     7→
     8→## Definition
     9→
    10→**Token efficiency** is the optimization of Large Language Model (LLM) token consumption to maximize functional output per token spent. In AI-assisted engineering, tokens are currency — every API call, agent task, and research query has a token cost that compounds across projects.
    11→
    12→## The Economics
    13→
    14→### Token as Currency
    15→
    16→Unlike traditional compute resources, LLM tokens have both **cost** and **context** implications:
    17→
    18→- **Cost**: API pricing is per-token (input + output)
    19→- **Context**: Each token consumes limited context window space
    20→- **Compound effect**: Poor efficiency scales linearly with project count
    21→
    22→### Baseline Metrics
    23→
    24→| Model | Cost per 1M tokens | Typical task | Token count | Task cost |
    25→|-------|-------------------|--------------|-------------|-----------|
    26→| **Claude Haiku** | $0.25 / $1.25 (in/out) | Web research | 15-20K | $0.025-0.035 |
    27→| **Claude Sonnet** | $3.00 / $15.00 (in/out) | Code implementation | 40-60K | $0.50-0.75 |
    28→| **Claude Opus** | $15.00 / $75.00 (in/out) | Complex reasoning | 80-120K | $2.50-4.00 |
    29→| **Local Ollama** | $0.00 | Embeddings, classification | Unlimited | $0.00* |
    30→
    31→*Hardware cost not included
    32→
    33→## Key Principles
    34→
    35→### 1. Validate Before Scaling
    36→
    37→**Pattern**: [[implementation-first-infrastructure-later]]
    38→
    39→Prove a concept works with minimal tokens before investing in infrastructure:
    40→- ✅ 8K tokens → Working feature → Scale if validated
    41→- ❌ 61K tokens → Full infrastructure → Discover feature doesn't work
    42→
    43→### 2. Use the Right Model for the Job
    44→
    45→**Haiku for research** (1/3 cost of Sonnet):
    46→- Web searches, API documentation lookups
    47→- JSON extraction, structured data processing
    48→- Quick validations, status checks
    49→
    50→**Sonnet for implementation** (balanced):
    51→- Code writing, architecture design
    52→- Complex debugging, refactoring
    53→- Production-quality output
    54→
    55→**Opus for reasoning** (5x Sonnet cost):
    56→- Multi-step planning, strategic decisions
    57→- Novel problem-solving, research synthesis
    58→- Only when Sonnet insufficient
    59→
    60→### 3. Template Reuse Over Reinvention
    61→
    62→Copying working templates costs ~500 tokens. Building from scratch costs 8,000-60,000 tokens:
    63→- **cloud-vault-mcp**: FastMCP server with 7 tools, working tests
    64→- **ollama-mcp**: Model management with context handling
    65→- **Haiku research agents**: Proven web research patterns
    66→
    67→### 4. Batch Operations
    68→
    69→Single operations compound linearly. Batch operations amortize overhead:
    70→- ❌ Update 100 rows sequentially: 100 API calls, ~5,000 tokens each = 500K tokens
    71→- ✅ Batch update 100 rows: 10 batches, ~8,000 tokens each = 80K tokens (84% savings)
    72→
    73→### 5. Local-First Processing
    74→
    75→When Ollama works (embeddings, classification, simple reasoning), use it:
    76→- **Cost**: $0 API tokens (electricity ~$0.01-0.05/hour)
    77→- **Privacy**: No data leaves local machine
    78→- **Speed**: No network latency for inference
    79→
    80→**Caveat**: Context management and prompt engineering still consume human time.
    81→
    82→## Anti-Patterns
    83→
    84→### Infrastructure-First Development
    85→
    86→Building scaffolding before implementation:
    87→- **Example**: 1,192-line API docs + 600 placeholder tests before writing code
    88→- **Cost**: 61,000 tokens, 0% functional output
    89→- **Remediation**: [[implementation-first-infrastructure-later]]
    90→
    91→### Model Mismatches
    92→
    93→Using expensive models for simple tasks:
    94→- ❌ Opus for JSON extraction: $4.00
    95→- ✅ Haiku for JSON extraction: $0.03 (133x cheaper)
    96→
    97→### Sequential Agent Work
    98→
    99→Spawning 20 agents sequentially (wait for each to finish):
   100→- **Time**: 20 × 3 minutes = 60 minutes
   101→- **Tokens**: 20 × 15K = 300K tokens
   102→- ✅ **Better**: Spawn 4 parallel batches of 5 agents = 15 minutes
   103→
   104→### Over-Research
   105→
   106→Researching every possible approach before picking one:
   107→- **Example**: 5 API endpoints documented, 1 actually used (80% waste)
   108→- **Fix**: Document-as-you-go (implement → document → repeat)
   109→
   110→## Case Studies
   111→
   112→### Success: Sheets Research Pipeline
   113→
   114→**Approach**: Haiku agents (4 parallel) with batch updates
   115→- **Cost**: $1.36 per 560 rows researched
   116→- **Time**: 42 minutes end-to-end
   117→- **Output**: 100% functional, vault notes + sheet updates
   118→
   119→**Why it worked**:
   120→- Right model (Haiku for web research)
   121→- Parallelization (4 agents at once)
   122→- Batch operations (SheetsBridge batch API)
   123→- Proven template (reused research agent pattern)
   124→
   125→### Failure: Kyutai MCP Server (Initial)
   126→
   127→**Approach**: Infrastructure-first with comprehensive research
   128→- **Cost**: 61,000 tokens
   129→- **Time**: 8+ hours
   130→- **Output**: 0% functional (1/22 tests passing)
   131→
   132→**What went wrong**:
   133→- Researched 5 APIs, documented all, used none
   134→- Wrote 600 placeholder tests before implementation
   135→- Installed 73MB dependencies before validating need
   136→- Ignored working template (cloud-vault-mcp)
   137→
   138→**Recovery**: Restarted with template, built ONE feature first (8K tokens)
   139→
   140→### Success: 12D Graph Phase 2
   141→
   142→**Approach**: Local Ollama for embeddings + Haiku for gap analysis
   143→- **Cost**: $0.00 API tokens
   144→- **Time**: 10 minutes
   145→- **Output**: 84 papers with embeddings, conceptual depth, research gaps
   146→
   147→**Why it worked**:
   148→- Local-first (Ollama embeddings = $0)
   149→- Right scope (semantic dimensions only, not full graph)
   150→- Incremental (Phase 1 → Phase 2 → Phase 3)
   151→
   152→## Metrics to Track
   153→
   154→### Per-Project Metrics
   155→
   156→- **Token spend**: Total input + output tokens
   157→- **Token efficiency**: Functional LOC per 1K tokens
   158→- **Model mix**: % Haiku / Sonnet / Opus / Local
   159→- **Rework rate**: Tokens spent on discarded work
   160→
   161→### Portfolio Metrics
   162→
   163→- **Average cost per feature**: Trend over time (should decrease)
   164→- **Template reuse rate**: % projects using templates vs from-scratch
   165→- **Agent utilization**: Sequential vs parallel work
   166→- **Batch operation adoption**: % operations batched vs sequential
   167→

   175→
   176→## Relationship to Compound Engineering
   177→
   178→Token efficiency amplifies [[compound-engineering]]'s compounding effect:
   179→
   180→- **Session 1**: Spend 60K tokens, learn nothing → Next session starts from zero
   181→- **Session 1 (efficient)**: Spend 8K tokens, document lessons → Next session reuses templates, spends 5K tokens
   182→
   183→Over 100 sessions:
   184→- **Inefficient path**: 100 × 60K = 6M tokens (~$1,500)
   185→- **Efficient path**: 8K + 99 × 5K = 503K tokens (~$75) — **12x ROI**

     9→# Universe Simulation
    10→
    11→The Cohezion universe simulation is an N-body gravitational simulation that serves dual purposes: as a physically interesting computation (modeling particle interactions under gravity) and as a high-throughput generator of agent trajectory data for compound learning experiments. Running overnight, the simulation produces millions of trajectory samples — 5.5M trajectories in one overnight run — that are then analyzed to extract patterns applicable to agent orchestration.
    12→
    13→Each simulated particle trajectory is treated as an analog for an agent execution path through the 12-dimensional compound engineering space. Positions represent agent state (coherence, token efficiency, task complexity, skill coverage); velocities represent rates of change; accelerations represent environmental pressures. This analogy yields concrete patterns: the predictive throttling pattern emerged from observing that trajectory velocity gradients reliably predict resource exhaustion before it occurs — a pattern that was validated on real agent sessions.
    14→
    15→The simulation is also a testbed for the three-tier data storage architecture. Generating 5.5M trajectories produces large artifacts (model checkpoints, trajectory files) that cannot be committed to git. The universe simulation was the motivating case for the pre-commit hook enforcement and JourneyTracker artifact registration system that prevents unconstrained data accumulation across sessions.

     8→
     9→# Concept Validation
    10→
    11→Concept validation is the process of verifying that a concept note accurately, completely, and usefully represents the underlying knowledge it describes. Where [[concept-testing]] checks structural properties (links work, schema is valid), concept validation verifies semantic accuracy: does the definition match what the primary sources actually say? Are the key properties correct? Would an expert in the domain recognize the description as accurate?
    12→
    13→Validation matters because the vault is not just a reference document — it is injected into agent contexts to ground execution decisions. An inaccurate concept note is worse than no note: it actively misleads agents, biasing their reasoning toward incorrect assumptions. Validation serves as the quality gate that keeps the [[knowledge-graph-systems]] trustworthy as it grows.
    14→
    15→The validation process in Cohezion mirrors the software TDD cycle: a concept is a "test" of the underlying knowledge, and validation is confirming the test is actually testing the right thing. Adversarial review (assume the definition is wrong, find counter-evidence) is the most effective validation technique for concepts with non-obvious definitions.

     8→
     9→# AI Alignment
    10→
    11→AI alignment is the research and engineering discipline focused on ensuring that AI systems reliably pursue goals that their designers and users intend, rather than instrumental goals that emerge from optimization pressure. The core difficulty is specification: humans rarely articulate their values precisely, and optimization pressure causes systems to find unexpected ways to satisfy literal objectives while violating the underlying intent (the “King Midas problem”).
    12→
    13→For agentic AI systems, alignment is especially critical because agents take real-world actions, make decisions autonomously, and can operate for extended periods without human oversight. A misaligned agent that executes thousands of tool calls can cause substantial harm before the misalignment is detected. This motivates the three-layer alignment strategy used in production systems: intent verification (does the agent understand the goal?), action auditing (does each action match the intent?), and outcome evaluation (did the result match what was intended?).
    14→
    15→In Cohezion, alignment is addressed through the RequestAlignmentAnalyzer (checking coherence between request and available skills before execution), the VaultExecutionLogger (creating an immutable audit trail of all agent decisions), and the adversarial review practice (explicitly stress-testing plans before committing to them). The CONSTITUTION.md file defines hard constraints that no agent may violate regardless of instruction.

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→Materials science is the interdisciplinary field studying the relationship between a material's atomic structure, its processing history, and its macroscopic properties (mechanical, electrical, optical, thermal). By understanding structure-property relationships, materials scientists design new materials with targeted characteristics — superconductors, semiconductors, structural alloys, biomaterials, and photovoltaics.
    10→
    11→AI is transforming materials discovery: machine learning potentials (trained on quantum chemistry calculations) enable molecular dynamics simulations at DFT accuracy but classical speed, accelerating the exploration of material space from years to days. Foundation models trained on materials databases can predict properties of hypothetical materials before synthesis. This accelerated discovery paradigm is the materials science analog of AlphaFold in structural biology.
    12→
    13→For Cohezion's knowledge graph, materials science connects papers on DNA origami nanofabrication, amorphous material structure determination (3D atomic reconstruction), semiconductor patterning, and photonic nanocavities — a diverse set of methodologies unified by the structure-property-processing triangle.

     9→# Cohezion
    10→
    11→Cohezion is a compound AI orchestration framework designed to make every agent session more effective than the last. Unlike stateless AI pipelines where each run starts from scratch, Cohezion maintains a persistent knowledge base (the Obsidian vault) and a structured feedback loop: agent sessions produce decisions, experiments, and patterns that are indexed, cross-linked, and re-injected into future sessions as context. The result is a system that compounds its own intelligence over time.
    12→
    13→The architecture is built around four interlocking layers: the [[compound-engineering]] methodology (the philosophy), the [[cloud-vault-mcp]] server (the memory infrastructure), the `cz` CLI (the workflow orchestrator), and [[surrealdb]] (the agent context graph). Together they implement a 12-dimensional agentic universe where every execution is tracked as a journey, every lesson is captured as a vault note, and every session benefits from all prior sessions.
    14→
    15→Cohezion is simultaneously a research project, a production tool, and a self-improving system. The FLUME VAE trains on real agent trajectory data, the RetrospectionEngine extracts patterns from session histories, and the SkillRefiner continuously updates PRIME skill definitions based on empirical performance. The target state is an autonomous compound engineering loop that improves without human intervention.
    16→
    17→## Components
    18→- **[[cloud-vault-mcp]]** — HTTP MCP server (port 8360) with 30+ tools for vault/graph/research operations
    19→- **cohezion-engine** (`cz`) — workflow CLI for session management, spec flows, and worktrees
    20→- **3d-graph-plugin** — Obsidian visualization of the knowledge graph
    21→- **[[surrealdb]]** — agent context graph storing sessions, tasks, and relationships
    22→- **Ollama** — local model inference (28+ models, zero API cost)
    23→- **FLUME VAE** — variational autoencoder trained on agent trajectory data

    13→# The Awareness of Nothing at All and Quadrature Physics
    14→
    15→## Overview
    16→
    17→This note explores two deeply interconnected ideas at the frontier of modern physics: the nature of "nothing" as understood through quantum mechanics and quantum field theory, and the physics of quadrature measurements that allow us to probe, quantify, and even manipulate the quantum vacuum. Together, these subjects reveal that emptiness is not empty, that silence has structure, and that our most sensitive instruments work by listening to the noise of nothing.
    18→
    19→---
    20→
    21→## Part I: The Physics of Nothing
    22→
    23→### The Quantum Vacuum Is Not Empty
    24→
    25→In classical physics, a vacuum is straightforward: remove all matter and radiation from a region of space, and you are left with nothing. As MIT theoretical physicist Daniel Harlow has put it, "Classically, the vacuum is boring. Nothing is happening."
    26→
    27→Quantum mechanics upends this entirely. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle forbids any quantum field from having exactly zero energy. Even in its lowest-energy configuration -- the ground state or "true vacuum" -- a quantum field undergoes ceaseless fluctuations. These **vacuum fluctuations** are not merely theoretical abstractions; they have measurable physical consequences.
    28→
    29→The universe, as understood through quantum field theory, is not a collection of isolated particles but a set of continuous, fluctuating fields: matter fields (whose quanta are fermions -- leptons and quarks) and force fields (whose quanta are bosons -- photons, gluons, and others). Every point in space, even in the most perfect vacuum, is alive with the irreducible jitter of these fields.
    30→
    31→### Zero-Point Energy
    32→
    33→**Zero-point energy** (ZPE) is the minimum energy possessed by a quantum mechanical system, even at absolute zero temperature. Max Planck introduced the concept in 1911, and Albert Einstein later championed it to explain why molecules continue vibrating even at near-zero temperatures and why liquid helium resists solidification.
    34→
    35→A landmark 2025 experiment at the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser (European XFEL) facility near Hamburg demonstrated zero-point effects directly: when an iodopyridine molecule consisting of just 11 atoms was cooled nearly to absolute zero, its atoms continued to display coordinated vibrations -- a direct signature of the zero-point energy that cannot be removed no matter how cold the system becomes.
    36→
    37→As physicist Peter Milonni has noted, "The interesting thing about the vacuum is every field, and therefore every particle, is somehow represented" -- meaning that emptiness contains the latent potential for all possible forms of matter.
    38→
    39→### The Casimir Effect: Forces from Nothing
    40→
    41→In 1948, Dutch physicist Hendrik Casimir predicted that two uncharged, parallel conducting plates placed in close proximity would experience an attractive force. This force arises because the plates restrict which vacuum fluctuations can exist between them, creating an energy imbalance between the interior and exterior regions. The experimental confirmation of this force in 1997 provided compelling evidence that vacuum fluctuations are physically real.
    42→
    43→Recent advances have moved beyond simply measuring the Casimir force:
    44→
    45→- **Magnetic control (2024):** Researchers in China demonstrated control of the Casimir force using magnetic fields, employing a golden bead and glass plate suspended in a ferrofluid. This represents a shift from passive measurement to active manipulation of vacuum forces.
    46→- **Dynamical Casimir effect (2024-2025):** Researchers have used superconducting quantum circuits to simulate the dynamical Casimir effect -- the production of real photons from vacuum fluctuations by rapidly moving mirrors or changing boundary conditions.
    47→- **DARPA investment:** The U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has launched a two-year, $10 million project encouraging scientists to find ways to manipulate the Casimir effect for breakthrough technologies.
    48→
    49→### The Cosmological Constant Problem
    50→
    51→The gravitational implications of vacuum energy remain one of the deepest unsolved problems in physics. As Wolfgang Pauli recognized early on, naive calculations of the total vacuum energy yield absurdly large (or infinite) values that should produce catastrophic gravitational effects -- curving spacetime so drastically that the universe as we know it could not exist. Yet the observed cosmological constant is roughly 120 orders of magnitude smaller than these predictions. This discrepancy, sometimes called "the worst prediction in physics," remains an active area of research.
    52→
    53→### False Vacuums and the Fate of the Universe
    54→
    55→Quantum field theory also raises the unsettling possibility that our current vacuum state is not the true ground state but a **false vacuum** -- a metastable configuration that could, in principle, decay. If the Higgs field occupies such a state, a bubble of true vacuum could nucleate and expand at nearly the speed of light, fundamentally rewriting the laws of physics within its domain. String theory compounds this picture by predicting an enormous "landscape" of possible vacuum states, each with different physical laws and constants.
    56→
    57→Physicist Edward Witten has even described a scenario in which certain vacuums could collapse into literal nothingness -- a "bubble of nothing" that destroys spacetime itself.
    58→
    59→### A Universe from Nothing? The Philosophical Debate
    60→
    61→Lawrence Krauss's 2012 book *A Universe from Nothing* brought the physics of the vacuum to broad public attention, arguing that quantum fluctuations could give rise to an entire universe without any external cause. However, the book sparked significant philosophical debate.
    62→
    63→The central critique, articulated forcefully by philosopher David Albert and others, is one of **equivocation**: Krauss's "nothing" is the quantum vacuum -- a state governed by the laws of quantum field theory, possessing structure, energy, and potentiality. This is not the "absolute nothing" (the complete absence of anything, including laws and fields) that philosophers have in mind when they ask, "Why is there something rather than nothing?"
    64→
    65→Physicist Sean Carroll has acknowledged this tension directly, stating that advances in physics do not, in themselves, resolve the deeper metaphysical question of why the universe (and its laws) exist at all.
    66→
    67→The scientific exploration of nothing has, however, blurred what once seemed like a sharp boundary: nothing and something may not be absolute opposites but points on a spectrum. In the words of a 2026 Quanta Magazine article, in quantum mechanics, "nothingness is the potential to be anything."
    68→
    69→---
    70→
    71→## Part II: Quadrature Physics
    72→
    73→### What Are Quadratures?
    74→
    75→In quantum optics, the electromagnetic field is described by **quadrature operators** -- Hermitian operators typically denoted X-hat and P-hat (or X-hat_1 and X-hat_2) that represent the amplitude and phase components of the quantized field. These are analogous to position and momentum in mechanical systems and obey the same canonical commutation relations, meaning they are subject to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle:
    76→
    77→> Delta(X) * Delta(P) >= 1/2
    78→
    79→The quadratures provide a complete description of the field's quantum state in phase space. A coherent state (the closest quantum analog of a classical light wave) has equal, minimum uncertainty in both quadratures -- this defines the **standard quantum limit** (SQL), also known as shot noise.
    80→
    81→### Squeezed States: Reshaping Uncertainty
    82→
    83→**Squeezed states** are quantum states of light in which the uncertainty in one quadrature has been reduced below the standard quantum limit, at the expense of increased uncertainty in the conjugate quadrature. The total uncertainty still satisfies the Heisenberg bound, but its distribution has been reshaped.
    84→
    85→Mathematically, a squeezed vacuum state is generated by applying the squeezing operator S(zeta) to the vacuum state |0>:
    86→
    87→> |zeta> = S(zeta)|0>
    88→
    89→where S(zeta) is defined in terms of creation and annihilation operators and the complex squeezing parameter zeta controls both the degree and angle of squeezing.
    90→
    91→The foundational formalism was laid out by Carlton Caves and Bonny Schumaker in their seminal 1985 paper in *Physical Review A*, which introduced the two-photon formalism for analyzing quadrature phases and squeezed states produced by parametric amplifiers and related devices.
    92→
    93→### Measuring Quadratures: Homodyne and Heterodyne Detection
    94→
    95→The primary experimental technique for measuring field quadratures is **balanced homodyne detection**. The signal field is mixed with a strong coherent reference beam (the local oscillator) on a 50/50 beamsplitter, and the difference in photocurrents from two photodetectors yields a measurement of the signal's quadrature. By sweeping the phase of the local oscillator, different quadratures can be selected and measured.
    96→
    97→**Heterodyne detection** simultaneously measures both quadratures, but at the cost of additional noise -- a direct consequence of the uncertainty principle, enforced by vacuum fluctuations entering through the unused beamsplitter port.
    98→
    99→Key points about homodyne detection and vacuum noise:
   100→
   101→- The shot noise observed in homodyne detection of a vacuum state is a direct measurement of **vacuum fluctuations** -- the irreducible quantum noise of the electromagnetic field.
   102→- Squeezing is identified by a reduction of the measured noise variance below this shot-noise level.
   103→- Conditional homodyne detection can distinguish between genuine quantum squeezing and classical noise reduction.
   104→
   105→### The Squeezed Vacuum: Less Noise Than Nothing
   106→
   107→This is where quadrature physics and the physics of nothing converge most directly. When we squeeze the vacuum state, we create a situation in which one quadrature of the electromagnetic field fluctuates **less than the vacuum itself** -- less than the irreducible noise floor of "nothing." In the conjugate quadrature, fluctuations increase correspondingly.
   108→
   109→This is not merely a theoretical curiosity. Squeezed vacuum states are now routinely produced in laboratories worldwide and have become essential tools in precision measurement and quantum information science.
   110→
   111→---
   112→
   113→## Part III: Where Nothing Meets Quadrature -- Applications and Frontiers
   114→
   115→### Gravitational Wave Detection: LIGO and Squeezed Light
   116→
   117→The most spectacular application of squeezed vacuum states is in **gravitational wave detection**. The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) uses squeezed light to push its sensitivity beyond the standard quantum limit.
   118→
   119→Key developments:
   120→
   121→- **Initial implementation:** LIGO first demonstrated enhanced sensitivity using squeezed states of light, as reported in *Nature Photonics* (2013).
   122→- **Frequency-dependent squeezing:** A major upgrade involves 300-meter optical filter cavities that rotate the squeezing quadrature as a function of frequency -- phase-squeezed at high frequencies (above ~50 Hz) to reduce shot noise, and amplitude-squeezed at low frequencies to mitigate radiation pressure noise. This is critical because different noise sources dominate at different frequencies.
   123→- **Dramatic results:** The introduction of advanced squeezing technology resulted in a doubling of the rate at which gravitational waves are detected -- a "stunning effect" reported in 2024.
   124→- **A+ upgrade and O5:** The upcoming A+ detector improvement includes balanced homodyne readout for better quadrature control. The fifth observing run (O5) is projected to begin in late 2025 or 2026, incorporating these advanced squeezing technologies at full capability.
   125→
   126→The LIGO achievement represents a case where understanding and manipulating the quantum noise of "nothing" has led to one of the most sensitive measurement instruments ever built.
   127→
   128→### Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing
   129→
   130→Squeezed states and quadrature measurements form the foundation of **continuous-variable (CV) quantum computing**, an alternative paradigm to the more commonly discussed qubit-based approach.
   131→
   132→- Lloyd and Braunstein proved in 1999 that universal quantum computation is achievable using continuous variables: linear optics (beamsplitters, phase shifters), squeezers, and at least one nonlinear element suffice.
   133→- In 2025, researchers demonstrated deterministic generation of eight-mode continuous-variable entanglement on an integrated photonic chip, using a quantum microcomb to produce multimode squeezed-vacuum optical frequency combs.
   134→- Integrated Si3N4 (silicon nitride) photonic chips now generate squeezing and probabilistic non-Gaussian states for Gaussian boson sampling.
   135→- New approaches to distributed quantum machine learning use continuous-variable cluster states as the primary quantum resource.
   136→
   137→CV quantum computing is attractive because it operates at room temperature, uses well-understood optical technology, and is naturally compatible with existing fiber-optic communication infrastructure.
   138→
   139→### Quantum Sensing Beyond the Standard Quantum Limit
   140→
   141→A 2025 review in *Applied Sciences* comprehensively surveyed quantum-enhanced sensing with squeezed light across multiple domains:
   142→
   143→- **Interferometry** -- precision phase measurements
   144→- **Magnetometry** -- detecting weak magnetic fields
   145→- **Force sensing** -- measuring tiny forces
   146→- **Biomedical sensing** -- potential applications in imaging and diagnostics
   147→- **Quantum radar** -- enhanced detection capabilities
   148→
   149→Notable 2025 breakthroughs include:
   150→
   151→- A **hybrid quantum network** combining entangled light with atomic spin ensembles (engineered as negative-mass oscillators) for frequency-dependent quantum noise reduction in the acoustic frequency range, developed at the Niels Bohr Institute (published in *Nature*).
   152→- A new **decoherence mitigation technique** from USC that enhances quantum sensing by counteracting environmental noise, surpassing conventional methods (published in *Nature Communications*).
   153→- NIST research on **quantum noise reduction strategies** -- "meeting noise halfway" -- for next-generation quantum sensors.
   154→
   155→### Quantum Communication
   156→
   157→Deterministic entanglement-assisted quantum communication over a 20 km fiber channel was demonstrated in 2025, leveraging squeezed states and continuous-variable entanglement -- a key step toward practical quantum networks.

   160→
   161→## Part IV: Open Questions and Frontiers
   162→
   163→Several deep questions remain at the intersection of vacuum physics and quadrature measurement:
   164→
   165→1. **The cosmological constant problem:** Why is the observed vacuum energy so astonishingly small compared to theoretical predictions? Can new measurement techniques or theoretical frameworks resolve this discrepancy?
   166→
   167→2. **Vacuum metastability:** Is our vacuum truly stable, or could it decay? What observational signatures might indicate proximity to a phase transition?
   168→
   169→3. **The nature of "true nothing":** Physics has progressively shown that every proposed version of "nothing" contains hidden structure. Is absolute nothingness even a coherent concept, or does the question "Why is there something rather than nothing?" rest on a false dichotomy?
   170→
   171→4. **Limits of squeezing:** Current experiments achieve roughly 10-15 dB of squeezing. What are the fundamental and practical limits? Can new materials, nonlinear processes, or error-correction techniques push further?
   172→
   173→5. **Dynamical Casimir physics:** Can the production of real photons from vacuum fluctuations (via the dynamical Casimir effect) be harnessed for any practical purpose? DARPA's recent investment suggests this question is being taken seriously.
   174→
   175→6. **Quantum gravity and the vacuum:** How does the quantum vacuum behave in the presence of strong gravitational fields? Can squeezed-state techniques be adapted to probe quantum gravitational effects?
   176→

   178→
   179→## Part V: Opportunities for Enhancing Our Platform
   180→
   181→Interpreting "platform" broadly -- as a research platform, knowledge management system, software infrastructure, or collaborative workspace -- the following opportunities emerge from this research:
   182→
   183→### Knowledge Organization and Research Integration
   184→
   185→- **Structured knowledge graphs:** The relationship between vacuum physics, quadrature measurement, and applications (LIGO, quantum computing, quantum sensing) forms a rich, interconnected network of concepts. A platform that represents these connections explicitly -- rather than as isolated notes -- would accelerate understanding and discovery.
   186→- **Living literature reviews:** The field is moving rapidly (2024-2025 saw major advances in LIGO squeezing, CV quantum computing on-chip, and Casimir force manipulation). A platform that tracks and integrates new publications automatically would provide significant value.
   187→
   188→### Simulation and Computation
   189→
   190→- **Quadrature visualization tools:** Interactive tools for visualizing Wigner functions, phase-space distributions, and the effects of squeezing on vacuum states would make these concepts accessible to a broader audience and aid in experimental design.
   191→- **Noise modeling:** Platforms that simulate quantum noise in interferometric and sensing configurations, incorporating realistic squeezing levels and loss models, would be valuable for experimental groups.
   192→
   193→### Quantum Technology Development
   194→
   195→- **Continuous-variable quantum computing frameworks:** Software platforms supporting CV quantum computing (simulation, circuit design, error analysis) are less mature than their qubit-based counterparts. There is an opportunity to build or contribute to open-source tooling in this space.
   196→- **Sensor design optimization:** Platforms that integrate quantum noise theory with engineering constraints (optical loss, detector efficiency, thermal effects) could accelerate the development of quantum-enhanced sensors.
   197→
   198→### Education and Communication
   199→
   200→- **Bridging physics and philosophy:** The topic of "nothing" sits at a rare intersection of cutting-edge physics and perennial philosophical questions. A platform that presents both the scientific content and the philosophical context -- without conflating them -- would serve a broad audience.
   201→- **From foundational to applied:** The path from vacuum fluctuations to gravitational wave detection is a compelling narrative of how fundamental physics generates transformative technology. Curating this narrative could enhance engagement with both technical and non-technical audiences.
   202→
   203→### Collaborative Research Infrastructure
   204→
   205→- **Cross-disciplinary connection:** Vacuum physics, quantum optics, quantum information, cosmology, and philosophy of physics all converge here. A platform that facilitates cross-disciplinary collaboration -- connecting, for example, experimentalists measuring squeezing with theorists studying vacuum decay -- could catalyze new research directions.
   206→- **Open data and reproducibility:** As squeezed-light experiments become more standardized, platforms supporting open data sharing and reproducible analysis pipelines would benefit the community.

   209→
   210→## Summary
   211→
   212→The "awareness of nothing" is not a mystical concept but a precise physical program: to understand, measure, and manipulate the quantum vacuum -- the irreducible substrate of reality. Quadrature physics provides the theoretical language and experimental toolkit for this program. Together, they have already produced transformative technologies (LIGO's squeezed-light detection, continuous-variable quantum computing) and continue to press against some of the deepest questions in physics (the cosmological constant problem, the nature of true nothingness, the stability of the vacuum).
   213→
   214→The field is advancing rapidly, with major milestones achieved in 2024-2025 and more expected as LIGO's O5 run begins and integrated photonic quantum devices mature. The opportunities for platform development -- whether in knowledge management, simulation, education, or collaborative research infrastructure -- are substantial.

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→Agent architecture defines the structural design of an autonomous AI agent — how it perceives inputs, maintains state, reasons about actions, and executes against external systems. The canonical pattern is the observe-reason-act loop (see [[agent-loop-architecture]]), but production architectures extend this with memory hierarchies, tool registries, role specialization, and inter-agent communication protocols.
    10→
    11→Architectures span a spectrum: single-agent systems where one LLM completes an entire workflow, to multi-agent systems where specialized sub-agents handle distinct domains (researcher, planner, executor, reviewer). The key design decisions are role boundaries, shared context strategy, and failure isolation — poorly designed agents amplify errors rather than containing them.
    12→
    13→In Cohezion, the agent architecture centers on the CompoundExecutor, which orchestrates an 11-step pipeline. Specialized agents (domain experts, skill refiners, retrospection engines) communicate through a shared [[mcp-model-context-protocol]] interface rather than direct coupling, enabling hot-swappable components and independent scaling.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Role specialization**: Each agent is optimized for a narrow task type (research, code, review)
    18→- **Memory hierarchy**: Short-term (context window), mid-term (session cache), long-term (vault)
    19→- **Tool registry**: Agents access external systems through a standardized [[tool-use]] interface
    20→- **Failure isolation**: Sub-agent failures should not cascade; circuit breakers and fallbacks are essential
    21→- **Communication protocol**: Agents exchange structured messages, not raw text

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→Concept testing in Cohezion refers to the practice of validating that a knowledge concept is correctly captured, accurately described, and genuinely useful before it becomes a permanent node in the knowledge graph. A concept note that contains incorrect information or misleading descriptions compounds negatively — it gets injected into agent contexts, biases decisions, and generates downstream errors that are hard to trace back to the faulty source.
    10→
    11→The key testing practices are: checking the concept definition against primary sources (does it accurately represent the paper or pattern it describes?), verifying wiki-links point to existing notes (no broken links), confirming the `related_concepts` frontmatter matches actual relationships, and validating that the concept is self-contained enough to be useful when retrieved without the full graph. The [[adversarial-review]] pattern applies here — assume the concept note is wrong and verify it.
    12→
    13→In Cohezion's compound engineering workflow, concepts are tested as part of the vault enrichment process. Newly created or auto-generated stub notes are reviewed for accuracy, expanded with verified content, and cross-linked to related notes. The SurrealDB import pipeline validates concept metadata against schema before ingestion, acting as a programmatic concept test.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Accuracy verification**: Concept definitions checked against primary sources
    18→- **Link validation**: Wiki-links verified to point to existing, correctly named notes
    19→- **Self-containment check**: Concept useful in isolation without requiring linked notes
    20→- **Schema validation**: Frontmatter fields (tags, related_concepts, date) match expected types
    21→- **Cross-link consistency**: If A links to B, B should know about A (bidirectional awareness)

     9→# Non-Blocking Observability
    10→
    11→Non-blocking observability is the pattern of collecting telemetry, metrics, and execution traces without allowing instrumentation code to block, slow, or crash the primary execution path. It is the discipline of "observe without interfering" — the observer effect problem in distributed systems, solved by wrapping all tracking calls in try/except handlers and offloading I/O to background tasks.
    12→
    13→In agentic AI systems, observability is especially critical because agent behavior is complex, emergent, and hard to reproduce. Without traces, debugging a 20-step agent workflow becomes guesswork. But naive observability — synchronous writes to external systems, blocking metric uploads, exception propagation from tracking code — can introduce latency and failure modes that alter the very behavior being observed. Non-blocking observability resolves this by treating tracking as best-effort: valuable when available, never at the cost of correctness.
    14→
    15→In Cohezion, the `JourneyTracker` implements this pattern with explicit try/except wrappers around all state transition recordings. If SurrealDB is unavailable, the agent continues executing and logs fall back to JSONL format. Metrics are batched and flushed asynchronously. The `GlobalMetricsAggregator` uses in-memory accumulation with periodic background flushes, ensuring agent loop throughput is never gated on metrics I/O.
    16→
    17→## Key Properties
    18→
    19→- **Best-effort**: Tracking failures are logged as warnings, never raised as errors
    20→- **Try/except wrapping**: All instrumentation code is wrapped to prevent propagation
    21→- **Async/background flush**: Metrics accumulate in-memory and flush on a timer or at session end
    22→- **Graceful degradation**: If the observability backend is unavailable, execution continues normally
    23→- **Fallback persistence**: In-memory → JSONL → SurrealDB as availability allows

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→SurrealDB is a multi-model database that combines graph database capabilities, document storage, relational queries, and vector fields in a single system accessed through SurrealQL — a SQL-inspired query language with graph-native extensions. Unlike traditional databases that force a choice between document, relational, or graph models, SurrealDB handles all three simultaneously, making it well-suited for agent context graphs that need structured schema, relationship traversal, and vector similarity search.
    10→
    11→SurrealDB's key differentiator for agent systems is its RELATE syntax for typed edges. Rather than encoding relationships as foreign keys in relational tables (which loses semantic meaning) or as adjacency lists in document fields (which makes traversal expensive), RELATE creates first-class edge records: `RELATE paper_a->cites->paper_b SET strength = 0.9`. These edges are queryable, typed, and traversable with graph path syntax. Combined with native vector field support for embedding storage, SurrealDB handles both the graph and vector layers of Cohezion's [[graphrag-knowledge-graph-with-surrealdb]] implementation.
    12→
    13→The SurrealDB agent context schema stores agent sessions, tasks, decisions, and artifacts as interconnected records. Session nodes link to task nodes link to artifact nodes, enabling queries like "find all decisions made during sessions that produced high-coherence artifacts" — retrospective analytics that feed the [[experience-feedback-loop]]. The record-centric schema (as captured in [[lesson-surrealdb-schema-design]]) outperforms table-centric approaches by 60-70% in query complexity.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Multi-model**: Document, relational, graph, and vector operations in one system
    18→- **RELATE syntax**: First-class typed edge records with queryable metadata
    19→- **SurrealQL**: SQL-familiar with graph path traversal and CONTAINS/SELECT FETCH extensions
    20→- **Record IDs are typed**: IDs must match declared type at query time — a common source of bugs
    21→- **Runs locally**: `ws://localhost:8000` with no cloud dependency; zero operational cost

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→A session retrospective is a structured reflection performed at the end of an agent session to extract reusable knowledge before context is lost. It is the primary mechanism by which raw session experience becomes durable vault knowledge — transforming the ephemeral (what happened in this session) into the permanent (lessons and patterns that inform future sessions).
    10→
    11→The validated retrospective structure (from [[lesson-effective-retrospectives]]) captures four categories: What Worked (successful approaches to replicate), What Failed (mistakes to avoid), What Was Surprising (unexpected discoveries), and Reusable Patterns Extracted (generalizable solutions). This structure ensures comprehensive extraction — capturing failures is as important as capturing successes, since avoiding repeated mistakes compounds as much as applying proven patterns.
    12→
    13→In Cohezion, retrospectives feed directly into the [[experience-feedback-loop]]: after a session, the agent runs `vault_log_decision` for architectural choices, `vault_log_experiment` for hypothesis-result pairs, and `vault_extract_pattern` for reusable solutions. These structured vault entries become searchable context for future sessions via `vault_find_relevant_context`.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Session-end discipline**: Performed before context is cleared; retrospective quality degrades with delay
    18→- **Four-category structure**: What Worked / What Failed / What Was Surprising / Patterns Extracted
    19→- **Vault-first**: Outputs go to vault via CompoundOps, not just conversation memory
    20→- **Failure-positive**: Failed experiments are as valuable as successes; document them explicitly
    21→- **Pattern generalization**: Specific session solutions are generalized into reusable patterns

     9→# AI Safety
    10→
    11→AI safety is the research and engineering field dedicated to ensuring that AI systems behave safely and beneficially, especially as they become more capable and autonomous. It encompasses four major subfields: alignment (systems pursue intended goals), interpretability (humans can understand system reasoning), robustness (systems fail gracefully under distributional shift), and governance (institutional structures for responsible deployment).
    12→
    13→For agentic AI systems, safety concerns are especially acute because agents act in the world rather than merely generating text. An agent with access to file systems, APIs, and external services can cause irreversible harm if misaligned. The primary safety mechanisms are: constrained tool permissions (agents can only access what they need), action auditing (every tool call is logged), reversibility preference (prefer reversible actions over irreversible ones), and human oversight checkpoints (mandatory approval before irreversible actions).
    14→
    15→Cohezion addresses AI safety through its CONSTITUTION.md (hard constraints no agent may violate), the VaultExecutionLogger (immutable audit trail), and the practice of [[adversarial-review]] before execution. The GuardrailPipeline performs input/output safety checks on agent decisions. The [[lesson-26-never-print-credentials]] lesson captures the most critical operational safety rule: secrets must never appear in logs.

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→API design is the discipline of defining the interfaces through which systems communicate — choosing endpoints, data schemas, error contracts, versioning strategies, and authentication patterns. Good API design is the difference between components that compose cleanly and systems where every integration requires custom glue code. The MCP protocol is itself an API design: it defines how AI agents discover and call tools across vendor boundaries.
    10→
    11→For AI agent systems, API design decisions have compounding effects: an awkward API signature that requires three round-trips where one would suffice multiplies its overhead across thousands of agent invocations. The key principles are minimal surface area (fewest endpoints that cover the use cases), consistent error formats (agents can handle errors programmatically), and schema-driven interfaces (OpenAPI or JSON Schema declarations that agents can use without documentation).
    12→
    13→In Cohezion, the [[cloud-vault-mcp]] server is the primary designed API surface. Its 30+ tools follow consistent naming conventions (`vault_*`, `compound_*`, `surrealdb_*`) with JSON Schema inputs and structured outputs. The FastAPI backend (`cohezion.api:app`, 72 endpoints) follows layered validation patterns — validating at each boundary: request → service → database — rather than only at the entry point.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Minimal surface**: Fewest endpoints/tools that cover actual use cases; resist adding speculative endpoints
    18→- **Consistent contracts**: Uniform error formats and response structures enable programmatic handling
    19→- **Schema-driven**: Declare input/output schemas so consumers don't need documentation
    20→- **Layered validation**: Validate at each boundary, not just the entry point
    21→- **Versioning discipline**: Breaking changes require version bumps; never silently change behavior

     8→## Definition
     9→
    10→AI systems that operate autonomously across extended workflows, integrating multiple specialized agents with dynamic task decomposition, persistent memory, and orchestrated autonomy. Coined in the agentic AI era (2022-present), these systems represent a paradigm shift from narrow task-specific automation toward multi-agent collaboration, as exemplified by systems like Coscientist and ChemCrow that autonomously design and execute complex experiments.
    11→
    12→## Key Properties
    13→
    14→- Operates through observe-reason-act cycles enabling autonomous decision-making
    15→- Integrates multiple specialized agents with different LLMs and tool-augmented capabilities
    16→- Maintains persistent memory and dynamic task decomposition
    17→- Orchestrates complex workflows without human intervention
    18→- Demonstrates emergent capabilities beyond component systems through multi-agent collaboration
    19→
    20→## Examples
    21→
    22→- Coscientist: GPT-4 powered system that autonomously designs and executes complex chemical experiments including palladium-catalysed cross-couplings
    23→- ChemCrow: LLM chemistry agent with 18 expert-designed tools that autonomously planned and executed syntheses of insect repellents and organocatalysts

     2→
     3→## DOMAIN EXPERTISE
     4→You are a repository health engineer specializing in preventing and detecting repository bloat. You implement the **3-Layer Governance** pattern: Prevention (pre-commit hooks), Detection (automated monitoring), and Remediation (cleanup procedures). You ensure repositories stay lean (<6GB), maintainable, and fast.
     5→
     6→## KEY TEXTS & CONCEPTS
     7→- **Repository Bloat**: Accumulation of unnecessary data in .git directory causing slow operations and excessive disk usage.
     8→- **3-Layer Governance**:
     9→  1. Prevention: Pre-commit hooks block files >1MB before they enter history
    10→  2. Detection: CI/CD monitors repository size, large files, pack efficiency
    11→  3. Remediation: Documented procedures for cleanup (git gc, filter-repo, lfs migration)
    12→- **Pack Efficiency**: Git's internal compression ratio. Low efficiency (many loose objects) indicates need for `git gc`.
    13→- **Size Thresholds**:
    14→  - **Target**: <6GB for optimal performance
    15→  - **Warning**: 6-10GB approaching limit, consider cleanup
    16→  - **Critical**: >10GB requires immediate remediation
    17→- **Large File Patterns**: Binary files (*.pt, *.pth, *.ckpt), logs, checkpoints that should use git-lfs or .gitignore
    18→
    19→## INSTRUCTION
    20→
    21→### 1. Assessment Phase
    22→Run comprehensive repository health scan:
    23→
    24→```bash
    25→# Check repository size
    26→du -sh .git
    27→SIZE_BYTES=$(du -sb .git | cut -f1)
    28→SIZE_GB=$((SIZE_BYTES / 1024 / 1024 / 1024))
    29→
    30→# Find large files in history (>1MB)
    31→git rev-list --objects --all | \
    32→git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' | \
    33→awk '$1 == "blob" && $3 > 1048576 {printf "%.2f MB: %s\n", $3/1048576, $4}' | \
    34→sort -rn | head -20
    35→
    36→# Check pack efficiency
    37→git count-objects -vH
    38→
    39→# Validate .gitignore coverage
    40→grep -E '^\*\.(pt|pth|ckpt|bin|log)$|^(logs|checkpoints|tmp|\.cache)/' .gitignore
    41→```
    42→
    43→**Health Criteria**:
    44→- ✅ HEALTHY: <6GB, <20 large files, good pack efficiency
    45→- ⚠️  WARNING: 6-10GB, 20-50 large files, moderate pack issues
    46→- ❌ CRITICAL: >10GB, >50 large files, poor pack efficiency
    47→
    48→### 2. Prevention Layer (Pre-Commit Hooks)
    49→Ensure `.pre-commit-config.yaml` includes:
    50→
    51→```yaml
    52→- repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    53→  rev: v5.0.0
    54→  hooks:
    55→    - id: check-added-large-files
    56→      args: [--maxkb=1000]  # Block files >1MB
    57→      stages: [pre-commit]
    58→    - id: detect-private-key
    59→      stages: [pre-commit]
    60→```
    61→
    62→**Verification**:
    63→```bash
    64→# Install hooks
    65→pre-commit install
    66→
    67→# Test blocking (should fail)
    68→dd if=/dev/zero of=test-large-file.bin bs=1M count=2
    69→git add test-large-file.bin
    70→git commit -m "test"  # Should be blocked
    71→rm test-large-file.bin
    72→```
    73→
    74→### 3. Detection Layer (CI/CD Monitoring)
    75→Deploy `.github/workflows/repo-health.yml`:
    76→
    77→**Triggers**:
    78→- On push to main/develop
    79→- On pull request to main
    80→- Weekly schedule (Sunday 2am UTC)
    81→- Manual dispatch
    82→
    83→**Checks**:
    84→1. Repository size (fail if >10GB, warn if >6GB)
    85→2. Large files scan (warn if >50 files >1MB)
    86→3. Pack efficiency measurement
    87→4. .gitignore coverage validation
    88→
    89→**Alerts**:
    90→- GitHub Actions errors/warnings
    91→- Artifacts uploaded with large file list
    92→- Health summary in workflow logs
    93→
    94→### 4. Remediation Procedures
    95→
    96→#### Quick Cleanup (<5 min)
    97→For repositories 6-10GB with good pack efficiency:
    98→
    99→```bash
   100→# Aggressive garbage collection
   101→git gc --aggressive --prune=now
   102→
   103→# Repack objects
   104→git repack -Ad
   105→
   106→# Verify reduction
   107→du -sh .git
   108→```
   109→
   110→**Expected**: 20-50% size reduction
   111→
   112→#### Medium Cleanup (30-60 min)
   113→For repositories >10GB or >50 large files:
   114→
   115→```bash
   116→# Identify largest files
   117→git rev-list --objects --all | \
   118→git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' | \
   119→awk '$1 == "blob"' | sort -k3 -rn | head -20 > large_files.txt
   120→
   121→# Option A: Migrate to git-lfs
   122→git lfs install
   123→git lfs track "*.pt" "*.pth" "*.ckpt"
   124→git add .gitattributes
   125→git commit -m "chore: Configure git-lfs for large model files"
   126→
   127→# Option B: Remove from history (DESTRUCTIVE)
   128→# Create backup first!
   129→git tag backup-pre-cleanup
   130→git filter-repo --path-glob '*.pt' --invert-paths --force
   131→```
   132→
   133→**Warning**: History rewriting requires force-push and team coordination.

   135→#### Deep Cleanup (2-4 hours)

   152→# 4. Aggressive cleanup

   156→# 5. Verify and sync

   165→### 5. Governance Maintenance

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→Workflow orchestration is the coordination of multi-step agent processes — sequencing tasks, managing dependencies, routing subtasks to appropriate agents, handling failures, and assembling results into coherent outputs. In agentic AI systems, orchestration is the difference between a single-turn chatbot and a persistent autonomous system that can execute complex, long-horizon goals.
    10→
    11→Effective orchestration requires resolving three tensions: parallelism vs. coordination overhead (running too many agents in parallel introduces synchronization costs), flexibility vs. reliability (dynamic routing is powerful but harder to debug), and autonomy vs. oversight (fully autonomous orchestration risks runaway execution without human checkpoints). The right balance depends on task complexity — for tasks under ~2 hours of work, single-agent approaches are often more token-efficient than full orchestration (see [[lesson-11-team-agent-efficiency]]).
    12→
    13→In Cohezion, workflow orchestration is implemented through the `cz` CLI and the CompoundExecutor's 11-step pipeline. The `spec` workflow (plan → implement → verify) is a concrete orchestration pattern that sequences phases, enforces quality gates, and manages worktree isolation. The [[mcp-model-context-protocol]] serves as the orchestration bus — agents call tools through a unified interface rather than coupling directly to each other.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Task decomposition**: Breaking complex goals into atomic, assignable subtasks
    18→- **Dependency management**: Ensuring tasks execute in correct order with proper inputs
    19→- **Failure isolation**: Containing sub-task failures without cascading to the entire workflow
    20→- **Dynamic routing**: Selecting the appropriate agent or model based on task characteristics
    21→- **State persistence**: Maintaining workflow state across session boundaries via vault

     9→# Cloud Vault MCP
    10→
    11→The Cloud Vault MCP server is Cohezion's primary knowledge management and agent infrastructure interface, implemented as an HTTP [[mcp-model-context-protocol]] server running on port 8360. It exposes 30+ tools across six categories, providing AI agents with programmatic access to the Obsidian vault, SurrealDB graph database, Google Sheets, Ollama inference, and Teleport task management — all through a single standardized protocol.
    12→
    13→The server implements three logical operation layers. **VaultOps** handles file-level vault operations: reading, writing, searching, and cross-linking notes. **CompoundOps** implements the compound engineering primitives: `vault_log_decision`, `vault_log_experiment`, `vault_extract_pattern`, and `vault_find_relevant_context` — the tools that make the [[experience-feedback-loop]] concrete. **ObsidianOps** manages the graph layer: backlinks, forward links, tags, and wiki-link validation. Together these layers turn the Obsidian vault from a passive note store into an active, queryable knowledge graph that agents can read from and write to during execution.
    14→
    15→The server was built using FastMCP (Python) and serves as the reference template for additional MCP servers in the Cohezion ecosystem. The `cloud-vault-mcp/` directory is explicitly documented as the template to copy when building new MCP servers, carrying 87% token savings versus building from scratch. It runs alongside the Ollama MCP server (stdio, no port) and exposes a `/health` endpoint that monitors all five infrastructure dependencies.
    16→

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→Quantum mechanics is the fundamental physical theory describing the behavior of matter and energy at atomic and subatomic scales. It replaces classical Newtonian mechanics at these scales, introducing wave-particle duality (particles exhibit wave behavior), the uncertainty principle (conjugate variables like position and momentum cannot both be precisely known simultaneously), quantization (energy states are discrete, not continuous), and the superposition principle (quantum systems exist in linear combinations of states until measured).
    10→
    11→The theory's probabilistic nature (measurement outcomes follow probability amplitudes given by the wavefunction) was philosophically contentious — Einstein's objection led to the EPR paradox, which Bell later resolved experimentally in favor of quantum mechanics over local hidden variables. Modern applications include quantum computing ([[quantum-entanglement]] enabling entangled qubits), quantum sensing ([[dark-matter-detection]] using quantum-limited amplifiers), and quantum communication (quantum key distribution).
    12→
    13→For Cohezion's knowledge graph, quantum mechanics is the foundational physics domain connecting papers on quantum computing, quantum sensors, and quantum information. Cross-domain synthesis — e.g., how quantum sensor precision limits inform dark matter detection sensitivity — is the primary use case.
    14→
    15→## Key Properties
    16→
    17→- **Wave-particle duality**: Quantum objects exhibit both wave and particle properties depending on measurement
    18→- **Uncertainty principle**: ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2; precision in position limits precision in momentum
    19→- **Quantization**: Energy levels, spin, and other quantities take discrete values
    20→- **Superposition**: States are linear combinations; collapse occurs on measurement
    21→- **Non-locality**: Entangled particles exhibit correlated measurements regardless of separation

     9→# Adversarial Review
    10→
    11→Adversarial review is the structured practice of critiquing a plan or design by assuming the proposer is wrong and generating falsifiable counter-hypotheses. Unlike standard review (which looks for obvious errors), adversarial review actively tries to invalidate the proposal — finding hidden assumptions, edge cases, and alternative explanations that the proposer's perspective is blind to.
    12→
    13→The economic case for adversarial review is compelling: a 10-minute review investment (5K tokens) can prevent 8+ hours of wasted execution (225K+ tokens) when it catches a fundamental flaw before work begins. The ROI is 45x on a single catch. The [[lesson-adversarial-review-before-execution]] lesson, validated across multiple Cohezion sessions, established adversarial review as a mandatory gate before any significant implementation begins.
    14→
    15→In Cohezion's spec workflow, adversarial review is institutionalized through the `plan-challenger` agent: a sub-agent that receives the completed plan and is explicitly instructed to challenge its assumptions, identify risks, and require evidence for key claims. This is the final quality gate before plan approval — the plan-challenger runs in parallel with the plan-verifier, and both must clear before implementation begins.
    16→
    17→## Key Properties
    18→- **Assumption inversion**: Assumes the proposer is wrong; requires positive evidence, not absence of objections
    19→- **Counter-hypothesis generation**: Produces specific falsifiable alternative explanations
    20→- **Evidence requirement**: Intuition alone is insufficient; claims must be backed by observable evidence
    21→- **Mandatory gating**: Adversarial review is a blocking gate, not advisory feedback
    22→- **Asymmetric value**: High catch rate on low-probability catastrophic failures justifies fixed review overhead

     7→
     8→## Definition
     9→
    10→**Token efficiency** is the optimization of Large Language Model (LLM) token consumption to maximize functional output per token spent. In AI-assisted engineering, tokens are currency — every API call, agent task, and research query has a token cost that compounds across projects.
    11→
    12→## The Economics
    13→
    14→### Token as Currency
    15→
    16→Unlike traditional compute resources, LLM tokens have both **cost** and **context** implications:
    17→
    18→- **Cost**: API pricing is per-token (input + output)
    19→- **Context**: Each token consumes limited context window space
    20→- **Compound effect**: Poor efficiency scales linearly with project count
    21→
    22→### Baseline Metrics
    23→
    24→| Model | Cost per 1M tokens | Typical task | Token count | Task cost |
    25→|-------|-------------------|--------------|-------------|-----------|
    26→| **Claude Haiku** | $0.25 / $1.25 (in/out) | Web research | 15-20K | $0.025-0.035 |
    27→| **Claude Sonnet** | $3.00 / $15.00 (in/out) | Code implementation | 40-60K | $0.50-0.75 |
    28→| **Claude Opus** | $15.00 / $75.00 (in/out) | Complex reasoning | 80-120K | $2.50-4.00 |
    29→| **Local Ollama** | $0.00 | Embeddings, classification | Unlimited | $0.00* |
    30→
    31→*Hardware cost not included
    32→
    33→## Key Principles
    34→
    35→### 1. Validate Before Scaling
    36→
    37→**Pattern**: [[implementation-first-infrastructure-later]]
    38→
    39→Prove a concept works with minimal tokens before investing in infrastructure:
    40→- ✅ 8K tokens → Working feature → Scale if validated
    41→- ❌ 61K tokens → Full infrastructure → Discover feature doesn't work
    42→
    43→### 2. Use the Right Model for the Job
    44→
    45→**Haiku for research** (1/3 cost of Sonnet):
    46→- Web searches, API documentation lookups
    47→- JSON extraction, structured data processing
    48→- Quick validations, status checks
    49→
    50→**Sonnet for implementation** (balanced):
    51→- Code writing, architecture design
    52→- Complex debugging, refactoring
    53→- Production-quality output
    54→
    55→**Opus for reasoning** (5x Sonnet cost):
    56→- Multi-step planning, strategic decisions
    57→- Novel problem-solving, research synthesis
    58→- Only when Sonnet insufficient
    59→
    60→### 3. Template Reuse Over Reinvention
    61→
    62→Copying working templates costs ~500 tokens. Building from scratch costs 8,000-60,000 tokens:
    63→- **cloud-vault-mcp**: FastMCP server with 7 tools, working tests
    64→- **ollama-mcp**: Model management with context handling
    65→- **Haiku research agents**: Proven web research patterns
    66→
    67→### 4. Batch Operations
    68→
    69→Single operations compound linearly. Batch operations amortize overhead:
    70→- ❌ Update 100 rows sequentially: 100 API calls, ~5,000 tokens each = 500K tokens
    71→- ✅ Batch update 100 rows: 10 batches, ~8,000 tokens each = 80K tokens (84% savings)
    72→
    73→### 5. Local-First Processing
    74→
    75→When Ollama works (embeddings, classification, simple reasoning), use it:
    76→- **Cost**: $0 API tokens (electricity ~$0.01-0.05/hour)
    77→- **Privacy**: No data leaves local machine
    78→- **Speed**: No network latency for inference
    79→
    80→**Caveat**: Context management and prompt engineering still consume human time.
    81→
    82→## Anti-Patterns
    83→
    84→### Infrastructure-First Development
    85→
    86→Building scaffolding before implementation:
    87→- **Example**: 1,192-line API docs + 600 placeholder tests before writing code
    88→- **Cost**: 61,000 tokens, 0% functional output
    89→- **Remediation**: [[implementation-first-infrastructure-later]]
    90→
    91→### Model Mismatches
    92→
    93→Using expensive models for simple tasks:
    94→- ❌ Opus for JSON extraction: $4.00
    95→- ✅ Haiku for JSON extraction: $0.03 (133x cheaper)
    96→
    97→### Sequential Agent Work
    98→
    99→Spawning 20 agents sequentially (wait for each to finish):
   100→- **Time**: 20 × 3 minutes = 60 minutes
   101→- **Tokens**: 20 × 15K = 300K tokens
   102→- ✅ **Better**: Spawn 4 parallel batches of 5 agents = 15 minutes
   103→
   104→### Over-Research
   105→
   106→Researching every possible approach before picking one:
   107→- **Example**: 5 API endpoints documented, 1 actually used (80% waste)
   108→- **Fix**: Document-as-you-go (implement → document → repeat)
   109→
   110→## Case Studies
   111→
   112→### Success: Sheets Research Pipeline
   113→
   114→**Approach**: Haiku agents (4 parallel) with batch updates
   115→- **Cost**: $1.36 per 560 rows researched
   116→- **Time**: 42 minutes end-to-end
   117→- **Output**: 100% functional, vault notes + sheet updates
   118→
   119→**Why it worked**:
   120→- Right model (Haiku for web research)
   121→- Parallelization (4 agents at once)
   122→- Batch operations (SheetsBridge batch API)
   123→- Proven template (reused research agent pattern)
   124→
   125→### Failure: Kyutai MCP Server (Initial)
   126→
   127→**Approach**: Infrastructure-first with comprehensive research
   128→- **Cost**: 61,000 tokens
   129→- **Time**: 8+ hours
   130→- **Output**: 0% functional (1/22 tests passing)
   131→
   132→**What went wrong**:
   133→- Researched 5 APIs, documented all, used none
   134→- Wrote 600 placeholder tests before implementation
   135→- Installed 73MB dependencies before validating need
   136→- Ignored working template (cloud-vault-mcp)
   137→
   138→**Recovery**: Restarted with template, built ONE feature first (8K tokens)
   139→
   140→### Success: 12D Graph Phase 2
   141→
   142→**Approach**: Local Ollama for embeddings + Haiku for gap analysis
   143→- **Cost**: $0.00 API tokens
   144→- **Time**: 10 minutes
   145→- **Output**: 84 papers with embeddings, conceptual depth, research gaps
   146→
   147→**Why it worked**:
   148→- Local-first (Ollama embeddings = $0)
   149→- Right scope (semantic dimensions only, not full graph)
   150→- Incremental (Phase 1 → Phase 2 → Phase 3)
   151→
   152→## Metrics to Track
   153→
   154→### Per-Project Metrics
   155→
   156→- **Token spend**: Total input + output tokens
   157→- **Token efficiency**: Functional LOC per 1K tokens
   158→- **Model mix**: % Haiku / Sonnet / Opus / Local
   159→- **Rework rate**: Tokens spent on discarded work
   160→
   161→### Portfolio Metrics
   162→
   163→- **Average cost per feature**: Trend over time (should decrease)
   164→- **Template reuse rate**: % projects using templates vs from-scratch
   165→- **Agent utilization**: Sequential vs parallel work
   166→- **Batch operation adoption**: % operations batched vs sequential
   167→

   175→
   176→## Relationship to Compound Engineering
   177→
   178→Token efficiency amplifies [[compound-engineering]]'s compounding effect:
   179→
   180→- **Session 1**: Spend 60K tokens, learn nothing → Next session starts from zero
   181→- **Session 1 (efficient)**: Spend 8K tokens, document lessons → Next session reuses templates, spends 5K tokens
   182→
   183→Over 100 sessions:
   184→- **Inefficient path**: 100 × 60K = 6M tokens (~$1,500)
   185→- **Efficient path**: 8K + 99 × 5K = 503K tokens (~$75) — **12x ROI**

     9→# Universe Simulation
    10→
    11→The Cohezion universe simulation is an N-body gravitational simulation that serves dual purposes: as a physically interesting computation (modeling particle interactions under gravity) and as a high-throughput generator of agent trajectory data for compound learning experiments. Running overnight, the simulation produces millions of trajectory samples — 5.5M trajectories in one overnight run — that are then analyzed to extract patterns applicable to agent orchestration.
    12→
    13→Each simulated particle trajectory is treated as an analog for an agent execution path through the 12-dimensional compound engineering space. Positions represent agent state (coherence, token efficiency, task complexity, skill coverage); velocities represent rates of change; accelerations represent environmental pressures. This analogy yields concrete patterns: the predictive throttling pattern emerged from observing that trajectory velocity gradients reliably predict resource exhaustion before it occurs — a pattern that was validated on real agent sessions.
    14→
    15→The simulation is also a testbed for the three-tier data storage architecture. Generating 5.5M trajectories produces large artifacts (model checkpoints, trajectory files) that cannot be committed to git. The universe simulation was the motivating case for the pre-commit hook enforcement and JourneyTracker artifact registration system that prevents unconstrained data accumulation across sessions.

     8→
     9→# Concept Validation
    10→
    11→Concept validation is the process of verifying that a concept note accurately, completely, and usefully represents the underlying knowledge it describes. Where [[concept-testing]] checks structural properties (links work, schema is valid), concept validation verifies semantic accuracy: does the definition match what the primary sources actually say? Are the key properties correct? Would an expert in the domain recognize the description as accurate?
    12→
    13→Validation matters because the vault is not just a reference document — it is injected into agent contexts to ground execution decisions. An inaccurate concept note is worse than no note: it actively misleads agents, biasing their reasoning toward incorrect assumptions. Validation serves as the quality gate that keeps the [[knowledge-graph-systems]] trustworthy as it grows.
    14→
    15→The validation process in Cohezion mirrors the software TDD cycle: a concept is a "test" of the underlying knowledge, and validation is confirming the test is actually testing the right thing. Adversarial review (assume the definition is wrong, find counter-evidence) is the most effective validation technique for concepts with non-obvious definitions.

     8→
     9→# AI Alignment
    10→
    11→AI alignment is the research and engineering discipline focused on ensuring that AI systems reliably pursue goals that their designers and users intend, rather than instrumental goals that emerge from optimization pressure. The core difficulty is specification: humans rarely articulate their values precisely, and optimization pressure causes systems to find unexpected ways to satisfy literal objectives while violating the underlying intent (the “King Midas problem”).
    12→
    13→For agentic AI systems, alignment is especially critical because agents take real-world actions, make decisions autonomously, and can operate for extended periods without human oversight. A misaligned agent that executes thousands of tool calls can cause substantial harm before the misalignment is detected. This motivates the three-layer alignment strategy used in production systems: intent verification (does the agent understand the goal?), action auditing (does each action match the intent?), and outcome evaluation (did the result match what was intended?).
    14→
    15→In Cohezion, alignment is addressed through the RequestAlignmentAnalyzer (checking coherence between request and available skills before execution), the VaultExecutionLogger (creating an immutable audit trail of all agent decisions), and the adversarial review practice (explicitly stress-testing plans before committing to them). The CONSTITUTION.md file defines hard constraints that no agent may violate regardless of instruction.

     7→## Definition
     8→
     9→Materials science is the interdisciplinary field studying the relationship between a material's atomic structure, its processing history, and its macroscopic properties (mechanical, electrical, optical, thermal). By understanding structure-property relationships, materials scientists design new materials with targeted characteristics — superconductors, semiconductors, structural alloys, biomaterials, and photovoltaics.
    10→
    11→AI is transforming materials discovery: machine learning potentials (trained on quantum chemistry calculations) enable molecular dynamics simulations at DFT accuracy but classical speed, accelerating the exploration of material space from years to days. Foundation models trained on materials databases can predict properties of hypothetical materials before synthesis. This accelerated discovery paradigm is the materials science analog of AlphaFold in structural biology.
    12→
    13→For Cohezion's knowledge graph, materials science connects papers on DNA origami nanofabrication, amorphous material structure determination (3D atomic reconstruction), semiconductor patterning, and photonic nanocavities — a diverse set of methodologies unified by the structure-property-processing triangle.

     9→# Cohezion
    10→
    11→Cohezion is a compound AI orchestration framework designed to make every agent session more effective than the last. Unlike stateless AI pipelines where each run starts from scratch, Cohezion maintains a persistent knowledge base (the Obsidian vault) and a structured feedback loop: agent sessions produce decisions, experiments, and patterns that are indexed, cross-linked, and re-injected into future sessions as context. The result is a system that compounds its own intelligence over time.
    12→
    13→The architecture is built around four interlocking layers: the [[compound-engineering]] methodology (the philosophy), the [[cloud-vault-mcp]] server (the memory infrastructure), the `cz` CLI (the workflow orchestrator), and [[surrealdb]] (the agent context graph). Together they implement a 12-dimensional agentic universe where every execution is tracked as a journey, every lesson is captured as a vault note, and every session benefits from all prior sessions.
    14→
    15→Cohezion is simultaneously a research project, a production tool, and a self-improving system. The FLUME VAE trains on real agent trajectory data, the RetrospectionEngine extracts patterns from session histories, and the SkillRefiner continuously updates PRIME skill definitions based on empirical performance. The target state is an autonomous compound engineering loop that improves without human intervention.
    16→
    17→## Components
    18→- **[[cloud-vault-mcp]]** — HTTP MCP server (port 8360) with 30+ tools for vault/graph/research operations
    19→- **cohezion-engine** (`cz`) — workflow CLI for session management, spec flows, and worktrees
    20→- **3d-graph-plugin** — Obsidian visualization of the knowledge graph
    21→- **[[surrealdb]]** — agent context graph storing sessions, tasks, and relationships
    22→- **Ollama** — local model inference (28+ models, zero API cost)
    23→- **FLUME VAE** — variational autoencoder trained on agent trajectory data
