purpose: Machine-readable vault map for agent session startup
---

# Vault Manifest

**Read this first.** This file tells you where everything lives, where to put your output, and what conventions to follow.

## Directory Map

### Content Directories (where knowledge lives)

| Directory | Purpose | Put Here When... | Naming | Required Frontmatter |
|-----------|---------|-------------------|--------|---------------------|
| `concepts/` | Core definitions, frameworks, techniques | Defining a reusable idea, technology, or methodology | `kebab-case.md` (no date prefix) | `title`, `date`, `tags[]` |
| `papers/` | Research papers, articles, external sources | Summarizing external research with citations | `kebab-case-descriptive-title.md` | `title`, `date`, `tags[]` |
| `decisions/` | Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) | Recording a choice with context, alternatives, consequences | `YYYY-MM-DD-decision-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `status`, `tags[]` |
| `patterns/` | Reusable solutions and code patterns | Documenting a repeatable solution to a recurring problem | `kebab-case-pattern-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `tags[]` |
| `experiments/` | Hypothesis testing and results | Testing a hypothesis with method, results, learnings | `YYYY-MM-DD-experiment-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `status`, `tags[]` |
| `projects/` | Project-level tracking and plans | Tracking a multi-session effort with goals and status | `YYYY-MM-DD-project-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `status`, `tags[]` |
| `lessons/` | Lessons learned from mistakes/discoveries | Capturing something learned the hard way — prevents repeat mistakes | `kebab-case-lesson-title.md` | `title`, `date`, `tags[]`, `severity` |

### Workflow Directories (where work happens)

| Directory | Purpose | Put Here When... | Naming |
|-----------|---------|-------------------|--------|
| `inbox/` | Unsorted intake — triage point | Dropping raw ideas, unprocessed content, or agent output that needs classification | Any `.md` name |
| `daily/` | Daily notes, session logs, checkpoints | Recording a session's work, daily standup, or checkpoint | `YYYY-MM-DD-*.md` |
| `sessions/` | Formal session records with structured metadata | Documenting a compound engineering session with metrics | `session-NNN-*.md` |
| `missions/` | Multi-agent coordinated tasks | Orchestrating multiple agents toward a shared goal | `mission-name.md` or dated |
| `retrospectives/` | Post-session analysis | Reviewing what worked, what didn't, and why | `YYYY-MM-DD-retrospective.md` |
| `Agents/` | Agent execution records and walkthroughs | Storing agent run artifacts, traces, walkthroughs | `AgentName/UUID/` subdirs |

### Navigation Directories (how to find things)

| Directory | Purpose | Key Files |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
| `concepts/MOC-*.md` | Maps of Content — curated topic indexes | 8 MOCs: agentic-ai, quantum-physics, vault-architecture, platform-infrastructure, machine-learning, astrophysics, compound-engineering, safety-alignment |

### Infrastructure Directories (tooling, not content)

| Directory | Purpose | Agent Action |
|-----------|---------|--------------|
| `teleport/` | Cloud-to-local file sync (tasks + results) | Use for cross-environment transfers |
| `docs/` | Long-form documentation, brand guides | Reference only — don't create here without asking |
| `meta/` | Self-recording, compound demos | Specialized — check before writing |
| `specs/` | Formal specifications | For major system designs |
| `benchmarks/` | Performance benchmarking | For measurement data |
| `research/` | Research guides and API specs | For structured research output |
| `templates/` | Note templates (anti-patterns, etc.) | Copy, don't modify |
| `tools/` | Cohezion engine CLI source | Code, not notes |
| `obsidian-plugin/` | 3D graph visualization plugin | Code, not notes |
| `mcp-server/` | MCP server source | Code, not notes |

---

## Output Routing Rules

**When you produce output, route it to the correct directory:**

```
I found a new technique/technology    → concepts/
I summarized external research        → papers/
I made an architectural choice        → decisions/
I documented a reusable solution      → patterns/
I tested a hypothesis                 → experiments/
I'm tracking a multi-session effort   → projects/
I learned something the hard way      → lessons/
I have raw/unstructured content       → inbox/     (vault keeper will triage)
I'm logging today's session work      → daily/
I ran a multi-agent mission           → missions/
I'm reviewing what worked/didn't      → retrospectives/
I don't know where this goes          → inbox/     (always safe default)
```

**When in doubt, use `inbox/`.** The vault keeper triages inbox items into their proper location with correct frontmatter and cross-links.

---

## Conventions

### Frontmatter (YAML)

Every note in a content directory MUST have frontmatter:

```yaml
---
title: "Note Title"
date: 2026-03-04
tags: [tag1, tag2, tag3]
---
```

**Tags are ALWAYS arrays** — never comma-separated strings.

**Status values by directory:**
- `decisions/`: `proposed` → `accepted` → `deprecated` | `rejected`
- `experiments/`: `in-progress` → `complete` | `failed`
- `projects/`: `active` → `complete` → `archived`

### Cross-References

Use Obsidian wiki-links: `[[note-name]]`

- Use bare filename (no path prefix): `[[machine-learning]]` not `[[concepts/machine-learning]]`
- Link at first mention of a concept
- Every note should have 3+ outbound wiki-links
- Every new note must be linked FROM at least one existing note (no orphans)

### Templates

Directories with `_template.md` files: `decisions/`, `patterns/`, `experiments/`, `projects/`, `daily/`

Copy the template when creating a new note in these directories.

---

## Quick Start for Agents

### Starting a session:
1. Read this manifest (you're doing it now)
2. Check `inbox/` for items needing triage
3. Load the relevant MOC for your task: `concepts/MOC-*.md`
4. Check `lessons/` for past mistakes related to your task

### During your session:
5. Create notes in the correct directory per routing rules above
6. Add `[[wiki-links]]` to connect every new note to 1-3 existing notes
7. Use proper frontmatter with tags as arrays

### Ending a session:
8. Log session summary to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD-session-id.md`
9. If you discovered something reusable, add it to `lessons/` or `patterns/`
10. Any raw output that needs triage → `inbox/`

---

## Vault Health Invariants

A healthy vault maintains:
- **0 orphan notes** in content directories
- **0 frontmatter issues** (missing or malformed)
- **0 broken wiki-links** (pointing to non-existent notes)
- **< 10% thin notes** (under 3KB) per directory
- **8+ Maps of Content** covering major topic clusters
- **6+ wiki-links per note** on average

The `/vault-keeper` skill enforces these automatically.

---

## Key Entry Points

| Need | Start Here |
|------|------------|
| Agent architecture & multi-agent systems | `[[MOC-agentic-ai]]` |
| Quantum mechanics, computing, sensors | `[[MOC-quantum-physics]]` |
| Vault structure, linking, health | `[[MOC-vault-architecture]]` |
| MCP, SurrealDB, CI/CD, infrastructure | `[[MOC-platform-infrastructure]]` |
| ML, transformers, optimization | `[[MOC-machine-learning]]` |
| Space, JWST, cosmology | `[[MOC-astrophysics]]` |
| Compound sessions, retrospectives | `[[MOC-compound-engineering]]` |
| AI safety, alignment, guardrails | `[[MOC-safety-alignment]]` |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# PostToolUse hook: Proactive vault keeper checks on .md files.
#
# Two modes, same script:
#   Write/Edit → per-file checks + vault-wide pulse (60s cooldown)
#   Read       → vault-wide pulse only (5 min cooldown)
#
# Any agent touching vault .md files gets health awareness injected.
# Alerts are prefixed with VAULT_KEEPER: so the agent can detect and act on them.

VAULT_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"

# ── Extract tool info from stdin JSON ─────────────────────────────────────────
stdin_json=$(cat)

if ! command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    exit 0
fi

tool_name=$(echo "$stdin_json" | jq -r '.tool_name // empty' 2>/dev/null)
file_path=$(echo "$stdin_json" | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' 2>/dev/null)

# Only run for .md files inside the vault
[[ -z "$file_path" ]] && exit 0
[[ "$file_path" != *.md ]] && exit 0
[[ "$file_path" != "$VAULT_ROOT"* ]] && exit 0

# Skip tooling directories
[[ "$file_path" == *"/obsidian-plugin/"* ]] && exit 0
[[ "$file_path" == *"/mcp-server/"* ]] && exit 0
[[ "$file_path" == *"/tools/"* ]] && exit 0
[[ "$file_path" == *"/.claude/"* ]] && exit 0

# ── Mode-specific cooldown ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [[ "$tool_name" == "Read" ]]; then
    COOLDOWN_FILE="/tmp/vault-keeper-read-$(id -u).last"
    COOLDOWN_SECONDS=300
else
    COOLDOWN_FILE="/tmp/vault-keeper-write-$(id -u).last"
    COOLDOWN_SECONDS=60
fi

if [[ -f "$COOLDOWN_FILE" ]]; then
    last_run=$(cat "$COOLDOWN_FILE" 2>/dev/null)
    now=$(date +%s)

    case "$dir_name" in

                fi
            fi
            ;;

    name="${basename_md%.md}"

            alerts="${alerts}VAULT_KEEPER: new note has no inbound links — ${rel_path}\n"
        fi
    fi
fi

# ── Output alerts ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [[ -n "$alerts" ]]; then
    echo -e "$alerts"
fi

exit 0

# Vault Manifest

**Read this first.** This file tells you where everything lives, where to put your output, and what conventions to follow.

## Directory Map

### Content Directories (where knowledge lives)

| Directory | Purpose | Put Here When... | Naming | Required Frontmatter |
|-----------|---------|-------------------|--------|---------------------|
| `concepts/` | Core definitions, frameworks, techniques | Defining a reusable idea, technology, or methodology | `kebab-case.md` (no date prefix) | `title`, `date`, `tags[]` |

| `decisions/` | Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) | Recording a choice with context, alternatives, consequences | `YYYY-MM-DD-decision-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `status`, `tags[]` |
| `patterns/` | Reusable solutions and code patterns | Documenting a repeatable solution to a recurring problem | `kebab-case-pattern-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `tags[]` |
| `experiments/` | Hypothesis testing and results | Testing a hypothesis with method, results, learnings | `YYYY-MM-DD-experiment-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `status`, `tags[]` |
| `projects/` | Project-level tracking and plans | Tracking a multi-session effort with goals and status | `YYYY-MM-DD-project-name.md` | `title`, `date`, `status`, `tags[]` |
| `lessons/` | Lessons learned from mistakes/discoveries | Capturing something learned the hard way — prevents repeat mistakes | `kebab-case-lesson-title.md` | `title`, `date`, `tags[]`, `severity` |

### Workflow Directories (where work happens)

| Directory | Purpose | Put Here When... | Naming |
|-----------|---------|-------------------|--------|
| `inbox/` | Unsorted intake — triage point | Dropping raw ideas, unprocessed content, or agent output that needs classification | Any `.md` name |
| `daily/` | Daily notes, session logs, checkpoints | Recording a session's work, daily standup, or checkpoint | `YYYY-MM-DD-*.md` |
| `sessions/` | Formal session records with structured metadata | Documenting a compound engineering session with metrics | `session-NNN-*.md` |
| `missions/` | Multi-agent coordinated tasks | Orchestrating multiple agents toward a shared goal | `mission-name.md` or dated |
| `retrospectives/` | Post-session analysis | Reviewing what worked, what didn't, and why | `YYYY-MM-DD-retrospective.md` |
| `Agents/` | Agent execution records and walkthroughs | Storing agent run artifacts, traces, walkthroughs | `AgentName/UUID/` subdirs |

### Navigation Directories (how to find things)

| Directory | Purpose | Key Files |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
| `concepts/MOC-*.md` | Maps of Content — curated topic indexes | 8 MOCs: agentic-ai, quantum-physics, vault-architecture, platform-infrastructure, machine-learning, astrophysics, compound-engineering, safety-alignment |

### Infrastructure Directories (tooling, not content)

| Directory | Purpose | Agent Action |
|-----------|---------|--------------|
| `teleport/` | Cloud-to-local file sync (tasks + results) | Use for cross-environment transfers |
| `docs/` | Long-form documentation, brand guides | Reference only — don't create here without asking |
| `meta/` | Self-recording, compound demos | Specialized — check before writing |
| `specs/` | Formal specifications | For major system designs |
| `benchmarks/` | Performance benchmarking | For measurement data |
| `research/` | Research guides and API specs | For structured research output |
| `templates/` | Note templates (anti-patterns, etc.) | Copy, don't modify |
| `tools/` | Cohezion engine CLI source | Code, not notes |
| `obsidian-plugin/` | 3D graph visualization plugin | Code, not notes |
| `mcp-server/` | MCP server source | Code, not notes |

---

## Output Routing Rules

**When you produce output, route it to the correct directory:**

```
I found a new technique/technology    → concepts/
I summarized external research        → papers/
I made an architectural choice        → decisions/
I documented a reusable solution      → patterns/
I tested a hypothesis                 → experiments/
I'm tracking a multi-session effort   → projects/
I learned something the hard way      → lessons/
I have raw/unstructured content       → inbox/     (vault keeper will triage)
I'm logging today's session work      → daily/
I ran a multi-agent mission           → missions/
I'm reviewing what worked/didn't      → retrospectives/
I don't know where this goes          → inbox/     (always safe default)
```

**When in doubt, use `inbox/`.** The vault keeper triages inbox items into their proper location with correct frontmatter and cross-links.

---

## Conventions

### Frontmatter (YAML)

Every note in a content directory MUST have frontmatter:

```yaml
---
title: "Note Title"
date: 2026-03-04
tags: [tag1, tag2, tag3]
---
```

**Tags are ALWAYS arrays** — never comma-separated strings.

**Status values by directory:**
- `decisions/`: `proposed` → `accepted` → `deprecated` | `rejected`
- `experiments/`: `in-progress` → `complete` | `failed`
- `projects/`: `active` → `complete` → `archived`

### Cross-References

Use Obsidian wiki-links: `[[note-name]]`

- Use bare filename (no path prefix): `[[machine-learning]]` not `[[concepts/machine-learning]]`
- Link at first mention of a concept
- Every note should have 3+ outbound wiki-links
- Every new note must be linked FROM at least one existing note (no orphans)

### Templates

Directories with `_template.md` files: `decisions/`, `patterns/`, `experiments/`, `projects/`, `daily/`

Copy the template when creating a new note in these directories.

---

## Quick Start for Agents

### Starting a session:
1. Read this manifest (you're doing it now)
2. Check `inbox/` for items needing triage
3. Load the relevant MOC for your task: `concepts/MOC-*.md`
4. Check `lessons/` for past mistakes related to your task

### During your session:
5. Create notes in the correct directory per routing rules above
6. Add `[[wiki-links]]` to connect every new note to 1-3 existing notes
7. Use proper frontmatter with tags as arrays

### Ending a session:
8. Log session summary to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD-session-id.md`
9. If you discovered something reusable, add it to `lessons/` or `patterns/`
10. Any raw output that needs triage → `inbox/`

---

## Vault Health Invariants

A healthy vault maintains:
- **0 orphan notes** in content directories
- **0 frontmatter issues** (missing or malformed)
- **0 broken wiki-links** (pointing to non-existent notes)
- **< 10% thin notes** (under 3KB) per directory
- **8+ Maps of Content** covering major topic clusters
- **6+ wiki-links per note** on average

The `/vault-keeper` skill enforces these automatically.

| Compound sessions, retrospectives | `[[MOC-compound-engineering]]` |
| AI safety, alignment, guardrails | `[[MOC-safety-alignment]]` |

```

**When in doubt, use `inbox/`.** The vault keeper triages inbox items into their proper location with correct frontmatter and cross-links.

## Canvas Files (Multimodal Assets)

**Notes explain. Canvases show.** When a topic has complex relationships, spatial layout reveals structure that prose cannot. Create `.canvas` files alongside their companion `.md` notes.

### When to Create a Canvas

| Signal | Canvas Type |
|--------|-------------|
| MOC with 10+ linked notes | **Relationship map** — nodes for notes, edges for connections |
| Architecture or system design | **Architecture diagram** — groups for layers, text cards for components |
| Decision with 3+ alternatives | **Decision landscape** — cards per option, edges to trade-offs |
| Research cluster spanning domains | **Domain map** — grouped by field, edges for cross-domain links |
| Vault keeper nudges you | The hook detected 10+ outbound links — the note wants a canvas |

### Naming and Placement

Canvas files live **alongside their companion note**:
- `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.md` → `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.canvas`
- `decisions/2026-03-05-pick-database.md` → `decisions/2026-03-05-pick-database.canvas`
- Standalone canvases (no companion note) → `canvas/` directory

### JSON Format

Obsidian canvas files are JSON with `nodes` and `edges`:

```json
{
  "nodes": [
    {"id":"unique-id", "type":"file", "file":"concepts/machine-learning.md", "x":0, "y":0, "width":250, "height":60},
    {"id":"label-1",   "type":"text", "text":"## Key Insight\n\nMarkdown content here", "x":300, "y":0, "width":300, "height":120, "color":"4"},
    {"id":"group-1",   "type":"group","label":"ML Cluster", "x":-50, "y":-50, "width":600, "height":250, "color":"2"}
  ],
  "edges": [
    {"id":"edge-1", "fromNode":"unique-id", "toNode":"label-1", "label":"informs"}
  ]
}
```

**Node types:**
- `file` — link to a vault note (opens on click). Use `"file": "path/to/note.md"`
- `text` — inline markdown card. Use `"text": "## Title\n\nContent"`
- `group` — visual grouping box. Use `"label": "Group Name"`

**Colors:** `"1"` red, `"2"` orange, `"3"` yellow, `"4"` green, `"5"` cyan, `"6"` purple, or hex `"#RRGGGG"`

**Layout tips:** Use x/y grid spacing of ~300px horizontal, ~150px vertical. Groups should surround their children with ~50px padding.

Here's what I found about **Gemini CLI's GEMINI.md context files**:

## Overview

Context files, which use the default name `GEMINI.md`, are a powerful feature for providing instructional context to the Gemini model. You can use these files to give project-specific instructions, define a persona, or provide coding style guides.

The Gemini CLI is an open-source AI agent that brings the power of Gemini directly into your terminal, allowing you to perform a wide range of tasks such as coding, problem-solving, and task management using natural language.

## What is GEMINI.md?

The Context (`GEMINI.md`) refers to the conversational memory or state that the Gemini model maintains during an ongoing interaction. Provide project-specific instructions to the model using `GEMINI.md` files. Use `/init` to generate a starter file. The CLI loads these files hierarchically, allowing for general and specific contexts. You can see the combined context with `/memory show`.

## How GEMINI.md Works

`GEMINI.md` is described as your "handbook" — it usually explains the purpose of the project, how to use the Gemini CLI, and may include setup steps, usage notes, or best practices. It's where you go to understand why and how things work.

## Organizing Context

You can organize context by importing other Markdown files. For example, a main project context file might include general instructions like "All Python code must be PEP 8 compliant" and import component-specific style guides via `@./src/frontend/react-style-guide.md` and `@./src/backend/fastapi-style-guide.md`. You can also create a `.geminiignore` file in your project's root to exclude files and directories from Gemini's tools, similar to `.gitignore`.

## Memory Commands

Key memory-related commands include `/memory show` (show what Gemini remembers), `/memory add <text>` (add custom notes), and `/memory refresh` (reload GEMINI.md files).

## Cross-Tool Compatibility Discussion

There's an active discussion in the Gemini CLI community about standardizing context files across different AI coding tools. Right now, users working in teams that use more than one agentic coding tool have to set up `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, Cursor rules, etc. Codex already changed from `codex.md` to `AGENTS.md`.

# Obsidian Embed Syntax Guide

## Core Embed Format
Add an exclamation mark (`!`) before an internal link to embed content.

## Notes, Headings & Blocks
- **Full note:** `![[Internal links]]`
- **Heading:** `![[Internal links#Link to a heading in a note]]`
- **Block:** `![[Internal links#^b15695]]`

## Images
- **Basic:** `![[Engelbart.jpg]]`
- **Custom dimensions:** `![[Engelbart.jpg|100x145]]` (width x height)
- **Width only:** `![[Engelbart.jpg|100]]` (scales proportionally)
- **External image:** `![250](https://example.com/image.jpg)`

## Audio Files
```md
![[Excerpt from Mother of All Demos (1968).ogg]]
```

## PDFs
- **Basic:** `![[Document.pdf]]`
- **Specific page:** `![[Document.pdf#page=3]]`
- **Custom height:** `![[Document.pdf#height=400]]`

## Lists
First, add a block identifier to the list:
```md
- list item 1
- list item 2
^my-list-id
```

Then embed: `![[My note#^my-list-id]]`

## Bonus Feature
"On desktop, you can also drag and drop supported files directly into your note to embed them automatically."

# Tags in Notes: Complete Guide

## Syntax & Creation

Tags are created using a hash symbol followed by a keyword. You can add them inline in editors or via YAML properties formatted as lists:
```yaml
tags:
  - recipe
  - cooking
```

Valid characters include letters, numbers, underscores, hyphens, and forward slashes. "Tags must contain at least one non-numerical character," so #1984 won't work, but #y1984 will. Tags ignore case sensitivity, though they display with their original casing.

For multi-word tags, use: camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, or kebab-case (no spaces allowed).

## Nested Tag Hierarchies

Nested tags use forward slashes to establish relationships, like `#inbox/to-read` and `#inbox/processing`. The parent tag `#inbox` will match all nested variations in searches, creating an organizational structure visible in the Tags view plugin.

## Finding & Using Tags

Search functionality includes:
- **Search plugin**: Use "tag:#meeting" as an operator or click tags directly in notes
- **Tags view**: Select "Tags: Show tags" from the command palette to browse organized tags
- **Bases functions**: The `hasTag()` function recognizes both parent and nested tags

Tags appear wherever notes use the properties feature or inline hashtag notation.

# Obsidian Callouts: Complete Reference

## Basic Syntax
Callouts use blockquote syntax with a type identifier. The fundamental structure is:
```markdown
> [!type] Optional Title
> Content goes here
```

## Supported Callout Types

| Type | Aliases | Usage |
|------|---------|-------|
| note | — | `[!note]` |
| abstract | summary, tldr | `[!abstract]` |
| info | — | `[!info]` |
| todo | — | `[!todo]` |
| tip | hint, important | `[!tip]` |
| success | check, done | `[!success]` |
| question | help, faq | `[!question]` |
| warning | caution, attention | `[!warning]` |
| failure | fail, missing | `[!failure]` |
| danger | error | `[!danger]` |
| bug | — | `[!bug]` |
| example | — | `[!example]` |
| quote | cite | `[!quote]` |

## Key Features

**Custom Titles:** Add text after the type identifier:
```markdown
> [!tip] Custom Title Here
> Content body
```

**Foldable Callouts:** Use `+` (expanded by default) or `-` (collapsed by default):
```markdown
> [!warning]- Collapsed warning
> Hidden content appears when expanded
```

**Nested Callouts:** Layer callouts using multiple `>` symbols:
```markdown
> [!question] Outer callout
> > [!todo] Middle level
> > > [!example] Inner level
```

**Title-Only Callouts:** Omit the body:
```markdown
> [!tip] Just a title
```

## Custom Callout Definition

Create custom types via CSS:
```css
.callout[data-callout="custom-name"] {
    --callout-color: 0, 0, 0;
    --callout-icon: lucide-icon-name;
}
```

Support markdown, wikilinks, and embeds within callout content. Unsupported types default to the note style.

# Markdown Formatting Syntax Guide

## Headings
- `# Heading 1` through `###### Heading 6`

## Text Styling
| Style | Syntax |
|-------|--------|
| Bold | `**text**` or `__text__` |
| Italic | `*text*` or `_text_` |
| Bold + Italic | `***text***` or `___text___` |
| Strikethrough | `~~text~~` |
| Highlight | `==text==` |
| Escape formatting | `\` before special characters |

## Paragraphs & Line Breaks
- **Paragraphs**: Separate with blank lines
- **Line breaks**: Two trailing spaces + Enter, or Shift+Enter
- **Strict line breaks**: Single Enter combines lines; double Enter creates separate paragraphs

## Links
- Internal: `[[Note name]]` or `[text](file.md)`
- External: `[text](URL)`
- With spaces: `[text](URL%20with%20spaces)` or `[text](<URL with spaces>)`

## Images
- `![alt text](URL)` 
- With dimensions: `![alt|640x480](URL)`

## Code
- Inline: `` `code` ``
- Block: ` ```language ` (three or more backticks)
- Indent block: Tab or 4 spaces

## Lists
- Unordered: `-`, `*`, or `+`
- Ordered: `1.` or `1)`
- Tasks: `- [ ]` (incomplete) or `- [x]` (complete)
- Nested: Indent items with Tab

## Other Elements
- **Quotes**: `> text`
- **Horizontal rules**: `***`, `---`, or `___`
- **Footnotes**: `[^label]` with `[^label]: definition`
- **Inline footnotes**: `^[footnote text]`
- **Comments**: `%% text %%`

# Obsidian Properties & Frontmatter Reference

## Overview
"Properties allow you to organize information about a note" containing structured data like text, links, dates, checkboxes, and numbers.

## Supported Property Types

1. **Text** – Single-line text without markdown rendering. Can include URLs and internal links (must be quoted).
   ```yaml
   title: A New Hope
   link: "[[Episode IV]]"
   ```

2. **List** – Multiple values with hyphens and spaces. Supports text, numbers, and internal links.
   ```yaml
   cast: 
     - Mark Hamill
     - Harrison Ford
   ```

3. **Number** – Literal integers or decimals only (no expressions).
   ```yaml
   year: 1977
   pie: 3.14
   ```

4. **Checkbox** – Boolean values (`true`/`false`/indeterminate).
   ```yaml
   favorite: true
   ```

5. **Date** – ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).
   ```yaml
   date: 2020-08-21
   ```

6. **Date & time** – ISO format with timestamp.
   ```yaml
   time: 2020-08-21T10:30:00
   ```

7. **Tags** – Special list type for the `tags` property only.
   ```yaml
   tags:
     - journal
     - personal
   ```

## Default Properties

| Property | Type | Purpose |
|----------|------|---------|
| `tags` | List | Categorization |
| `aliases` | List | Alternative note names |
| `cssclasses` | List | Custom styling via CSS snippets |
| `publish` | Boolean | Obsidian Publish selection |
| `permalink` | Text | Custom URL slug |
| `description` | Text | Preview text for links |
| `image`/`cover` | Text | Social media preview image |

## Format
Properties use YAML syntax at file start, wrapped by `---` delimiters. JSON is also supported but converts to YAML.

## Limitations
"Nested properties," bulk-editing, and markdown rendering within properties are unsupported.

# Obsidian File Formats

## Natively Supported Formats

**Markdown & Notes:**
- Markdown (`.md`)
- Bases (`.base`)

**Canvas:**
- JSON Canvas (`.canvas`)

**Embedded Media (natively rendered):**
- Images: `.avif`, `.bmp`, `.gif`, `.jpeg`, `.jpg`, `.png`, `.svg`, `.webp`
- Audio: `.flac`, `.m4a`, `.mp3`, `.ogg`, `.wav`, `.webm`, `.3gp`
- Video: `.mkv`, `.mov`, `.mp4`, `.ogv`, `.webm`
- PDF: `.pdf`

## Extended Support

"You can extend Obsidian to support other file formats using Community plugins." This allows users to add functionality beyond the built-in file types.

## Key Notes

- The page indicates that "many file types — including images, audio, video, and PDFs — can be embedded directly into your notes"
- Audio and video playback depends on device codec availability
- Desktop and mobile have different embedding workflows (drag-and-drop vs. attachment options)

# Internal Link Syntax in Obsidian

## Wiki-link Format
- Basic: `[[Three laws of motion]]`
- With extension: `[[Three laws of motion.md]]`

## Heading Links
- Same note: `[[#Preview a linked file]]`
- Another note: `[[About Obsidian#Links are first-class citizens]]`
- Subheadings: `[[Help and support#Questions and advice#Report bugs]]`
- Search headers: `[[## team]]`

## Block References
- Basic syntax: `[[2023-01-01#^37066d]]`
- Human-readable: `[[2023-01-01#^quote-of-the-day]]`
- Search blocks: `[[^^block]]`

## Link Display Text (Wiki-link)
- Custom text: `[[Example|Custom name]]`
- With heading: `[[Example#Details|Section name]]`

## Markdown Format
- Basic: `[Three laws of motion](Three%20laws%20of%20motion)`
- With extension: `[Three laws of motion](Three%20laws%20of%20motion.md)`
- Custom display: `[Custom name](Example.md)`
- With heading: `[Section name](Example.md#Details)`

## Embedded Content
- Prefix with exclamation: `![[filename]]` (embeds linked content)

## Key Constraint
"A string which contains the following characters may not work as a link: `# | ^ : %% [[ ]]`"

# CSS Snippets in Obsidian: Complete Guide

## Location & Storage
CSS snippets are stored in the vault's configuration folder. Obsidian automatically searches this location for CSS files.

## Adding Snippets

**Desktop Process:**
1. Access Settings → Appearance → CSS snippets
2. Select "Open snippets folder"
3. Create a CSS file with your snippet content
4. Click "Reload snippets" to detect the file
5. Toggle to enable the snippet

**Mobile/Tablet Process:**
1. Use a file manager to locate your vault
2. Navigate to the configuration folder
3. Create a `snippets` folder if needed
4. Add your CSS file to this folder
5. Open Settings → Appearance → CSS snippets
6. Tap "Reload snippets" then enable via toggle

**Alternative Methods:**
- Sync changes across devices using Obsidian's sync service
- Use community plugins to create snippets within the app

## Key Features

**Automatic Updates:** "Once enabled, Obsidian will automatically detect changes to CSS snippets and apply them when you save the file."

**No Restart Required:** Changes take effect immediately without restarting the application.

## What Can Be Styled

- Heading colors and sizes
- UI element appearance
- Note-specific styling via CSS classes
- Various interface components through CSS variables

## Styling Methods

**1. CSS Variables:** Modify predefined variables like `--h1-color`, `--h2-color`, etc.

**2. Custom CSS Classes:** Assign custom classes to notes using the `cssclasses` property to apply note-specific styling.

## Examples

**Heading Color Example:**
```css
body {
  --h1-color: red;
  --h2-color: orange;
}
```

**CSS Class Example:**
```css
.red-border img {
   border-color: #ff0000;
}
```

## Validation
Use tools like the CSS Validation Service to ensure CSS files are properly formatted, as invalid CSS will not function.

# Advanced Formatting Features

## Tables
Create tables using vertical bars (`|`) and hyphens (`-`) for headers. The syntax supports:
- Basic structure: `| Column | Column |` with `| --- | --- |` for headers
- Optional outer bars (recommended for readability)
- Content formatting using bold, italics, links, and embeds
- Text alignment via colons: `:--` (left), `:--:` (center), `--:` (right)

**Example:**
```md
| Left | Center | Right |
| :-- | :--: | --: |
| Content | Content | Content |
```

## Diagrams (Mermaid)
Create flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and timelines using "mermaid" code blocks. Key features:
- Use `graph TD` syntax for flowcharts
- Apply `internal-link` class to create clickable note links: `class Biology,Chemistry internal-link;`
- Special characters in note names require double quotes: `class "⨳ special" internal-link;`

## Math/LaTeX (MathJax)
Insert mathematical expressions using:
- **Block math**: Surround with `$$..$$`
- **Inline math**: Wrap with single `$...$`

# Obsidian URI Scheme Reference

## Protocol Format
`obsidian://action?param1=value&param2=value`

All values require proper URI encoding (e.g., `/` → `%2F`, space → `%20`).

## Actions & Parameters

### 1. **open** - Open vault or note
Opens an Obsidian vault or specific file within it.

**Key Parameters:**
- `vault`: vault name or ID
- `file`: filename or path from vault root
- `path`: absolute file system path (overrides vault/file)
- `paneType`: `tab`, `split`, or `window` (desktop only)
- `prepend`/`append`: adds content to file top/end

**Examples:**
- `obsidian://open?vault=my%20vault`
- `obsidian://open?vault=my%20vault&file=my%20note`
- Deep linking: `Note%23Heading` navigates to heading; `Note%23%5EBlock` navigates to block

### 2. **new** - Create note
Creates a new note with optional content.

**Key Parameters:**
- `vault`: vault name or ID
- `name`/`file`: filename or path
- `content`: note contents
- `clipboard`: uses clipboard content instead
- `silent`: creates without opening
- `append`/`overwrite`: handles existing files
- `x-success`: callback URL parameter

**Examples:**
- `obsidian://new?vault=my%20vault&name=my%20note`
- `obsidian://new?vault=my%20vault&file=path%2Fto%2Fmy%20note`

### 3. **daily** - Create/open daily note
Requires Daily notes plugin enabled.

**Parameters:** Accepts same parameters as `new` action

**Example:**
- `obsidian://daily?vault=my%20vault`

### 4. **unique** - Create unique note
Requires Unique note creator plugin enabled.

**Parameters:**
- `vault`: vault name or ID
- `content`/`clipboard`: note contents
- `paneType`: UI placement option

**Example:**
- `obsidian://unique?vault=my%20vault&content=Hello%20World`

### 5. **search** - Open search
Opens search interface with optional query.

**Parameters:**
- `vault`: vault name or ID
- `query`: search term (optional)

**Examples:**
- `obsidian://search?vault=my%20vault`
- `obsidian://search?vault=my%20vault&query=Obsidian`

### 6. **choose-vault** - Open vault manager
No parameters required.

**Example:**
- `obsidian://choose-vault`

### 7. **hook-get-address** - Hook integration
Used with Hook productivity app.

**Parameters:**
- `vault`: vault name or ID (optional)
- `x-success`/`x-error`: callback URLs

**Example:**
- `obsidian://hook-get-address`

## Shorthand Formats
- `obsidian://vault/my%20vault/my%20note` (equivalent to open action)
- `obsidian:///absolute/path/to/my%20note` (equivalent to path parameter)

## x-callback-url Response
When `x-success` is provided, callback includes:
- `name`: filename without extension
- `url`: obsidian:// URI
- `file`: file:// URL (desktop only)

# Template Features Summary

## Core Functionality
Templates is a core plugin enabling insertion of "pre-defined snippets of text into your active note."

## Available Template Variables

| Variable | Function |
|----------|----------|
| `{{title}}` | Displays the active note's title |
| `{{date}}` | Inserts today's date (default: `YYYY-MM-DD`) |
| `{{time}}` | Inserts current time (default: `HH:mm`) |

## Format Customization
Date and time variables support custom formatting via Moment.js tokens. Syntax: `{{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}` or `{{time:HH:mm}}`. Default formats are configurable in Settings.

## Setup Requirements
1. Access Settings (bottom-left corner)
2. Navigate to Core plugins → Templates
3. Specify your template folder location

## Creating Templates
Place notes containing desired text in your template folder. Incorporate template variables for dynamic content like dates or titles.

## Insertion Process
1. Click "Insert template" in the ribbon
2. Select your desired template
3. The plugin inserts it at the cursor position

## Additional Integration
Template variables also function within Daily notes and Unique note creator plugins.

# Graph View Features in Obsidian

## Core Functionality
Graph view visualizes vault relationships through nodes (notes) and links (internal connections). Node size increases with reference count.

## Filters
- **Search files**: Filter notes by search terms
- **Tags**: Toggle tag visibility
- **Attachments**: Toggle attachment visibility
- **Existing files only**: Show only notes that exist in the vault
- **Orphans**: Toggle display of unlinked notes
- Excluded files (per vault settings) don't appear

## Groups
Organize and color-code note clusters through custom search-based groupings.

## Display Settings
- **Arrows**: Show link directionality
- **Text fade threshold**: Adjust note name transparency
- **Node size**: Scale circle sizes
- **Link thickness**: Adjust line widths
- **Animate**: Launch chronological time-lapse based on creation dates

## Forces (Physics Simulation)
- **Center force**: Graph compactness (higher = more circular)
- **Repel force**: Node spacing intensity
- **Link force**: Connection tightness (rubber band analogy)
- **Link distance**: Line length between notes

## Local Graph
Displays only notes connected to the active note, with adjustable depth levels to reveal progressively connected notes.

## Navigation & Interaction
- Zoom via scroll wheel or +/- keys
- Pan by dragging or arrow keys
- Shift+keyboard speeds up movement
- Hover to highlight connections
- Click to open notes
- Right-click for context menu

# Bookmark Features in Obsidian

## Bookmarkable Items
The plugin supports bookmarks for:
- Files and folders
- Graphs (excluding local graphs)
- Search queries
- Headings and blocks
- Web links (requires Web viewer enabled)

## Creating Bookmarks

**Files**: Right-click in File explorer and select "Bookmark," or use "Bookmark the active tab" in the Bookmarks panel.

**Folders**: Right-click folders in File explorer and choose the bookmark option.

**Searches**: Execute a search, then select the three-dot menu next to results and choose "Bookmark."

**Graphs**: Right-click the graph tab and select "Bookmark."

**Headings**: Right-click the heading and pick "Bookmark this heading," or use the Command palette command.

**Blocks**: Access via Command palette with "Bookmark block under cursor."

**Links**: Within Web viewer, use the address bar's three-dot menu or Command palette.

**Multiple files**: Select files using Alt+click or Shift+range selection, then right-click and bookmark together.

## Management Features

A bookmark opens an "Add bookmark" dialog where you assign optional titles and organize items into groups. The dialog becomes "Edit bookmark" for existing bookmarks.

Reorganize bookmarks by dragging them within the Bookmarks tab. Create groups using "New bookmark group," collapse/expand sections as needed, and remove items by right-clicking and selecting delete options.

# Obsidian Search: Complete Operator & Syntax Reference

## Boolean Operators
- **AND (implicit)**: `meeting work` returns files containing both terms
- **OR**: `meeting OR work` returns files with either term
- **NOT (negation)**: `-work` excludes a term from results
- **Parentheses**: `meeting (work OR meetup) personal` controls expression priority

## Search Operators

| Operator | Purpose | Example |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `file:` | Search filenames across vault | `file:.jpg` or `file:202209` |
| `path:` | Search file paths | `path:"Daily notes/2022-07"` |
| `content:` | Search file contents | `content:"happy cat"` |
| `match-case:` | Case-sensitive matching | `match-case:HappyCat` |
| `ignore-case:` | Case-insensitive matching | `ignore-case:ikea` |
| `tag:` | Find specific tags | `tag:#work` |
| `line:` | Match complete lines | `line:(mix flour)` |
| `block:` | Same-block matching | `block:(dog cat)` |
| `section:` | Same-section matching | `section:(dog cat)` |
| `task:` | Search tasks | `task:call` |
| `task-todo:` | Uncompleted tasks only | `task-todo:call` |
| `task-done:` | Completed tasks only | `task-done:call` |

## Property Search Syntax
- `[property]` - files containing that property
- `[property:value]` - specific property values
- `[property:null]` - empty properties
- `[status:Draft OR Published]` - multiple property values

## Advanced Features
- **Exact phrases**: Surround with quotes: `"star wars"`
- **Escaped quotes**: `"they said \"hello\" to them"`
- **Comparison operators**: `[duration:<5]` or `[duration:>5]`
- **Regular expressions**: Wrap in forward slashes: `/\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/`
- **Nested queries**: `task:(call OR email)`

# Canvas Features Overview

## Core Purpose
Canvas is Obsidian's core plugin for visual note-taking that provides "infinite space to lay out notes and connect them to other notes, attachments, and web pages." It enables users to "organize them in a 2D space" and "better understand the relationship between them."

## Card Types (Content You Can Add)

- **Text cards**: Markdown-based cards without file references; can include links and code blocks
- **Note cards**: References to vault files that can be dragged in or selected from the file explorer
- **Media cards**: Images, audio, and PDFs from your vault
- **Web page cards**: Embedded URLs that can be opened in your browser
- **Folder cards**: Adding a folder adds all its contained files to the canvas

## Card Management
Users can edit, delete, resize, duplicate, and swap cards. Cards support color customization and can be arranged by dragging, with options to snap or move in single directions.

## Connections
Lines connect cards to show relationships. Connection features include directional arrows, custom labels describing relationships, color coding, and navigation shortcuts to jump between connected cards.

## Organization
Groups allow related cards to be bundled together with custom names for better visual organization.

## File Format
Canvas data is "saved as `.canvas` files using the open file format JSON Canvas," making files portable and interoperable.

## Navigation
Pan using Space+drag or middle-mouse button; zoom via Space+scroll or control buttons, with fit-to-view and selection zoom options.

Here's a comprehensive overview of **OpenCode** — an AI coding agent built for the terminal:

## What is OpenCode?

OpenCode is a powerful AI coding agent built for the terminal. It is an open-source AI coding agent for the terminal with support for 75+ LLM providers.

## Key Features

### Agents
Agents are specialized AI assistants that can be configured for specific tasks and workflows. They allow you to create focused tools with custom prompts, models, and tool access. There are two types of agents in OpenCode: primary agents and subagents. Primary agents are the main assistants you interact with directly. You can cycle through them using the Tab key, or your configured switch_agent keybind. These agents handle your main conversation.

OpenCode comes with two built-in primary agents, Build and Plan.

### Context & Instructions
You should give OpenCode plenty of context and examples to help it understand what you want. Once it gives you a plan, you can give it feedback or add more details.

OpenCode includes an auto compact feature that automatically summarizes your conversation when it approaches the model's context window limit.

### Custom Commands
You can create custom commands by creating a file at `~/.config/opencode/commands/prime-context.md`, which creates a command called `user:prime-context`. OpenCode supports named arguments in custom commands using placeholders in the format `$NAME`.

### Configuration
The `.opencode` and `~/.config/opencode` directories use plural names for subdirectories: `agents/`, `commands/`, `modes/`, `plugins/`, `skills/`, `tools/`, and `themes/`. You can place your global OpenCode config in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, and use global config for user-wide server/runtime preferences like providers, models, and permissions.

### MCP (Model Context Protocol) Support
OpenCode implements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to extend its capabilities through external tools. MCP provides a standardized way for the AI assistant to interact with external services and tools.

MCP supports external tool integration via a standardized protocol and automatic tool discovery from MCP servers. It supports both `stdio` and `sse` server types with configuration in JSON format. MCP tools follow the same permission model as other tools, requiring user approval before execution.

### CLI Commands for MCP
You can add an MCP server to your configuration via the CLI. This command will guide you through adding either a local or remote MCP server. You can also list all configured MCP servers and their connection status. OpenCode also supports authenticating with an OAuth-enabled MCP server.

### Built-in Tools
Tools allow the LLM to perform actions in your codebase. OpenCode comes with a set of built-in tools, but you can extend it with custom tools or MCP servers. Key built-in tools include:

- Shell command execution in your project environment
- File modification using exact string replacements
- Fast content search across your codebase with full regex syntax and file pattern filtering
- File finding by pattern matching
- Web content fetching
- LSP server interaction for code intelligence features like definitions, references, hover info, and call hierarchy

### Additional Features
- **GitHub Integration**: OpenCode integrates with your GitHub workflow. You can mention `/opencode` or `/oc` in your comment, and OpenCode will execute tasks within your GitHub Actions runner.
- **Server Mode**: OpenCode can start an HTTP server that provides API access to its functionality without the TUI interface.
- **Web Interface**: It can also start an HTTP server and open a web browser to access OpenCode through a web interface.
- **Session Management**: You can show token usage and cost statistics for your OpenCode sessions.
- OpenCode is licensed under the MIT License.

# Unique Note Creator Plugin Features

The Unique note creator plugin offers the following capabilities:

1. **Time-based note naming**: Generates notes with timestamp-based names following the Zettelkasten method (format: YYYYMMDDHHmm)

2. **Collision handling**: "If a note with the same name exists, the new note uses the next available timestamp"

3. **Multiple creation methods**:
   - Ribbon button access for quick note creation
   - Command palette integration for keyboard-driven workflow

4. **Template support**: Users can designate a template file to populate new unique notes with predefined content rather than starting blank

5. **Configurable settings**: Plugin settings allow customization of the template file location through the Core plugins section in Settings

These features enable efficient note-taking with automatically organized timestamps while maintaining flexibility through templating options.

# HTML Support in Obsidian

## Supported HTML Tags
The documentation explicitly mentions these tags work in Obsidian:
- `<script>` (sanitized for security)
- `<div>`
- `<table>`
- `<tr>`
- `<td>`
- `<span>`
- `<a>`
- `<u>` (underline)
- `<s>` (strikethrough)
- `<iframe>` (for embedding web pages)
- HTML comments `<!-- -->`

## Key Limitations

**Markdown Processing:** "Obsidian does not render Markdown syntax inside HTML elements." This means bold, italics, and code formatting won't work within HTML tags.

**Block Structure:** HTML blocks must remain complete without blank lines. Breaking HTML with empty lines will prevent proper rendering.

**Inline Tag Behavior:** Tags like `<span>` and `<a>` have limited functionality; any apparent Markdown rendering occurs outside the HTML context, not within it.

## Security Restrictions

Obsidian implements HTML sanitization to prevent malicious code execution. The documentation warns that "an attacker could convince you to paste a text containing JavaScript that extracts sensitive information." The sanitization process blocks potentially harmful scripts while preserving safe HTML functionality for styling and formatting purposes.

# Note Management Features in Obsidian

## Creating Notes
Users can create new notes via:
- Keyboard shortcut: `Ctrl+N` (Windows/Linux) or `Cmd+N` (macOS)
- File explorer interface
- Command palette selection

After creation, "Enter the name of the note and then press `Enter` to start editing."

## Renaming Notes
To rename an active note:
- Click the note name at the editor top or press `F2`
- Input the new name and press `Enter`

**Automatic Link Updates:** When renaming, "Obsidian automatically updates all the links to that file." Users can also rename files through the File explorer without opening them first.

## Deleting Notes
Deletion methods include:
- Using **More options → Delete file** in the active note's upper right
- Selecting "Delete current file" from the Command palette
- File explorer interface

## Deletion Behavior Options
Users can configure deletion outcomes under Settings → Files & Links:
- **System trash** (default): Files move to OS trash for recovery
- **Obsidian trash**: Files go to a `.trash` folder within the vault
- **Permanently delete**: Immediate, irreversible deletion

## Important Consideration
"Obsidian will respect the filename limitations of the operating system you create the note on," so cross-device syncing requires OS-safe filenames.

# Daily Notes Features Summary

## Core Functionality
The Daily Notes plugin automatically opens or creates a note based on the current date, enabling journal entries, to-do lists, and daily logs. By default, notes follow a YYYY-MM-DD naming format.

## Access Methods
Users can open today's note via:
- Ribbon icon button
- Command palette command
- Custom hotkey assignment

## Configuration Options

**File Location**: The "New file location" setting allows users to organize daily notes into separate folders rather than keeping them in the root directory.

**Date Format Customization**: The date format feature supports momentJS syntax, enabling automatic subfolder organization. For example, a format of `YYYY/MMMM/YYYY-MMM-DD` creates nested folders by year and month (e.g., `2023/January/2023-Jan-01`).

## Template Integration
Users can create structured daily notes using templates:
1. Create a template note with desired content
2. Specify its location in Daily Notes plugin settings
3. The template applies automatically to newly created daily notes

Template variables like `{{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}` dynamically insert formatted dates.

## Integration with Date Properties
When a note contains a date property, the Daily Notes plugin automatically converts that date into a clickable link to the corresponding daily note in Live Preview mode, creating seamless cross-references within your vault.

# Obsidian Backlinks Plugin Features

## How Backlinks Work

A backlink represents a reverse reference: when Note A links to Note B, a backlink exists from B back to A. As explained, "A backlink for a note is a link from another note to that note."

## Linked Mentions

This feature displays "backlinks to the notes that contain an internal link to the active note." These are intentional references you've explicitly created through internal linking.

## Unlinked Mentions

This shows "backlinks to any unlinked occurrence of the name of the active note." This catches contextual references where the note title appears but isn't formally linked.

## Additional Options

The plugin provides customizable controls:
- Expand/collapse individual note results
- Toggle full paragraph context or truncated views
- Adjust mention sorting order
- Filter mentions using search terms

Note: Files matching excluded file patterns won't appear in unlinked mentions results.

# Outgoing Links Plugin Features

The Outgoing Links plugin is a core tool in Obsidian that displays connections from your current note. Here are its key capabilities:

## Main Features

**Links Section**: Displays all hyperlinks within the active note, allowing you to click through to connected documents.

**Unlinked Mentions**: This feature identifies text matching note names or their aliases that aren't yet formally linked. As described, this helps you "discover links you aren't aware of yet."

## Creating Connections

You can convert unlinked mentions into actual links by clicking the associated button for each potential connection.

## Helpful Notes

The plugin excludes files matching your vault's excluded file patterns from appearing in unlinked mentions. Additionally, if multiple notes share the same name, hovering over a button reveals the complete file path to distinguish between them.

A limitation exists with code blocks: while you can create links from unlinked mentions within code blocks, those links won't appear in the main Links section due to how code blocks function.

# Community Plugins in Obsidian

## How They Work

Community plugins extend Obsidian's functionality through third-party code. Users can browse, install, enable, and manage plugins through Settings. The platform requires users to disable Restricted Mode before installation, and plugins don't update automatically for security reasons.

## Installation & Management

The process involves opening Settings, browsing available plugins (either in-app or at obsidian.md/plugins), selecting a plugin, and installing it. Users can then enable the plugin and configure it with custom hotkeys or settings if available. Management options include toggling plugins on/off, checking for updates, and uninstalling.

## Security Considerations

As the documentation notes: "Community plugins run third-party code on your behalf that could potentially do harm." The Obsidian team implements security measures to prevent harmful plugins, detailed in their Plugin security documentation.

## Notable Information

While the provided content doesn't specifically mention Dataview or Templater, it confirms that plugins support additional file formats, third-party service integration, and configurable options. The documentation encourages developers to build plugins using Obsidian's plugin API.

Here's a comprehensive overview of how OpenCode AI CLI handles instructions files, AGENTS.md, and context loading at startup:

## OpenCode AI CLI: Instructions, AGENTS.md, and Context Loading

### AGENTS.md Instructions File

You can provide custom instructions to OpenCode by creating an AGENTS.md file. This is similar to Cursor's rules. It contains instructions that will be included in the LLM's context to customize its behavior for your specific project.

**Creating AGENTS.md:**
To create a new AGENTS.md file, you can run the `/init` command in OpenCode. You should commit your project's AGENTS.md file to Git. This will scan your project and all its contents to understand what the project is about and generate an AGENTS.md file with it. This helps OpenCode navigate the project better.

If you have an existing AGENTS.md file, this will try to add to it. You can also just create this file manually.

### File Locations

- **Project-level:** Place an AGENTS.md in your project root for project-specific rules. These only apply when you are working in this directory or its sub-directories.
- **Global rules:** You can also have global rules in a `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` file. This gets applied across all OpenCode sessions. Since this isn't committed to Git or shared with your team, we recommend using this to specify any personal rules that the LLM should follow.

### Claude Code Compatibility (CLAUDE.md Fallback)

For users migrating from Claude Code, OpenCode supports Claude Code's file conventions as fallbacks: Project rules: CLAUDE.md in your project directory (used if no AGENTS.md exists). Global rules: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (used if no ~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md exists). The first matching file wins in each category. For example, if you have both AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, only AGENTS.md is used. Similarly, ~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md takes precedence over ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

### Custom Instruction Files via opencode.json

You can specify custom instruction files in your opencode.json or the global ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json. This allows you and your team to reuse existing rules rather than having to duplicate them to AGENTS.md.

You can also use remote URLs to load instructions from the web. Remote instructions are fetched with a 5 second timeout. All instruction files are combined with your AGENTS.md files.

While OpenCode doesn't automatically parse file references in AGENTS.md, you can achieve similar functionality using the instructions field in opencode.json with paths and glob patterns. For monorepos or projects with shared standards, using opencode.json with glob patterns (like `packages/*/AGENTS.md`) is more maintainable than manual instructions.

### .opencode Directory Structure

The `.opencode` and `~/.config/opencode` directories use plural names for subdirectories: agents/, commands/, modes/, plugins/, skills/, tools/, and themes/. Singular names (e.g., agent/) are also supported for backwards compatibility.

You can also define agents using markdown files in `~/.config/opencode/agents/` or `.opencode/agents/`.

### Agent Skills (SKILL.md)

Agent skills let OpenCode discover reusable instructions from your repo or home directory. Skills are loaded on-demand via the native skill tool—agents see available skills and can load the full content when needed.

OpenCode searches these locations, walking up from your current working directory until it reaches the git worktree. It loads any matching `skills/*/SKILL.md` in `.opencode/` and any matching `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` or `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md` along the way. Global definitions are also loaded from `~/.config/opencode/skills/*/SKILL.md`, `~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`, and `~/.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md`.

### Startup Context Loading

When OpenCode starts up it loads the providers from the credentials file. And if there are any keys defined in your environments or a `.env` file in your project.

Remote config is loaded first, serving as the base layer. All other config sources (global, project) can override these defaults.

### Auto Compact Feature

OpenCode includes an auto compact feature that automatically summarizes your conversation when it approaches the model's context window limit.

# Bases Formula Functions and Syntax

## Operators

**Arithmetic:** `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` with parentheses for order of operations

**Comparison:** `>`, `<`, `==`, `!=` for evaluating values and dates

**Boolean:** `!` (not), `&&` (and), `||` (or) to combine conditions

## Functions by Category

**Global:** `if()`, `now()`, `date()`, `link()`, `max()`, `min()`

**String:** `contains()`, `replace()`, `split()`, `lower()`, `title()`

**Number:** `round()`, `ceil()`, `floor()`, `abs()`, `toFixed()`

**Date:** `format()`, `relative()`, `date()`, `time()`

**List:** `filter()`, `map()`, `sort()`, `join()`, `unique()`, `.length`

## Property References

- Note properties from frontmatter
- File properties: `file.name`, `file.size`, `file.mtime`
- Formula properties via `formula.formula_name`

## Data Types Supported

Strings, numbers, booleans, dates, lists, and objects

## Key Constraint

"A formula cannot reference itself directly or indirectly through other formulas."

# Obsidian Bases: Comprehensive Overview

## What It Is
Bases is a core plugin enabling database-like organization of notes. It allows users to "view, edit, sort, and filter files and their properties" through structured layouts.

## Core Functionality
- Data storage occurs in local Markdown files using properties
- Views are defined using Bases syntax (stored as `.base` files or embedded in code blocks)
- Supports organizing projects, travel plans, reading lists, and similar structured data

## Available Views
1. **Table** - Files displayed as rows; properties shown as columns
2. **List** - Files displayed with bulleted or numbered formatting
3. **Cards** - Grid layout enabling gallery-style displays with images
4. **Map** - Interactive map with files as pins

## Query & Calculation Capabilities
- **Filtering** - Restrict displayed files based on property values
- **Sorting** - Order files by specific properties
- **Grouping** - Organize files by property categories
- **Formulas** - "Create calculations using data from other properties"
- **Functions** - Dedicated functions available for formulas and filters

## Syntax & Implementation
Base structure is described through Bases syntax with standardized formatting. Community plugins can extend functionality with additional view types beyond the four built-in layouts.

# Templater: Template Language Overview

## Core Definition
Templater is a template language plugin for Obsidian that enables users to insert variables and function results into notes while executing JavaScript code. As described in the documentation: "Templater is a template language that lets you insert **variables** and **functions** results into your notes."

## Key Capabilities
The plugin automates manual tasks through powerful template creation. It processes dynamic content at note creation or insertion time, distinguishing it from static core templates.

## Available Modules
The documentation lists nine internal function modules:

- **tp.app** - Application-level operations
- **tp.config** - Configuration access
- **tp.date** - Date manipulation and formatting
- **tp.file** - File metadata (creation date, modification date, title)
- **tp.frontmatter** - YAML frontmatter handling
- **tp.hooks** - Event-based triggers
- **tp.obsidian** - Native Obsidian API integration
- **tp.system** - System command execution
- **tp.web** - Web-based functions (like fetching daily quotes)

## Syntax
Templates use delimiter syntax like `<% tp.file.title %>` to embed dynamic content. The plugin supports JavaScript execution within templates for complex logic.

## Function Types
Beyond internal modules, Templater supports user-defined functions via scripts and system commands, plus dynamic and execution commands for advanced automation.

# Dataview: Query Engine for Obsidian Vaults

## Overview
Dataview is a live indexing and query system for personal knowledge bases. It enables users to "add metadata to notes and query them with the Dataview Query Language to list, filter, sort or group data."

## Core Architecture

### Data Indexing
Dataview indexes metadata from two sources:
- **Implicit fields**: Automatically captured tags, bullet points, tasks, file properties
- **Explicit fields**: User-added via YAML frontmatter or inline syntax `[key:: value]`

Only indexed data is queryable—document body text isn't included.

### Query Types
Three query methods exist:
1. **Dataview Query Language (DQL)**: Primary declarative approach
2. **Inline queries**: Single-value displays with calculations
3. **JavaScript queries**: Custom logic against the Dataview API

## DQL Syntax Structure

A query requires:
- **Query Type** (mandatory): LIST, TABLE, TASK, or CALENDAR
- **FROM clause** (optional): Filters by tag, folder, or other sources
- **Data Commands** (optional): WHERE, GROUP BY, SORT, etc.

### Basic Example
```
LIST FROM #poems WHERE author = "Edgar Allan Poe"
```

### Operations
Dataview supports functions for calculations: "date operations, length counting, field transformations"—all computed within queries without modifying source files.

## Supported Query Capabilities
- Filtering and aggregation
- Sorting and grouping
- Dynamic calculations
- Multiple output formats (tables, lists, calendars)
- Link collection and analysis

## Documentation Structure
The plugin offers guides for metadata annotation, query language reference, JavaScript API documentation, and practical examples across hundreds of use cases.

# Vault Management in Obsidian

## Vault Creation

Obsidian supports two approaches for creating vaults:

1. **New vault**: Users can create a fresh vault by naming it and selecting a file system location through the Vault Switcher interface.

2. **From existing folder**: Users may convert an existing directory into a vault by selecting "Open folder as vault" in the Vault Manager.

## Folder Structure

A vault is fundamentally "a folder on your file system which contains your notes, attachments, and the configuration folder with Obsidian-specific settings." The vault's name and underlying folder name are identical—renaming one automatically renames the other.

## .obsidian Configuration Folder

The `.obsidian` folder stores all Obsidian-specific settings at the vault's root level. Key points:

- **Hidden by default**: Most operating systems conceal folders beginning with a period
- **Transferable**: Users can copy the `.obsidian` folder between vaults to replicate settings across different vaults
- **Settings management**: Access occurs through Settings → Community Plugins, where users can manage restricted mode and other configurations

The documentation notes that "You may need to restart Obsidian to apply the changes" when transferring configuration folders between vaults.

# Command Palette in Obsidian

## Overview
The Command Palette is a core plugin that enables users to execute commands via keyboard without navigating menus. It provides access to all available commands and their associated keyboard shortcuts.

## Basic Usage
To invoke the Command Palette, press `Ctrl+P` (Windows/Linux) or `Cmd+P` (macOS). Users can also access it through the Ribbon interface. After opening, type the command name, use arrow keys to navigate results, and press Enter to execute.

## Key Features

**Fuzzy Matching:** The search function supports fuzzy matching, meaning you don't need exact command names. For instance, searching "scf" will locate the Save current file command, matching partial letters across the name.

**Recent Commands:** Starting in version 1.8.3, frequently used commands appear prioritized at the top of the palette, though the fuzzy matching algorithm still applies. When filtering begins, shorter command names receive priority over recency.

## Pinned Commands
For frequently accessed commands, users can pin them to the top of the Command Palette for quick access without typing. This feature is configured through Settings > Command palette (under Plugin options). Alternatively, assigning custom hotkeys provides another method for rapid command execution.

# Obsidian Editing Shortcuts Summary

Obsidian provides default keyboard shortcuts for text navigation and editing that vary by operating system. These shortcuts "cannot be customized within Obsidian" but customizable commands are available through the Hotkeys feature.

## Key Shortcut Categories

**Common Actions** include copy, cut, paste, undo, and redo operations across both platforms (Ctrl/Cmd variants).

**Text Editing** covers insertion and deletion tasks like creating new lines and removing characters or words. Windows/Linux uses `Ctrl+Shift+K` to delete entire lines, while macOS uses the same combination.

**Text Navigation** enables cursor movement by character, word, line, page, and document. Windows/Linux relies on Ctrl+arrow keys for word jumping, whereas macOS uses Option+arrow keys for equivalent functionality.

**Text Selection** allows users to extend selections incrementally using Shift combinations paired with navigation shortcuts.

**macOS-Specific Features** include dedicated text formatting shortcuts: `Cmd+B` for bold and `Cmd+I` for italic text—unavailable in the Windows/Linux documentation provided.

The platform differences reflect each operating system's standard conventions, with macOS using Command and Option keys versus Windows/Linux using Control and Ctrl modifiers.

# Slash Commands in Obsidian

**What it is:**
Slash commands is a core plugin enabling users to execute commands by typing a forward slash (`/`) at the line start or after blank space.

**How to use it:**
1. Type `/` in the editor
2. Enter your desired command name to search available options
3. Use arrow keys to navigate results
4. Press Enter to execute

You can exit the search with `Esc` or `Space` without running anything.

**Key feature:**
The plugin supports fuzzy matching, similar to the Command palette. This allows you to find commands without knowing exact names—for instance, typing "scf" locates the "Save current file" command.

# Slides Plugin Overview

The Slides plugin is a core feature that transforms markdown notes into presentations.

## Starting a Presentation

You can initiate presentations through two methods:

1. **File menu**: Right-click a note's tab and select "Start presentation"
2. **Command palette**: Open with `Ctrl+P` (or `Cmd+P` on Mac), search for "Start presentation," and press Enter

## Navigation Controls

Movement through slides uses several options:
- Click the directional arrows in the bottom-right corner
- Press keyboard arrow keys
- Press Spacebar to advance to the next slide
- Press `Escape` or click the X button to exit the presentation

## Creating Slides

"To separate slides, enter `---` at the start of a line surrounded by newlines."

The plugin accepts any valid markdown file. Slides support standard formatting including italicized and bold text using regular markdown syntax.

## Example Structure

A basic presentation uses horizontal dividers (`---`) to mark slide boundaries, allowing you to organize content logically across multiple slides within a single markdown document.

# Aliases in Obsidian: Complete Information

## Definition and Purpose
Aliases serve as alternative names for notes, enabling reference through different titles. They're useful for acronyms, nicknames, and multilingual references.

## How to Define Aliases

Add aliases to a note's YAML frontmatter as a list:
```
---
aliases:
  - Doggo
  - Woofer
  - Yapper
---
```

## Linking Behavior

When linking via alias, Obsidian converts the reference into a pipe-format link showing the note's actual title and the alias as display text. For example: `[[Artificial Intelligence|AI]]` rather than simply `[[AI]]`. This design ensures compatibility with other applications supporting Wikilink format.

## Finding Unlinked References

The Backlinks feature identifies unlinked mentions of aliases throughout your vault. Converting these unlinked mentions into links automatically applies the alias as display text.

## Key Distinction

Aliases differ from changing link display text, which modifies appearance only for that specific link instance, whereas aliases create reusable alternative names across the entire vault.

# Folding Features Overview

## Primary Folding Functionality

The application supports collapsing sections to improve note navigation. Users can fold headings and indented lists by hovering over content and selecting the arrow control on the left side.

## Key Features

**Manual Folding:**
- "You can fold headings and indented lists by hovering the mouse cursor over the section you want to fold"
- Folded sections display an arrow indicator at all times

**Configuration:**
Users can customize folding behavior through Settings → Editor, where they can disable "Fold indent" or "Fold heading" options independently.

**Bulk Operations:**
Two commands in the Command Palette manage multiple sections simultaneously:
- "Fold all headings and lists" collapses every section
- "Unfold all headings and lists" expands every section

**Keyboard-Based Folding:**
For users preferring keyboard controls, hotkeys can be assigned to:
- **Fold less** — expands at the cursor position
- **Fold more** — collapses the section containing the cursor

## Use Cases

Folding enhances workflow by creating outlines and allowing users to concentrate on specific content areas within large documents.

To avoid repeatedly uploading the same large file, use Claude's Files API (in Beta since April 14, 2025) to store it once and reference it by file_id thereafter. Anthropic launched the Files API in public beta, enabling you to upload files and reference them in the Messages API and code execution tool.

## MCP (Model Context Protocol) Support

Anthropic open-sourced the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a new standard for connecting AI assistants to the systems where data lives, including content repositories, business tools, and development environments. Its aim is to help frontier models produce better, more relevant responses.

### Key MCP Features
- The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between their data sources and AI-powered tools. The 2025 updates to Claude and MCP focus on enterprise readiness and performance improvements. Anthropic has expanded the MCP ecosystem with enhanced support for remote server deployments, letting organizations host MCP services in cloud environments while maintaining security and compliance requirements. The introduction of streamable HTTP transport alongside traditional Server-Sent Events provides better reliability and performance for enterprise deployments.

The Model Context Protocol specification is evolving rapidly. Current version is 2025-03-26. Breaking changes happen as the spec matures. Keep this in mind when building systems that depend on MCP.

(Note: the legacy `.cursorrules` file still works but is no longer recommended.) Cursor has transitioned to a newer rules system:

That said, a `.cursorrules` file tells Cursor the house rules for your project, and it remains functional for those who haven't migrated.

### MCP (Model Context Protocol) Support

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that standardizes how applications provide context and tools to LLMs. Think of MCP as a plugin system for Cursor — it allows you to extend the Agent's capabilities by connecting it to various data sources and tools through standardized interfaces.

**History & Adoption:**

Someone could push a modified `.cursor/mcp.json` to a shared repository, swapping a legitimate command for a malicious one. This was fixed in Cursor 1.3, July 2025.

Best practices include: keep Cursor current, disable auto-run, restrict credentials, pin package versions, and audit third-party servers before adding them.

When MCP integrations + comprehensive rule sets + carefully fed context/prompts come together, next-gen models will be able to handle tasks exceeding 30 minutes.

## AGENTS.md and the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)

### What is AGENTS.md?

Released by OpenAI in August 2025, AGENTS.md is a simple, universal standard that gives AI coding agents a consistent source of project-specific guidance needed to operate reliably across different repositories and toolchains. Essentially, AGENTS.md began as a practical solution to a familiar problem — Codex needed a predictable way to find project-specific instructions, such as coding conventions, build steps, and testing requirements, to help agents work safely and effectively in a codebase.

The format is described as a lightweight Markdown file designed to live alongside README.md. It offers a simple, interoperable standard that gives AI coding agents a consistent source of project-specific guidance needed to operate reliably across different repositories and toolchains. This markdown-based convention makes agent behavior far more predictable across diverse repositories and build systems.

### Adoption

Since its release in August 2025, AGENTS.md has been adopted by more than 60,000 open-source projects and agent frameworks including Amp, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Factory, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Jules and VS Code among others — reflecting growing alignment around shared, vendor-neutral conventions as agents enter production.

### The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)

On December 9, 2025, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), and founding contributions of three leading projects driving innovation in open source AI: Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP), Block's goose, and OpenAI's AGENTS.md.

The AAIF provides a neutral, open foundation to ensure agentic AI evolves transparently and collaboratively.

### Three Founding Projects

1. **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** – from Anthropic: An open protocol that enables seamless integration between AI systems and external data sources, providing a standardized way for AI agents to access context.

2. **goose** – from Block: Released in early 2025, goose is an open source, local-first AI agent framework that combines language models, extensible tools, and standardized MCP-based integration to provide a structured, reliable, and trusted environment for building and executing agentic workflows.

3. **AGENTS.md** – from OpenAI: An open format for guiding coding agents. It is used by more than 20,000 open source projects and serves as a README for agents: a dedicated, predictable place to provide the context and instructions to help AI coding agents work on projects.

### Membership

Platinum members include Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI. Gold members include Adyen, Arcade.dev, Cisco, Datadog, Docker, Ericsson, IBM, JetBrains, Okta, Oracle, Runlayer, Salesforce, SAP, Shopify, Snowflake, Temporal, Tetrate, and Twilio Inc.

### Purpose and Vision

AAIF is not trying to build agents themselves. Its job is narrow and important: maintain the shared infrastructure, protocols, formats, and conventions that allow thousands of agents, frameworks, and tools to work together reliably — including protocols that define how agents connect to tools, APIs, and data; formats that make agent instructions and context portable; and conventions that align behavior across different runtimes and repositories.

The larger vision is more ambitious: If tools like MCP, AGENTS.md, and Goose become standard infrastructure, the agent landscape could shift from closed platforms to an open, mix-and-match software world reminiscent of the interoperable systems that built the modern web.
