Now I have comprehensive data from all the major documentation pages. Here is the complete catalog:

---

## Comprehensive Catalog of Obsidian Features Beyond Plain Markdown

### 1. File Formats Natively Supported

Obsidian natively recognizes and renders the following file types (not just `.md`):

| Category | Extensions |
|----------|-----------|
| **Notes** | `.md` (Markdown) |
| **Databases** | `.base` (Bases) |
| **Visual canvas** | `.canvas` (JSON Canvas format) |
| **Images** | `.avif`, `.bmp`, `.gif`, `.jpeg`, `.jpg`, `.png`, `.svg`, `.webp` |
| **Audio** | `.flac`, `.m4a`, `.mp3`, `.ogg`, `.wav`, `.webm`, `.3gp` |
| **Video** | `.mkv`, `.mov`, `.mp4`, `.ogv`, `.webm` |
| **Documents** | `.pdf` |

All media files can be embedded inline in notes. Community plugins can extend this list further.

---

### 2. Embed Syntax

Embeds use `!` before an internal link:

```markdown
# Embed an entire note
![[Note Name]]

# Embed a specific heading from a note
![[Note Name#Heading]]

# Embed a specific block
![[Note Name#^block-id]]

# Embed an image
![[image.jpg]]

# Embed image with custom dimensions (width x height)
![[image.jpg|640x480]]

# Embed image with width only (proportional scaling)
![[image.jpg|300]]

# External image with width
![250](https://example.com/image.jpg)

# Embed audio
![[recording.mp3]]

# Embed PDF
![[document.pdf]]

# Embed PDF at a specific page
![[document.pdf#page=3]]

# Embed PDF with custom height
![[document.pdf#height=400]]

# Embed a list (requires block ID on the list)
![[Note Name#^my-list-id]]
```

Block IDs are added by placing `^block-id` at the end of any block (paragraph, list, etc.):

```markdown
This is a paragraph I want to reference. ^my-block-id

- list item 1
- list item 2
^my-list-id
```

---

### 3. Callouts / Admonitions

Syntax uses blockquote with a type identifier:

```markdown
> [!note] Optional Title
> Content here
```

**All built-in callout types:**

| Type | Aliases |
|------|---------|
| `note` | -- |
| `abstract` | `summary`, `tldr` |
| `info` | -- |
| `todo` | -- |
| `tip` | `hint`, `important` |
| `success` | `check`, `done` |
| `question` | `help`, `faq` |
| `warning` | `caution`, `attention` |
| `failure` | `fail`, `missing` |
| `danger` | `error` |
| `bug` | -- |
| `example` | -- |
| `quote` | `cite` |

**Foldable callouts** (collapsed by default with `-`, expanded by default with `+`):

```markdown
> [!warning]- Click to expand
> Hidden content

> [!tip]+ Click to collapse
> Visible by default content
```

**Nested callouts:**

```markdown
> [!question] Outer
> > [!todo] Middle
> > > [!example] Inner
```

**Custom callout types** via CSS:

```css
.callout[data-callout="custom-name"] {
    --callout-color: 0, 0, 0;
    --callout-icon: lucide-icon-name;
}
```

---

### 4. Query Languages

#### Bases (Core Plugin, `.base` files)

Obsidian's built-in database/query system. Creates structured views of vault notes using their properties.

**Views:** Table, List, Cards (gallery with images), Map (interactive pins)

**Capabilities:** Filtering, sorting, grouping, formulas

**Formula operators:**
- Arithmetic: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`
- Comparison: `>`, `<`, `==`, `!=`
- Boolean: `!`, `&&`, `||`

**Formula functions:**
- Global: `if()`, `now()`, `date()`, `link()`, `max()`, `min()`
- String: `contains()`, `replace()`, `split()`, `lower()`, `title()`
- Number: `round()`, `ceil()`, `floor()`, `abs()`, `toFixed()`
- Date: `format()`, `relative()`, `date()`, `time()`
- List: `filter()`, `map()`, `sort()`, `join()`, `unique()`, `.length`

**Property references:** `file.name`, `file.size`, `file.mtime`, plus any frontmatter property

**Tag function:** `hasTag()` recognizes both parent and nested tags

#### Dataview (Community Plugin)

The most popular query plugin. Provides three query modes:

1. **DQL (Dataview Query Language):**
   ```dataview
   TABLE author, date, rating
   FROM #books
   WHERE rating >= 4
   SORT date DESC
   ```
   Query types: `LIST`, `TABLE`, `TASK`, `CALENDAR`
   Data commands: `FROM`, `WHERE`, `SORT`, `GROUP BY`, `FLATTEN`, `LIMIT`

2. **Inline queries:** `` `= this.file.name` `` for single-value displays

3. **DataviewJS:** Full JavaScript access to the Dataview API in `dataviewjs` code blocks

**Metadata sources:** YAML frontmatter, inline fields `[key:: value]`, implicit file metadata (tags, tasks, creation date, etc.)

---

### 5. Properties / Frontmatter

YAML frontmatter between `---` delimiters at the file start:

```yaml
---
title: My Note
date: 2026-03-05
status: active
tags: [decision, architecture]
aliases: [Alt Name, Another Name]
cssclasses: [wide-page, custom-theme]
publish: true
permalink: custom-url-slug
description: Preview text for link hover
image: path/to/preview.png
cover: path/to/cover.jpg
---
```

**Supported property types:**
- **Text** -- single-line string (URLs and internal links must be quoted: `"[[link]]"`)
- **List** -- YAML array with `-` items
- **Number** -- integers and decimals
- **Checkbox** -- `true`/`false`
- **Date** -- ISO format `YYYY-MM-DD`
- **Date & time** -- ISO format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss`
- **Tags** -- special list type for `tags` property only

**Natively understood properties:**

| Property | Type | Purpose |
|----------|------|---------|
| `tags` | List | Note categorization, searchable with `tag:` operator |
| `aliases` | List | Alternative names for linking (shows in autocomplete) |
| `cssclasses` | List | Apply CSS snippet classes to the note |
| `publish` | Boolean | Whether to include in Obsidian Publish |
| `permalink` | Text | Custom URL slug for Publish |
| `description` | Text | Preview/hover text for links |
| `image` / `cover` | Text | Social media preview image |

**Limitations:** No nested properties. No markdown rendering inside property values. JSON frontmatter auto-converts to YAML.

---

### 6. Templates

#### Core Templates Plugin

Template variables inserted at cursor position:

| Variable | Output | Custom format |
|----------|--------|---------------|
| `{{title}}` | Active note's title | -- |
| `{{date}}` | Today's date | `{{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}` |
| `{{time}}` | Current time | `{{time:HH:mm}}` |

Format uses Moment.js tokens. Templates are plain notes stored in a designated folder.

#### Templater (Community Plugin)

Far more powerful, with nine function modules:

| Module | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `tp.app` | Application-level ops | -- |
| `tp.config` | Configuration access | -- |
| `tp.date` | Date manipulation | `<% tp.date.now("YYYY-MM-DD") %>` |
| `tp.file` | File metadata | `<% tp.file.title %>`, `<% tp.file.creation_date() %>` |
| `tp.frontmatter` | YAML frontmatter access | `<% tp.frontmatter.status %>` |
| `tp.hooks` | Event triggers | -- |
| `tp.obsidian` | Native API access | -- |
| `tp.system` | System command execution | `<% tp.system.clipboard() %>` |
| `tp.web` | Web fetching | `<% tp.web.daily_quote() %>` |

Syntax: `<% tp.module.function() %>`. Supports JavaScript execution within templates, user-defined functions, and dynamic commands.

---

### 7. Mermaid Diagrams

Yes, Obsidian natively renders Mermaid diagrams in fenced code blocks:

````markdown
```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Start] --> B{Decision}
    B -->|Yes| C[Action 1]
    B -->|No| D[Action 2]
    C --> E[End]
    D --> E
```
````

**Obsidian-specific feature:** Apply `internal-link` class to make diagram nodes clickable vault links:

````markdown
```mermaid
graph TD
    Biology --> Chemistry
    class Biology,Chemistry internal-link;
```
````

For note names with special characters, use double quotes: `class "Special Note" internal-link;`

---

## Comprehensive Catalog of Obsidian Features Beyond Plain Markdown

### 1. File Formats Natively Supported

Obsidian natively recognizes and renders the following file types (not just `.md`):

| Category | Extensions |
|----------|-----------|
| **Notes** | `.md` (Markdown) |
| **Databases** | `.base` (Bases) |
| **Visual canvas** | `.canvas` (JSON Canvas format) |
| **Images** | `.avif`, `.bmp`, `.gif`, `.jpeg`, `.jpg`, `.png`, `.svg`, `.webp` |
| **Audio** | `.flac`, `.m4a`, `.mp3`, `.ogg`, `.wav`, `.webm`, `.3gp` |
| **Video** | `.mkv`, `.mov`, `.mp4`, `.ogv`, `.webm` |
| **Documents** | `.pdf` |

All media files can be embedded inline in notes. Community plugins can extend this list further.

---

### 2. Embed Syntax

Embeds use `!` before an internal link:

```markdown
# Embed an entire note
![[Note Name]]

# Embed a specific heading from a note
![[Note Name#Heading]]

# Embed a specific block
![[Note Name#^block-id]]

# Embed an image
![[image.jpg]]

# Embed image with custom dimensions (width x height)
![[image.jpg|640x480]]

# Embed image with width only (proportional scaling)
![[image.jpg|300]]

# External image with width
![250](https://example.com/image.jpg)

# Embed audio
![[recording.mp3]]

# Embed PDF
![[document.pdf]]

# Embed PDF at a specific page
![[document.pdf#page=3]]

# Embed PDF with custom height
![[document.pdf#height=400]]

# Embed a list (requires block ID on the list)
![[Note Name#^my-list-id]]
```

Block IDs are added by placing `^block-id` at the end of any block (paragraph, list, etc.):

```markdown
This is a paragraph I want to reference. ^my-block-id

- list item 1
- list item 2
^my-list-id
```

---

### 3. Callouts / Admonitions

Syntax uses blockquote with a type identifier:

```markdown
> [!note] Optional Title
> Content here
```

**All built-in callout types:**

| Type | Aliases |
|------|---------|
| `note` | -- |
| `abstract` | `summary`, `tldr` |
| `info` | -- |
| `todo` | -- |
| `tip` | `hint`, `important` |
| `success` | `check`, `done` |
| `question` | `help`, `faq` |
| `warning` | `caution`, `attention` |
| `failure` | `fail`, `missing` |
| `danger` | `error` |
| `bug` | -- |
| `example` | -- |
| `quote` | `cite` |

**Foldable callouts** (collapsed by default with `-`, expanded by default with `+`):

```markdown
> [!warning]- Click to expand
> Hidden content

> [!tip]+ Click to collapse
> Visible by default content
```

**Nested callouts:**

```markdown
> [!question] Outer
> > [!todo] Middle
> > > [!example] Inner
```

**Custom callout types** via CSS:

```css
.callout[data-callout="custom-name"] {
    --callout-color: 0, 0, 0;
    --callout-icon: lucide-icon-name;
}
```

### 4. Query Languages

#### Bases (Core Plugin, `.base` files)

Obsidian's built-in database/query system. Creates structured views of vault notes using their properties.

**Views:** Table, List, Cards (gallery with images), Map (interactive pins)

**Capabilities:** Filtering, sorting, grouping, formulas

**Formula operators:**
- Arithmetic: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`
- Comparison: `>`, `<`, `==`, `!=`
- Boolean: `!`, `&&`, `||`

**Formula functions:**
- Global: `if()`, `now()`, `date()`, `link()`, `max()`, `min()`
- String: `contains()`, `replace()`, `split()`, `lower()`, `title()`
- Number: `round()`, `ceil()`, `floor()`, `abs()`, `toFixed()`
- Date: `format()`, `relative()`, `date()`, `time()`
- List: `filter()`, `map()`, `sort()`, `join()`, `unique()`, `.length`

**Property references:** `file.name`, `file.size`, `file.mtime`, plus any frontmatter property

**Tag function:** `hasTag()` recognizes both parent and nested tags

The most popular query plugin. Provides three query modes:

1. **DQL (Dataview Query Language):**

   FROM #books
   WHERE rating >= 4
   SORT date DESC
   ```

   Data commands: `FROM`, `WHERE`, `SORT`, `GROUP BY`, `FLATTEN`, `LIMIT`

2. **Inline queries:** `` `= this.file.name` `` for single-value displays

3. **DataviewJS:** Full JavaScript access to the Dataview API in `dataviewjs` code blocks

**Metadata sources:** YAML frontmatter, inline fields `[key:: value]`, implicit file metadata (tags, tasks, creation date, etc.)

YAML frontmatter between `---` delimiters at the file start:

```yaml
---
title: My Note
date: 2026-03-05
status: active
tags: [decision, architecture]

The core Slides plugin converts any markdown note into a presentation. Slides are separated by `---` on its own line surrounded by blank lines.

Here's a comprehensive overview of the **AGENTS.md file format specification**, based on the latest information from 2025:

## What is AGENTS.md?

AGENTS.md is a simple, open format for guiding coding agents. Think of it as a README for agents. It is a standardized Markdown file that serves as a "README for agents" — a dedicated, predictable location for providing guidance to AI-powered development tools.

AGENTS.md emerged from collaborative efforts across the AI software development ecosystem, including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules from Google, Cursor, and Factory. AGENTS.md is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation.

## File Format & Structure

AGENTS.md uses standard Markdown syntax with no required fields or structure. The format prioritizes flexibility: "just standard Markdown. Use any headings you like; the agent simply parses the text you provide."

AGENTS.md is plain Markdown; headings provide semantic hints.

### Recommended Sections

Hitting six core areas puts you in the top tier: **commands, testing, project structure, code style, git workflow, and boundaries**.

Common section headings include:


- `# Build & Test` — exact commands for compiling and testing
- `# Architecture Overview` — short description of major modules
- `# Security` — auth flows, API keys, sensitive data
- `# Git Workflows` — branching, commit conventions, PR requirements
- `# Conventions & Patterns` — naming, folder layout, code style


### Best Practices for Content

1. **Put commands early:** Put relevant executable commands in an early section: `npm test`, `npm run build`, `pytest -v`. Include flags and options, not just tool names. Your agent will reference these often.

2. **Code examples over explanations:** One real code snippet showing your style beats three paragraphs describing it. Show what good output looks like.

3. **Set clear boundaries:** Tell AI what it should never touch (e.g., secrets, vendor directories, production configs, or specific folders). "Never commit secrets" was the most common helpful constraint.

4. **Be specific about your stack:** Say "React 18 with TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS" not "React project." Include versions and key dependencies.

5. **Describe capabilities, not paths:** Instead of documenting structure, describe capabilities. Give hints about where things might be and the overall shape of the project. File paths change constantly. If your AGENTS.md says "authentication logic lives in src/auth/handlers.ts" and that file gets renamed or moved, the agent will confidently look in the wrong place.

## Hierarchical / Monorepo Support

Place another AGENTS.md inside each package. Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence and every subproject can ship tailored instructions.

For example, at time of writing the main OpenAI repo has 88 AGENTS.md files.

You're not limited to a single AGENTS.md at the root. You can place AGENTS.md files in subdirectories, and they merge with the root level.

### Override Files (OpenAI Codex)

Codex builds an instruction chain when it starts. Discovery follows this precedence order: **Global scope** — in your Codex home directory (defaults to `~/.codex`), Codex reads `AGENTS.override.md` if it exists; otherwise, it reads `AGENTS.md`. Codex uses only the first non-empty file at this level. **Project scope** — starting at the project root (typically the Git root), Codex walks down to your current working directory. In each directory along the path, it checks for `AGENTS.override.md`, then `AGENTS.md`, then any fallback names.

## Example Sections in Practice

**Per-file commands** (to avoid slow full-project builds):

One thing that annoys me about most agents is that they try to run full project-wide build commands way too often. If you work on a non-trivial codebase, those commands can take minutes. Agents know the file paths they just edited, and most key commands can be run on a per-file basis. If you specify exactly the command formats to do that, you'll get much faster feedback.

**Test-first mode:**

On trickier tasks you may want the agent to create or update tests first, then code until green. You can nudge it with a short section.

**Design system integration:**

If your design system lives in a separate package, the agent will guess how to use it. Index your system so the agent learns component APIs, tokens, and examples. Then reference that output here.

## Tool Compatibility

AGENTS.md is supported by a wide and growing ecosystem:

Your AGENTS.md file is compatible with a growing ecosystem of AI coding agents and tools. Rather than introducing another proprietary file format, AGENTS.md uses a standard that works across the entire AI development ecosystem.

AGENTS.md is a small markdown file at the root of your repo that tells AI tools how your project works. Similar to tool-specific formats like `.cursorrules`, `.builderrules`, etc., AGENTS.md is a growing standard for putting rules that should apply to any agents in one place.

## Key Takeaway

The best agents are given a clear persona and, most importantly, a detailed operating manual. This manual must include executable commands, concrete code examples for styling, explicit boundaries, and specifics about your tech stack. Add detail when your agent makes mistakes. The best agent files grow through iteration, not upfront planning.

Here's a comprehensive overview of **Claude.ai Projects** — covering knowledge bases, custom instructions, system prompts, and files:

## What Are Claude Projects?

Claude Projects creates specialized workspaces within Claude. Each Project maintains its own custom instructions, document library, and conversation history. According to Anthropic's documentation, Projects function as "self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases."

Claude Projects is a feature available to Claude Pro, Team, and Enterprise subscribers that allows you to create dedicated workspaces for specific tasks or topics.

## Knowledge Base

Each project maintains its dedicated knowledge base — a document repository where you can upload relevant files, brand guidelines, and reference materials.

- **Supported file formats:** Projects accept multiple file formats: PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT, HTML, ODT, RTF, and EPUB.
- **File size & limits:** Individual files can reach 30MB, and users can upload unlimited files provided the total content remains within the context window.
- **Context window:** Each Project supports a 200,000-token context window, roughly equivalent to 500 pages of content.
- Additionally, Claude-generated content (code, analysis, drafts) can be added directly to the Project's knowledge base for future reference.

## Custom Instructions (System Prompt)

Custom instructions act as a persistent system prompt that applies to every conversation within the project.

In the "Project instructions" field, you define how Claude should behave within the workspace. Write clear instructions as if you're briefing an assistant. For example, you might specify tone, format, coding style, or analytical approaches.

Every chat in a project will automatically have access to your knowledge base and follow your custom instructions.

## How Projects Differ from Regular Chats

Standard Claude conversations are isolated—each new chat starts fresh with no memory of previous interactions. Projects maintain persistent context across all chats within that workspace, plus they have access to your uploaded knowledge base and follow your custom instructions automatically.

## Project Memory & Knowledge Base Files

A system prompt is your starting point — your best guess before you start working together. Project memory is what you learn through the work. The instructions you couldn't have written upfront because you didn't know you needed them yet.

You can ask Claude to create the memory for you, generate it as a Markdown file, and upload it to your project knowledge base.

Knowledge base files should be comprehensive documentation: detailed examples, edge cases, before/after comparisons, and decision trees.

1. Open Claude and locate "Projects" in the left sidebar. Click "Create Project" or "New Project." Choose a descriptive name — avoid generic labels like "Project 1." Use specific identifiers such as "Q4 Marketing Campaign" or "Python Codebase Documentation."
2. Go to the "Project Knowledge" section. Upload files like PDFs, DOCs, or text files.
3. Write detailed custom instructions. This step determines Project effectiveness. Avoid vague directives like "be helpful." Instead, provide specific guidance on tone, format, and behavior.

## API / SDK System Prompt Customization

For developers using the Claude Agent SDK, you can customize Claude's behavior by modifying system prompts using three approaches — output styles, systemPrompt with append, and custom system prompts. You can use the Claude Code preset with an append property to add your custom instructions while preserving all built-in functionality.

- **Research:** Researchers upload collections of papers, survey data, and interview transcripts. Instructions enforce academic citation standards and analytical rigor. Claude can then synthesize findings, identify contradictions, and detect patterns across the entire research corpus.

- **Content & Marketing:** Using Claude Project for content tasks helps ensure consistency in documentation style and format across all articles, using existing support documentation and product docs as resources.

This feature is **paid-only** — Claude Free users do not have access to Projects. This is a paid-tier-only feature.

## Claude.ai MCP Server Integration & Remote Tools Connectors

### What Are MCP Connectors?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard, created by Anthropic, for AI applications to connect to tools and data. Last November (2024), Anthropic launched MCP. Until then, support for MCP was limited to Claude Desktop through local servers. They then introduced Integrations, allowing Claude to work seamlessly with remote MCP servers across the web and desktop apps.

### Launch & Availability

Claude AI Connectors were originally launched on July 14, 2025. As of June 3, 2025, Integrations and Research became available on the Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans. Custom connectors using remote MCP are available on Claude and Claude Desktop for users on free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans. Free users are limited to one custom connector. This feature is currently in beta.

### How Remote MCP Servers Work

Remote MCP servers extend AI applications' capabilities beyond your local environment, providing access to internet-hosted tools, services, and data sources. By connecting to remote MCP servers, you transform AI assistants from helpful tools into informed teammates capable of handling complex, multi-step projects with real-time access to external resources.

Custom Connectors serve as the bridge between Claude and remote MCP servers. They allow you to connect Claude directly to the tools and data sources that matter most to your workflows.

### How to Connect

Open Claude in your browser and navigate to the settings page by clicking on your profile icon and selecting "Settings." Once in settings, locate and click on the "Connectors" section in the sidebar. Click the "Add custom connector" button, enter the remote MCP server URL, follow the authentication prompts provided by the server (which may redirect you to a third-party authentication provider), and Claude will establish a secure connection.

### Supported Transports & Authentication

Claude supports both SSE- and Streamable HTTP-based remote servers, although support for SSE may be deprecated in the coming months. Claude supports both authless and OAuth-based remote servers. Claude supports Dynamic Client Registration (DCR).

### Available Integrations

At launch, users could choose from Integrations for 10 popular services, including Atlassian's Jira and Confluence, Zapier, Cloudflare, Intercom, Asana, Square, Sentry, PayPal, Linear, and Plaid—with more to come.

Claude can now see your Asana tasks, read your Gmail, access your Notion docs, draft messages in Slack, and even create designs in Canva. The Connectors Directory has grown significantly since launch, including Microsoft 365 (Outlook, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams), currently available only on Team and Enterprise plans, requiring a one-time setup by a Microsoft Entra ID Global Administrator.

### 2026 Developments

In early 2026, Anthropic expanded significantly into healthcare, adding connectors to major health data platforms. A Salesforce Integration was confirmed following the January 2026 Slack-Salesforce partnership, with Agentforce 360, Data 360, and Commerce 360 connecting directly to Claude.

### Mobile Support

As of July, Claude for iOS and Android also supports remote MCP servers. Users can use tools, prompts, and resources from remote servers that they've already added via claude.ai, though users cannot add new servers directly from Claude Mobile.

### Cross-Platform Usage

Connectors work across Claude, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and the API (via the MCP Connector). If you've logged into Claude Code with a Claude.ai account, MCP servers you've added in Claude.ai are automatically available in Claude Code.

### Security Considerations

Custom connectors allow you to connect Claude to services that have not been verified by Anthropic, and allow Claude to access and take action in these services. When you add a custom connector, you'll typically go through an OAuth authentication process. This allows Claude to interact with the application on your behalf, without Claude ever seeing your actual password. You can revoke these permissions at any time by disconnecting the connector.

Here's a comprehensive overview of **Gemini CLI's MCP (Model Context Protocol) support and tools integration**:

## Overview

Gemini CLI features extensible MCP (Model Context Protocol) support for custom integrations. The official documentation provides a guide to configuring and using MCP servers with the Gemini CLI, where an MCP server is an application that exposes tools and resources through the Model Context Protocol, allowing it to interact with external systems and data sources. MCP servers act as a bridge between the Gemini model and your local environment or other services like APIs.

## Core Capabilities

Gemini CLI's MCP integration enables three key functions:

1. **Discover tools**: List available tools, their descriptions, and parameters through standardized schema definitions.
2. **Execute tools**: Call specific tools with defined arguments and receive structured responses.
3. **Access resources**: Read data from specific resources that the server exposes (files, API payloads, reports, etc.).

With an MCP server, you can extend the Gemini CLI's capabilities to perform actions beyond its built-in features, such as interacting with databases, APIs, custom scripts, or specialized workflows.

## Configuration

MCP servers are configured in `~/.gemini/settings.json` to extend Gemini CLI with custom tools, supporting integrations like GitHub, Slack, and databases.

The Gemini CLI uses the `mcpServers` configuration in your `settings.json` file to locate and connect to MCP servers. This configuration supports multiple servers with different transport mechanisms. You can configure MCP servers through the top-level `mcpServers` object for specific server definitions, and through the `mcp` object for global settings that control server discovery and execution.

## Rich Content Support

MCP tools are not limited to returning simple text. You can return rich, multi-part content, including text, images, audio, and other binary data in a single tool response, allowing you to build powerful tools that can provide diverse information to the model in a single turn.

## MCP Prompts as Slash Commands

In addition to tools, MCP servers can expose predefined prompts that can be executed as slash commands within the Gemini CLI. This allows you to create shortcuts for common or complex queries that can be easily invoked by name.

## FastMCP Integration (September 2025)

Gemini CLI now seamlessly integrates with FastMCP, Python's leading library for building MCP servers. As of FastMCP v2.12.3, you can install local STDIO transport MCP servers built with FastMCP using the `fastmcp install gemini-cli` command. It automatically handles the configuration, dependency management, and calls Gemini CLI's built-in MCP management system (`gemini mcp add`).

## Google's Managed MCP Servers (December 2025)

Google announced the release of fully-managed, remote MCP servers. Google's existing API infrastructure is now enhanced to support MCP, providing a unified layer across all Google and Google Cloud services. Developers can now simply point their AI agents or standard MCP clients like Gemini CLI to a globally-consistent and enterprise-ready endpoint.

## Installation

To get started: install Gemini CLI with `npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@latest`, and for Python-based MCP servers, install FastMCP v2.12.3 or later.

## Architecture Details

The system sanitizes and validates tool schemas for compatibility with the Gemini API, registers tools in the global tool registry with conflict resolution, and fetches and registers resources if the server exposes any. Some MCP servers expose contextual "resources" in addition to the tools and prompts, and Gemini CLI discovers these automatically and gives you the possibility to reference them in the chat.

## Building MCP Servers

You can build MCP servers in multiple languages:
- MCP is an open-source protocol that standardizes how LLMs like Gemini communicate with external tools and services, acting as a bridge allowing the AI to access real-world information. By building an MCP server, you are creating a custom plugin that Gemini CLI can discover and use, effectively teaching it new skills.
- Google provides codelabs for building MCP servers in **Go** and **Python** (via FastMCP).

Gemini CLI is fully open source (Apache 2.0), and the community is encouraged to share MCP servers and extensions.

Here's a comprehensive overview of how Gemini CLI's **GEMINI.md** file hierarchy works:

## GEMINI.md File Hierarchy in Gemini CLI

Instead of repeating instructions in every prompt, you can define them once in a context file. The CLI uses a hierarchical system to source context. It loads various context files from several locations, concatenates the contents of all found files, and sends them to the model with every prompt.

### Three Hierarchy Levels

The hierarchical loading order creates a cascade of instructions across three main levels:

1. **Global Context**
   - A file located at `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` provides user-wide rules that apply to all projects (e.g., "Always use TypeScript and Jest for testing").
   - The file at `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` is always read first.
   - Because `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` (global memory) is loaded for all sessions, you could put general preferences or information there. For example, "The user's name is Alice. Speak politely and avoid slang." Just be aware that global memory applies to all projects, so don't clutter it with project-specific info.

2. **Project/Ancestor Context (Upward Traversal)**
   - Gemini CLI searches from the current working directory upwards, loading any GEMINI.md files it finds until it reaches the project root.
   - Gemini reads from the current working directory, up to the project root. The GEMINI.md files are read from the topmost folder down to the current folder.
   - Project root is a folder with a `.git` folder. When it finds the root of the git repo it stops scanning upwards. In the case there isn't any git repo, then it scans all the way up to the user Home directory.

3. **Sub-directory Context (Downward Traversal)**
   - Gemini CLI also scans subdirectories below the current working directory, allowing for highly specific instructions for individual components or modules.
   - Next, Gemini CLI does a downward scan, recursively through all the subdirectories of the current folder and picks up the GEMINI.md files from there.

### Precedence

The CLI implements a sophisticated hierarchical memory system by loading context files from several locations. Content from files lower in this list (more specific) typically overrides or supplements content from files higher up (more general). The CLI combines GEMINI.md files from multiple locations. More specific files override general ones.

### Dynamic Context Loading

When a tool accesses a file or directory, the CLI automatically scans for GEMINI.md files in that directory and its ancestors up to a trusted root. This lets the model discover highly specific instructions for particular components only when they are needed.

### Managing Memory

You can interact with loaded context files using `/memory` commands:

- `/memory show`: Displays the full, concatenated content of the current hierarchical memory.
- `/memory refresh`: Forces a re-scan and reload of all GEMINI.md files from all configured locations.
- `/memory add <text>`: Appends your text to your global `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` file. This lets you add persistent memories on the fly.

### Modularizing with Imports

You can organize GEMINI.md files by importing other Markdown files with the `@file.md` syntax. This only supports `.md` files.

### Quick Initialization

Use `/init` to generate a starting GEMINI.md file for your project.

Here's a comprehensive overview of **Windsurf IDE's MCP (Model Context Protocol) support and configuration**:

## What is MCP in Windsurf?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI agents connect to external tools, data sources, and services through a unified interface. Instead of building custom integrations for every tool, MCP gives AI assistants like Windsurf's Cascade agent a single protocol for talking to databases, file storage, APIs, and more.

## Windsurf's MCP Integration Timeline

Windsurf added MCP support to its Cascade agent in 2025, making it one of the first AI-native code editors to adopt the protocol alongside Cursor and VS Code with GitHub Copilot. The integration means Cascade can read from your database, manage files in cloud storage, pull GitHub issues, or interact with any MCP-compatible service, all without leaving your editor.

## How It Works

MCP was designed to standardize the way AI models connect to various data sources, allowing for consistent access and collaboration among digital tools—similar to how a USB-C port supports a variety of devices.

For developers, this changes how you work with AI in your IDE. Instead of copying data between tools and pasting context into chat windows, you connect your tools once and let Cascade pull the context it needs on its own.

## Configuration

You can integrate MCP servers with Cascade to access custom tools like GitHub, databases, and APIs. Windsurf supports configuring stdio, HTTP, and SSE transports with admin controls for Teams.

You can use the MCP Marketplace for one-click installs, or manually edit the `mcp_config.json` file with the server configuration.

## Supported MCP Servers & Use Cases

MCP servers are bridges between Windsurf and external services. They give Windsurf's agents context beyond your codebase—databases, APIs, cloud infrastructure, and more. Key examples include:

- **CloudOps**: AWS and Heroku MCP servers give Windsurf insight into how the application is deployed and configured in the cloud. Additionally, access to logs and environment-specific behavior can help Windsurf improve reliability.
- **GitHub**: Agents can read pull requests, inspect issues, and understand commit history. This repository content does not live in the codebase, but influences how the code should change.
- **Stripe**: Visibility into billing flows, customers, subscriptions, invoices, and webhooks. Agents can debug and reason about how the billing logic interacts with the codebase.
- **Swagger**: When agents are able to read the API specs, they can build to existing endpoints, and parse the results based on actual responses from the API.

## Tool Limits

Note that each MCP provides a number of tools to Windsurf, and Windsurf places a cap of 100 tools that can be active. This might mean enabling and disabling MCPs during different phases of coding.

## MCP as an Industry Standard (2025–2026)

In December 2025, Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, and JetBrains IDEs are all MCP clients. The November 2025 spec update addressed the big ones—async operations, statelessness by default, server identity verification, and official extensions for auth. It's not perfect, but it's dramatically more secure than the early version.

## Key Resources

- **Official Windsurf MCP Docs**: [docs.windsurf.com/windsurf/cascade/mcp](https://docs.windsurf.com/windsurf/cascade/mcp)
- **Windsurf University Tutorial**: [windsurf.com/university/tutorials/configuring-first-mcp-server](https://windsurf.com/university/tutorials/configuring-first-mcp-server)

Here's a summary of what I found regarding Gemini CLI, AGENTS.md support, fallback compatibility, and CLAUDE.md:

## AGENTS.md as a Unified Standard

AGENTS.md is a collaborative effort first started by the folks at Sourcegraph, and which now includes big-name supporters including OpenAI and Google. AGENTS.md is a lightweight, Markdown-based standard that serves as a common instruction file for AI coding agents. Instead of scattering the same instructions across multiple tool-specific files, projects can maintain one AGENTS.md with setup commands, build steps, code conventions, and testing workflows.

## The Fragmentation Problem

Different AI coding platforms have created their own ways to store instructions (e.g., claude.md for Claude Code and gemini.md for Gemini CLI) which fragments guidance across multiple files. The same setup steps and style rules get duplicated in different formats, and the moment your project changes, those files drift out of sync.

Right now, users working in teams that use more than one agentic coding tool have to setup: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Cursor rules, etc. Codex already changed from codex.md to AGENTS.md.

## Fallback Compatibility via Symlinks

Those wishing to transition to AGENTS.md simply have to rename their existing agent instruction file (be it CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md) as AGENTS.md and create a symlink for backward compatibility: `mv CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md && ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md`. With this in place, new tools will read AGENTS.md, while older ones that still expect the old filename will keep working.

## Claude Code's Absence from AGENTS.md Support

There is one glaring absence — Claude Code. Anthropic's Claude Code repository has been inundated with requests to support AGENTS.md, and it's perhaps only a matter of time before it joins its rivals.

Another user suggested Anthropic could adopt a dual-file approach, defaulting to CLAUDE.md when it's present but falling back to AGENTS.md if it isn't. This ensures Claude Code retains its tailored features, while still working out-of-the-box on the thousands of repos that already use the open standard.

## Gemini CLI's Support and Configuration

Supporting AGENTS.md as a standard aligns perfectly with the Agent Rules initiative. This draws from proven standards like SemVer and EditorConfig, allowing developers to define rules once and reuse them across tools like Gemini, Claude, Codex, and Aider. Gemini CLI already supports configuring the context file (e.g., via settings.json as noted in the docs), so enabling AGENTS.md could be as simple as setting it as the default or a recommended option.

## Community Workarounds

One developer built a small tool that checks for the presence of CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md and .cursorrules in a folder, identifies the most recent one, and then creates hardlinks from the other 3 to that one. "It's ridiculous" they noted, also mentioning a small tool that creates hardlinks between various JSON files that all have mcpServer definitions.

## GEMINI.md Hierarchy in Gemini CLI

Gemini CLI uses GEMINI.md which plays a very important role. However, the best thing about Gemini CLI is that it is Open Source. This means there is no suspense on how the CLI behaves — you can actually see the code, understand the logic, and structure your instructions accordingly.

Gemini CLI also follows the hierarchy of GEMINI.md files. It goes up the folder tree and picks up any GEMINI.md file along the way and adds that context to the instructions too.

In summary, the ecosystem is moving toward AGENTS.md as a unified standard, with Gemini CLI and Codex already supporting it. The recommended fallback compatibility approach involves renaming your tool-specific file (CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md) to AGENTS.md and creating a symlink back to the original filename. Claude Code remains the notable holdout as of the latest reports, though community pressure continues to mount for Anthropic to adopt the standard.

Here's a comprehensive overview of the **Cursor Rules `.cursor` directory and `rules.mdc` format structure**:

## Directory Structure

All rule files must be placed in the `.cursor/rules/` directory at the root of your project. This specific location ensures Cursor can find and apply your rules automatically.

The typical directory layout looks like this:

`.cursor/` contains a `rules/` subdirectory with files like `base.mdc` (always applied), `frontend.mdc` (applied to frontend files), `api.mdc` (applied to API files), and `personal.mdc` (local overrides, gitignored).

## Naming Conventions

Follow the naming convention: use kebab-case for filenames, always use the `.mdc` extension, and make names descriptive of the rule's purpose.

## `.mdc` File Format

Cursor rules are Markdown files that inject persistent context into every AI request Cursor makes. Think of them as a permanent system prompt that runs before every conversation, every autocomplete suggestion, and every code generation.

Each `.mdc` file has a YAML frontmatter section that controls when the rule applies.

### Frontmatter Structure

The YAML frontmatter has three key fields:

The standardized rule file format includes YAML frontmatter (`description`, `globs`, `alwaysApply`) plus a Markdown body containing a title, step-by-step instructions, code examples, and guidelines.

The basic structure is:

```
---
description: Short description of the rule's purpose
globs: optional/path/pattern/**/*
alwaysApply: false
---

# Rule Title

Main content explaining the rule with markdown formatting.
```

### Frontmatter Fields Explained

1. **`description`** — A short description of what the rule does (optional but recommended).
2. **`globs`** — File path patterns that determine when the rule is applied. For example, `"src/components/**"` would apply only when working in that directory. Can be a string or a list.
3. **`alwaysApply`** — Boolean (`true`/`false`). When `true`, the rule applies to every AI request regardless of context.

### Rule Application Modes

Based on how the frontmatter is configured, rules can work in different ways:

- **Always applied**: `alwaysApply: true` — applies to every request.
- **Glob-scoped**: Uses `globs` patterns to apply only when working with matching files.
- **Description-based (Agent-requested)**: When `alwaysApply: false` and no globs, the rule may be pulled in by the AI agent based on the description's relevance.

## Legacy vs. New Format

The legacy `.cursorrules` format still works perfectly in 2025. Cursor's newer MDC format gives you more control.

You can commit the legacy format with `git add .cursorrules` or the MDC format with `git add .cursor/rules/`.

## Advanced Format (XML-structured)

Some developers use a more structured approach. One approach introduces a strict format for Cursor rules using YAML frontmatter and a pseudo-XML body. That format helps LLMs reliably follow rule files instead of guessing.

`rules.mdc` defines the schema for all `.mdc` rule files. If you're writing or maintaining Cursor rules, this file is the standard they must follow. It covers structure, grammar, examples, language, and relationships between rules.

## Recent Changes (Late 2025)

There have been reports that when creating a new project rule via Cursor settings, it creates an `.mdc` file instead of a `rules/x/RULE.md` file, which the official Cursor docs indicate should be the newer structure. This suggests Cursor may be transitioning to a `RULE.md` structure in subdirectories, though `.mdc` remains widely used.

## Key Takeaways

- The format enforces consistency and discoverability, prevents misplaced rules, enables scoped and safe application of rules through the `alwaysApply` flag and glob patterns, and improves maintainability and onboarding for contributors.
- When you describe your tech stack, coding conventions, and project constraints in a rules file, Cursor's AI applies them automatically — without you needing to repeat yourself on every prompt.

Here's a comprehensive overview of how JetBrains AI Assistant handles IDE instructions, context, and rules files:

## Project Rules Files

To configure project-specific rules, go to **Settings | Tools | AI Assistant | Rules**, click **New Project Rules File** and provide a name for the file. Alternatively, you can manually create the `.aiassistant/rules` folder in the project root and add a `.md` file there.

### Rule Activation Modes

Rules can be applied in different ways:

- **By model decision** – applied when the model considers the rule relevant. You must also provide an Instruction so AI Assistant can understand when the rule should be applied. For example, you can instruct AI Assistant to apply the rule only when you work with Java files.
- **By file patterns** – applied when a file referenced in the chat matches the specified file pattern (for example, `*.kt` or `src/**`). The pattern must be provided in the Patterns field.
- **Off** – the rule is inactive and not applied.

### How Rules Are Applied

By default, project rules are automatically added to the default prompt in each chat session, ensuring that AI Assistant Chat adheres to the provided guidelines. Project rules set to "Always" should automatically apply to AI Assistant chat sessions.

However, there are known cases where this doesn't always work as expected. To ensure your rules are consistently applied, especially for specific actions like "Generate Unit Tests," it is recommended to include or duplicate your rules directly in the Prompt Library.

You can also reference rules manually in chat: `@rule` adds a project rule into a prompt. You can either select a rule from the invoked popup or write the rule name manually.

## `.aicontext` Files (2026)

JetBrains now supports context files (`.aicontext`) and custom model selection per file type, but you must configure them manually.

AI Assistant reads `.aicontext` files to understand your project. You create one at your project root, defining your tech stack, naming conventions, custom patterns, and code style preferences in YAML format.

## `.aiignore` and `.noai` Files

You can prevent AI Assistant from accessing specific files or folders by configuring an `.aiignore` file. This ensures restricted files are not processed when AI gathers project context.

You can also create an empty file named `.noai` in the root directory of the project. When this file is present, all AI Assistant features are fully disabled for the project. Even if this project is opened in another IDE, the AI Assistant features will not be available.

## Context Management

By default, AI Assistant automatically gathers the context it needs to provide an answer. If you prefer to add the context manually, you can disable this behavior by clicking and disabling the "Enable Codebase Mode" setting. After that, you can add the relevant information manually via the button or using `@` references.

When the Codebase Mode is enabled, context is not gathered from files listed in `.gitignore` and `.aiignore`.

## Model Selection (2026)

JetBrains AI Assistant (2026 version) uses a hybrid model system — cloud LLMs for complex tasks and local models for code completion. You can configure model selection per file type under Settings → Tools → JetBrains AI Assistant → Model Selection (e.g., local model for code completion, Cloud GPT-4 for chat/refactoring).

## Key Configuration Files Summary

| File/Folder | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `.aiassistant/rules/*.md` | Project-specific rules in Markdown |
| `.aicontext` | Project context (tech stack, conventions, patterns) |
| `.aiignore` | Exclude files/folders from AI context |
| `.noai` | Fully disable AI Assistant for a project |

## Research Findings: How AI Coding Tools Interact with File-Based Knowledge Bases

### 1. Gemini CLI (Google)

**Instruction/context file:** `GEMINI.md`

**Hierarchy (3 levels, all concatenated):**
- **Global:** `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` -- user-wide rules, loaded first for all sessions
- **Project (upward traversal):** Starting from current working directory, walks up to the git root, loading every `GEMINI.md` found along the way. Content from more specific (deeper) files supplements or overrides more general (higher) files.
- **Sub-directory (downward traversal):** Also recursively scans subdirectories below the current working directory, picking up `GEMINI.md` files for component-specific instructions.
- **Dynamic loading:** When a tool accesses a file in a new directory, Gemini auto-discovers `GEMINI.md` files in that directory tree.

**Modular imports:** Supports `@file.md` syntax to import other markdown files (only `.md` files supported).

**Key commands:**
- `/init` generates a starter `GEMINI.md`
- `/memory show` displays combined context
- `/memory refresh` reloads all files
- `/memory add <text>` appends to global `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md`

**File formats:** Standard Markdown. No required fields or structure -- "just standard Markdown, use any headings you like."

**MCP support:** Full MCP support. Configured via `mcpServers` in `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Supports stdio and HTTP transports. Can return rich multi-part content (text, images, audio). MCP prompts can be exposed as slash commands. FastMCP integration added in September 2025. Google launched managed remote MCP servers in December 2025.

**AGENTS.md compatibility:** Active community discussion about adopting AGENTS.md as default. Gemini CLI's context file is configurable via `settings.json`, so pointing it at `AGENTS.md` is possible. The tool is listed as an AGENTS.md adopter.

**Cross-agent note:** `.geminiignore` (similar to `.gitignore`) excludes files from tool access.

- [Gemini CLI Cheatsheet](https://www.philschmid.de/gemini-cli-cheatsheet)

---

### 2. OpenCode (Open-Source AI CLI)

**Instruction/context file:** `AGENTS.md` (primary), with `CLAUDE.md` as fallback.

**Hierarchy:**
- **Project-level:** `AGENTS.md` in project root. Only applies when working in that directory or its sub-directories.
- **Global:** `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` for personal rules across all sessions (not committed to git).
- **Claude Code fallback:** If no `AGENTS.md` exists, reads `CLAUDE.md` in the project directory. If no `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, falls back to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. First matching file wins in each category -- if both exist, only `AGENTS.md` is used.
- **Custom instruction files:** `opencode.json` supports an `instructions` field with paths, glob patterns (e.g., `packages/*/AGENTS.md` for monorepos), and even remote URLs (fetched with 5-second timeout). All instruction files combine with `AGENTS.md`.

**Skills system:** OpenCode discovers reusable instructions from the repo via `SKILL.md` files. It searches `.opencode/skills/*/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`, and `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md` -- walking up from the current directory to the git worktree root and loading global definitions from `~/.config/opencode/skills/*/SKILL.md`.

**Directory structure:** `.opencode/` and `~/.config/opencode/` use plural subdirectories: `agents/`, `commands/`, `modes/`, `plugins/`, `skills/`, `tools/`, `themes/`.

**MCP support:** Full MCP support. Supports `stdio` and `sse` server types. Configuration in JSON format. CLI commands for adding, listing, and authenticating with MCP servers. OAuth support for remote MCP servers. MCP tools follow the same permission model as built-in tools.

**Built-in tools:** Shell execution, file modification (exact string replacements), regex content search, file finding by pattern, web content fetching, LSP server interaction (definitions, references, hover, call hierarchy).

**Auto compact:** Automatically summarizes conversation when approaching context window limits.

- [OpenCode Agents](https://opencode.ai/docs/agents/)
- [OpenCode Tools](https://opencode.ai/docs/tools/)
- [OpenCode Agent Skills](https://opencode.ai/docs/skills/)
- [OpenCode CLI](https://opencode.ai/docs/cli/)

### 3. Claude.ai (Web Interface)

**Instruction/context mechanism:** Claude Projects (paid feature: Pro, Team, Enterprise).

**How it works:**
- **Custom Instructions:** A persistent system prompt field that applies to every conversation within a project. Written as free-form text guidance (tone, format, coding style, analytical approaches).
- **Knowledge Base:** A per-project document repository. Upload relevant files as persistent reference material. Claude-generated content can also be added to the knowledge base.
- **Context window:** 200,000 tokens per project (~500 pages of content).

**Supported file formats for upload:**
- Documents: PDF, DOCX, TXT, HTML, ODT, RTF, EPUB
- Data: CSV, Excel (.xlsx, up to 30MB)
- Images: Standard image formats (multimodal)
- Code files: Various text-based code files
- Individual file limit: 30MB, unlimited files (as long as total fits within context window)

**MCP support:** Yes, via remote MCP connectors (beta). Available on all plans (free users limited to one custom connector). Supports SSE and Streamable HTTP transports. OAuth and authless authentication. Pre-built integrations for Jira, Confluence, Zapier, Slack, Asana, Linear, Sentry, Microsoft 365, and many more. **Cross-platform:** MCP servers added in Claude.ai are automatically available in Claude Code if logged in with same account.

- [Claude can now connect to your world (Anthropic announcement)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/integrations)

### 4. Cursor / Windsurf / JetBrains AI Assistant

#### Cursor

**Instruction files:**
- **Legacy:** `.cursorrules` (still functional, no longer recommended)
- **Current:** `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` files (MDC = Markdown with YAML frontmatter)
- **Possible newer format:** `.cursor/rules/x/RULE.md` subdirectory structure (emerging)

**`.mdc` format:**
```yaml
---
description: Short description of rule purpose
globs: src/components/**
alwaysApply: false
---
# Rule Title
Markdown content with instructions, code examples, guidelines.
```

**Rule activation modes:**
- `alwaysApply: true` -- applies to every AI request
- Glob-scoped -- applies only when working with files matching `globs` patterns
- Description-based (agent-requested) -- AI agent pulls in the rule based on relevance

**MCP support:** Full MCP support since 2025. Configured in `.cursor/mcp.json` (project-level) or Cursor settings (global). Supports stdio, HTTP, and SSE transports. One-click MCP server installation from curated marketplace. Resources support shipped in v1.6 (September 2025). Cap of 100 active MCP tools.

- [Cursor Rules (official docs)](https://cursor.com/docs/context/rules)

#### Windsurf

**Instruction files:**

**Rule structure:** Standard Markdown files. Rules can also be configured via Settings > Set Workspace AI Rules > Edit Rules.

**MCP support:** Full MCP support via Cascade agent. Configured in `mcp_config.json`. Supports stdio, HTTP, and SSE transports. MCP Marketplace for one-click installs. Cap of 100 active tools.

**Memories:** Windsurf stores persistent "memories" of prompts and projects for continuous context improvement.

Sources:
- [Windsurf Cascade MCP Integration (official docs)](https://docs.windsurf.com/windsurf/cascade/mcp)
- [Windsurf Rules Directory](https://windsurf.com/editor/directory)
- [awesome-windsurfrules (GitHub)](https://github.com/SchneiderSam/awesome-windsurfrules)
- [Windsurf Rules & Workflows best practices](https://www.paulmduvall.com/using-windsurf-rules-workflows-and-memories/)

#### JetBrains AI Assistant

**Instruction files:**
- **Project rules:** `.aiassistant/rules/*.md` -- Markdown files in a dedicated directory

**Rule activation modes:**
- By model decision -- AI decides relevance based on an instruction description

**MCP support:** Yes, JetBrains has MCP support as documented in their AI Assistant docs.

- [Rules settings reference (JetBrains)](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai-assistant/settings-reference-rules.html)
- [JetBrains AI Assistant MCP](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai-assistant/mcp.html)

---

### 5. AGENTS.md Convention (AAIF / Linux Foundation)

**Origin:** Created by OpenAI for Codex (August 2025). Donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation in December 2025.

**Adoption:** Over 60,000 open-source projects. Supported by 20+ tools including OpenAI Codex, Google Jules, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code/GitHub Copilot, Devin, Aider, Factory, Amp, Zed, Warp, and OpenCode.

**Format:** Standard Markdown. No required fields or structure -- completely flexible. Headings provide semantic hints but are not enforced.

**Recommended sections (from analysis of 2,500+ repositories):**
1. **Build & Test** -- exact commands (`npm test`, `pytest -v`) with flags and options
2. **Architecture Overview** -- short description of major modules
3. **Code Style / Conventions** -- naming, folder layout, style preferences (code examples > prose)
4. **Security** -- auth flows, API keys, sensitive data boundaries
5. **Git Workflows** -- branching, commit conventions, PR requirements
6. **Boundaries** -- what the agent should never touch (secrets, vendor directories, production configs)

**File placement and hierarchy:**
- Place at repository root (alongside `README.md`)
- **Monorepo support:** Place additional `AGENTS.md` in subdirectories. Agents read the nearest file in the directory tree; the closest one to the edited file takes precedence.
- **Override files (Codex):** `AGENTS.override.md` takes priority over `AGENTS.md` at each level. Discovery walks from global scope (`~/.codex/`) through project root down to current working directory.
- Explicit user chat prompts override everything.

**Key principles:**
- Describe capabilities, not paths (file paths change; capabilities persist)
- Code examples over prose explanations
- Put executable commands early -- agents will attempt to run them
- Be specific about tech stack versions
- Living document -- grow through iteration, not upfront planning

**How it differs from CLAUDE.md:**
- `CLAUDE.md` is Claude Code-specific; `AGENTS.md` is vendor-neutral
- `CLAUDE.md` supports `.claude/rules/*.md` directory structure for modular rules; `AGENTS.md` uses monorepo-style nesting
- `AGENTS.md` has no frontmatter or metadata convention; `CLAUDE.md` has no mandated format either but Claude Code reads from specific paths (`CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/`, `~/.claude/`)
- Claude Code does not currently read `AGENTS.md` (notable absence as of the latest reports)

**Compatibility approach (symlinks):**
```bash
mv CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md && ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
```
This lets new tools read `AGENTS.md` while older tools that expect `CLAUDE.md` continue working.

Sources:
- [AGENTS.md official site](https://agents.md/)
- [AGENTS.md GitHub repository](https://github.com/agentsmd/agents.md)
- [How to write a great agents.md (GitHub Blog)](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-to-write-a-great-agents-md-lessons-from-over-2500-repositories/)
- [Custom instructions with AGENTS.md (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md/)
- [AAIF announcement (Linux Foundation)](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation)
- [A Complete Guide To AGENTS.md](https://www.aihero.dev/a-complete-guide-to-agents-md)
- [Improve your AI code output with AGENTS.md (Builder.io)](https://www.builder.io/blog/agents-md)
- [AGENTS.md open standard (tessl.io)](https://tessl.io/blog/the-rise-of-agents-md-an-open-standard-and-single-source-of-truth-for-ai-coding-agents/)

---

### Cross-Agent Compatibility Summary

| Tool | Primary File | Fallback Files | MCP Support | Hierarchy |
|------|-------------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| **Claude Code** | `CLAUDE.md` + `.claude/rules/*.md` | None (does not read AGENTS.md) | Full (stdio, HTTP) | Global `~/.claude/` + project + parent dirs |
| **Gemini CLI** | `GEMINI.md` | Configurable; community pushing for AGENTS.md | Full (stdio, HTTP, SSE) | Global `~/.gemini/` + upward + downward traversal |
| **OpenCode** | `AGENTS.md` | `CLAUDE.md` (if no AGENTS.md exists) | Full (stdio, SSE, OAuth) | Global `~/.config/opencode/` + project root |
| **Cursor** | `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` | `.cursorrules` (legacy) | Full (stdio, HTTP, SSE) | Project `.cursor/` directory |
| **Windsurf** | `.windsurf/rules/*.md` | `.windsurfrules` (legacy) | Full (stdio, HTTP, SSE) | Global `~/.codeium/` + project root |
| **JetBrains** | `.aiassistant/rules/*.md` + `.aicontext` | None | Yes | Project `.aiassistant/` directory |
| **Claude.ai** | Project Instructions (web UI) + file uploads | N/A (cloud-based) | Yes (remote MCP connectors) | Per-project knowledge base |
| **OpenAI Codex** | `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.override.md` takes precedence | Yes | Global `~/.codex/` + directory walk |

### Implications for Cohezion Vault Accessibility

To make the vault maximally accessible across tools:

1. **Create an `AGENTS.md`** at the vault root as the vendor-neutral entry point. This is read by OpenCode, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI (configurable), and 20+ other tools. Keep it focused on build commands, project structure, and conventions.

2. **Maintain `CLAUDE.md`** for Claude Code-specific features (rules hierarchy, `.claude/` directory integration, skills). Claude Code does not read `AGENTS.md`.

3. **Consider a `GEMINI.md`** or symlink if Gemini CLI users need to work with the vault (or configure Gemini CLI to read `AGENTS.md` via `settings.json`).

4. **MCP is the universal integration layer.** Every single tool surveyed supports MCP. The existing Cloud Vault MCP Server on port 8360 is the strongest cross-tool integration point -- any tool with MCP support can query the vault programmatically without needing file-system conventions at all.

5. **Markdown is the universal format.** Every tool reads standard Markdown. YAML frontmatter is tool-specific (Cursor uses it in `.mdc`, JetBrains uses `.aicontext` in YAML), but plain Markdown body content is universally understood.

6. **The symlink approach** (`ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` or vice versa) is the community workaround for maintaining a single source of truth across tool-specific filenames. This works well when the instructions are generic enough to apply to any agent.

OAuth and authless authentication. Pre-built integrations for Jira, Confluence, Zapier, Slack, Asana, Linear, Sentry, Microsoft 365, and many more. Works on web, desktop, and mobile (mobile can use servers added via web, but cannot add new ones). Custom connectors allow connecting to any remote MCP server via URL.

**Files API:** In beta since April 2025. Upload files once via API and reference by `file_id` thereafter -- avoids repeated uploads.

**Cross-platform:** MCP servers added in Claude.ai are automatically available in Claude Code if logged in with same account.

**Key limitation for vault compatibility:** Claude.ai Projects requires manual file uploads or API integration. There is no automatic file-system scanning like CLI tools do. The knowledge base is cloud-based, not file-system-based.

Sources:
- [Claude AI File Upload formats and limits](https://www.datastudios.org/post/claude-ai-file-upload-and-reading-formats-limits-and-operational-structure)
- [Claude AI Connectors guide](https://max-productive.ai/blog/claude-ai-connectors-guide-2025/)
- [Get started with custom connectors using remote MCP](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-get-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp)
- [Pre-built web connectors using remote MCP](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11176164-pre-built-web-connectors-using-remote-mcp)
- [Building custom connectors via remote MCP servers](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11503834-building-custom-connectors-via-remote-mcp-servers)
- [Claude can now connect to your world (Anthropic announcement)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/integrations)

---

### 4. Cursor / Windsurf / JetBrains AI Assistant

#### Cursor

**Instruction files:**
- **Legacy:** `.cursorrules` (still functional, no longer recommended)
- **Current:** `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` files (MDC = Markdown with YAML frontmatter)
- **Possible newer format:** `.cursor/rules/x/RULE.md` subdirectory structure (emerging)

**`.mdc` format:**
```yaml
---
description: Short description of rule purpose
globs: src/components/**
alwaysApply: false
---
# Rule Title
Markdown content with instructions, code examples, guidelines.
```

**Rule activation modes:**
- `alwaysApply: true` -- applies to every AI request
- Glob-scoped -- applies only when working with files matching `globs` patterns
- Description-based (agent-requested) -- AI agent pulls in the rule based on relevance

**MCP support:** Full MCP support since 2025. Configured in `.cursor/mcp.json` (project-level) or Cursor settings (global). Supports stdio, HTTP, and SSE transports. One-click MCP server installation from curated marketplace. Resources support shipped in v1.6 (September 2025). Cap of 100 active MCP tools.

Sources:
- [Cursor Rules (official docs)](https://cursor.com/docs/context/rules)
- [Cursor MCP (official docs)](https://cursor.com/docs/context/mcp)
- [Cursor AI Complete Guide 2025 (Medium)](https://medium.com/@hilalkara.dev/cursor-ai-complete-guide-2025-real-experiences-pro-tips-mcps-rules-context-engineering-6de1a776a8af)
- [Cursor Rules Guide 2026](https://www.agentrulegen.com/guides/cursor-rules-guide)

#### Windsurf

**Instruction files:**
- **Legacy:** `.windsurfrules` (still functional)
- **Current:** `.windsurf/rules/rules.md` (and additional `.md` files in `.windsurf/rules/`)
- **Global rules:** `~/.codeium/windsurf/memories/global_rules.md`
- **Component rules:** Dedicated files at project root (e.g., `.cicdrules.md`, `.iamrolerules.md`)

**Rule structure:** Standard Markdown files. Rules can also be configured via Settings > Set Workspace AI Rules > Edit Rules.

**MCP support:** Full MCP support via Cascade agent. Configured in `mcp_config.json`. Supports stdio, HTTP, and SSE transports. MCP Marketplace for one-click installs. Cap of 100 active tools.

**Memories:** Windsurf stores persistent "memories" of prompts and projects for continuous context improvement.

Sources:
- [Windsurf Cascade MCP Integration (official docs)](https://docs.windsurf.com/windsurf/cascade/mcp)
- [Windsurf Rules Directory](https://windsurf.com/editor/directory)
- [awesome-windsurfrules (GitHub)](https://github.com/SchneiderSam/awesome-windsurfrules)
- [Windsurf Rules & Workflows best practices](https://www.paulmduvall.com/using-windsurf-rules-workflows-and-memories/)

#### JetBrains AI Assistant

**Instruction files:**
- **Project rules:** `.aiassistant/rules/*.md` -- Markdown files in a dedicated directory
- **Project context:** `.aicontext` -- YAML file defining tech stack, naming conventions, patterns
- **Exclusions:** `.aiignore` (exclude files from AI context), `.noai` (disable AI entirely)

**Rule activation modes:**
- By model decision -- AI decides relevance based on an instruction description
- By file patterns -- activated when referenced files match glob patterns (e.g., `*.kt`, `src/**`)
- Off -- inactive

**MCP support:** Yes, JetBrains has MCP support as documented in their AI Assistant docs.

Sources:
- [Configure project rules (JetBrains)](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai-assistant/configure-project-rules.html)
- [Rules settings reference (JetBrains)](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai-assistant/settings-reference-rules.html)
- [JetBrains AI Assistant MCP](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai-assistant/mcp.html)

---

### 5. AGENTS.md Convention (AAIF / Linux Foundation)

**Origin:** Created by OpenAI for Codex (August 2025). Donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation in December 2025.

**Adoption:** Over 60,000 open-source projects. Supported by 20+ tools including OpenAI Codex, Google Jules, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code/GitHub Copilot, Devin, Aider, Factory, Amp, Zed, Warp, and OpenCode.

**Format:** Standard Markdown. No required fields or structure -- completely flexible. Headings provide semantic hints but are not enforced.

**Recommended sections (from analysis of 2,500+ repositories):**
1. **Build & Test** -- exact commands (`npm test`, `pytest -v`) with flags and options
2. **Architecture Overview** -- short description of major modules
3. **Code Style / Conventions** -- naming, folder layout, style preferences (code examples > prose)
4. **Security** -- auth flows, API keys, sensitive data boundaries
5. **Git Workflows** -- branching, commit conventions, PR requirements
6. **Boundaries** -- what the agent should never touch (secrets, vendor directories, production configs)

**File placement and hierarchy:**
- Place at repository root (alongside `README.md`)
- **Monorepo support:** Place additional `AGENTS.md` in subdirectories. Agents read the nearest file in the directory tree; the closest one to the edited file takes precedence.
- **Override files (Codex):** `AGENTS.override.md` takes priority over `AGENTS.md` at each level. Discovery walks from global scope (`~/.codex/`) through project root down to current working directory.
- Explicit user chat prompts override everything.

**Key principles:**
- Describe capabilities, not paths (file paths change; capabilities persist)
- Code examples over prose explanations
- Put executable commands early -- agents will attempt to run them
- Be specific about tech stack versions
- Living document -- grow through iteration, not upfront planning

**How it differs from CLAUDE.md:**
- `CLAUDE.md` is Claude Code-specific; `AGENTS.md` is vendor-neutral
- `CLAUDE.md` supports `.claude/rules/*.md` directory structure for modular rules; `AGENTS.md` uses monorepo-style nesting
- `AGENTS.md` has no frontmatter or metadata convention; `CLAUDE.md` has no mandated format either but Claude Code reads from specific paths (`CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/`, `~/.claude/`)
- Claude Code does not currently read `AGENTS.md` (notable absence as of the latest reports)

**Compatibility approach (symlinks):**
```bash
mv CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md && ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
```
This lets new tools read `AGENTS.md` while older tools that expect `CLAUDE.md` continue working.

Sources:
- [AGENTS.md official site](https://agents.md/)
- [AGENTS.md GitHub repository](https://github.com/agentsmd/agents.md)
- [How to write a great agents.md (GitHub Blog)](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-to-write-a-great-agents-md-lessons-from-over-2500-repositories/)
- [Custom instructions with AGENTS.md (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md/)
- [AAIF announcement (Linux Foundation)](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation)
- [A Complete Guide To AGENTS.md](https://www.aihero.dev/a-complete-guide-to-agents-md)
- [Improve your AI code output with AGENTS.md (Builder.io)](https://www.builder.io/blog/agents-md)
- [AGENTS.md open standard (tessl.io)](https://tessl.io/blog/the-rise-of-agents-md-an-open-standard-and-single-source-of-truth-for-ai-coding-agents/)

---

### Cross-Agent Compatibility Summary

| Tool | Primary File | Fallback Files | MCP Support | Hierarchy |
|------|-------------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| **Claude Code** | `CLAUDE.md` + `.claude/rules/*.md` | None (does not read AGENTS.md) | Full (stdio, HTTP) | Global `~/.claude/` + project + parent dirs |
| **Gemini CLI** | `GEMINI.md` | Configurable; community pushing for AGENTS.md | Full (stdio, HTTP, SSE) | Global `~/.gemini/` + upward + downward traversal |
| **OpenCode** | `AGENTS.md` | `CLAUDE.md` (if no AGENTS.md exists) | Full (stdio, SSE, OAuth) | Global `~/.config/opencode/` + project root |
| **Cursor** | `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` | `.cursorrules` (legacy) | Full (stdio, HTTP, SSE) | Project `.cursor/` directory |
| **Windsurf** | `.windsurf/rules/*.md` | `.windsurfrules` (legacy) | Full (stdio, HTTP, SSE) | Global `~/.codeium/` + project root |
| **JetBrains** | `.aiassistant/rules/*.md` + `.aicontext` | None | Yes | Project `.aiassistant/` directory |
| **Claude.ai** | Project Instructions (web UI) + file uploads | N/A (cloud-based) | Yes (remote MCP connectors) | Per-project knowledge base |
| **OpenAI Codex** | `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.override.md` takes precedence | Yes | Global `~/.codex/` + directory walk |

### Implications for Cohezion Vault Accessibility

To make the vault maximally accessible across tools:

1. **Create an `AGENTS.md`** at the vault root as the vendor-neutral entry point. This is read by OpenCode, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI (configurable), and 20+ other tools. Keep it focused on build commands, project structure, and conventions.

2. **Maintain `CLAUDE.md`** for Claude Code-specific features (rules hierarchy, `.claude/` directory integration, skills). Claude Code does not read `AGENTS.md`.

3. **Consider a `GEMINI.md`** or symlink if Gemini CLI users need to work with the vault (or configure Gemini CLI to read `AGENTS.md` via `settings.json`).

4. **MCP is the universal integration layer.** Every single tool surveyed supports MCP. The existing Cloud Vault MCP Server on port 8360 is the strongest cross-tool integration point -- any tool with MCP support can query the vault programmatically without needing file-system conventions at all.

5. **Markdown is the universal format.** Every tool reads standard Markdown. YAML frontmatter is tool-specific (Cursor uses it in `.mdc`, JetBrains uses `.aicontext` in YAML), but plain Markdown body content is universally understood.

6. **The symlink approach** (`ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` or vice versa) is the community workaround for maintaining a single source of truth across tool-specific filenames. This works well when the instructions are generic enough to apply to any agent.

# Cohezion Vault

Knowledge base for the Cohezion agentic AI framework. Obsidian vault with 1,400+ notes, 11,000+ wiki-links, and 8 Maps of Content.

## Quick Orientation

**Read `VAULT_MANIFEST.md` first.** It maps every directory, explains output routing, and lists conventions. Each directory also has a `_index.md` with purpose, naming rules, and key notes.

## Structure

| Directory | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `concepts/` | Core definitions, frameworks, techniques |
| `papers/` | Research papers and external sources |
| `decisions/` | Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) |
| `patterns/` | Reusable solutions and code patterns |
| `lessons/` | Hard-won knowledge from mistakes |
| `experiments/` | Hypothesis testing and results |
| `projects/` | Multi-session project tracking |
| `inbox/` | Unsorted intake — safe default for any output |
| `daily/` | Session logs and daily notes |
| `canvas/` | Standalone visual canvases |

## Conventions

- **Frontmatter:** YAML with `title`, `date`, `tags` (always arrays: `[tag1, tag2]`)
- **Cross-references:** Obsidian wiki-links `[[note-name]]` — bare filename, no path prefix
- **Rich formats encouraged:** Mermaid diagrams, callouts (`> [!tip]`), LaTeX math, `.canvas` files
- **Templates:** `_template.md` in each content directory — copy when creating notes

## Output Routing

```
Research summaries       → papers/
Techniques/definitions   → concepts/
Architectural choices    → decisions/
Reusable solutions       → patterns/
Mistakes and learnings   → lessons/
Visual relationship maps → companion .canvas alongside .md, or canvas/
Don't know where it goes → inbox/
```

## Entry Points (Maps of Content)

| Topic | MOC |
|-------|-----|
| Agent architecture | `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.md` |
| Quantum physics | `concepts/MOC-quantum-physics.md` |
| Vault structure | `concepts/MOC-vault-architecture.md` |
| Infrastructure | `concepts/MOC-platform-infrastructure.md` |
| Machine learning | `concepts/MOC-machine-learning.md` |
| Astrophysics | `concepts/MOC-astrophysics.md` |
| Methodology | `concepts/MOC-compound-engineering.md` |
| AI safety | `concepts/MOC-safety-alignment.md` |

## Build Commands (Tooling)

```bash
# Cohezion Engine CLI
cd tools/cohezion-engine && uv pip install -e .
cz --help

# 3D Graph Plugin
cd obsidian-plugin/3d-graph-plugin && npm install && npm run dev

# MCP Server
cd mcp-server && pip install -e ".[dev]" && pytest
```

## MCP Integration

- **Cloud Vault MCP** on port 8360 — programmatic vault access (VaultOps, CompoundOps, ObsidianOps, SurrealDB)
- **Ollama MCP** on port 22360 — semantic search and embeddings

## Vault Health

The vault maintains these invariants automatically:
- 0 orphan notes, 0 frontmatter issues, 0 broken links
- 8+ Maps of Content, 6+ avg wiki-links per note
- Proactive hooks detect and alert on violations

## See Also

- `VAULT_MANIFEST.md` — full directory map, rich format specs, agent workflow
- `CLAUDE.md` — Claude Code-specific instructions and tool conventions

## Output Routing Rules

**When you produce output, route it to the correct directory:**

```
I found a new technique/technology    → concepts/
I summarized external research        → papers/
I made an architectural choice        → decisions/
I documented a reusable solution      → patterns/
I tested a hypothesis                 → experiments/
I'm tracking a multi-session effort   → projects/
I learned something the hard way      → lessons/
I have raw/unstructured content       → inbox/     (vault keeper will triage)
I'm logging today's session work      → daily/
I ran a multi-agent mission           → missions/
I'm reviewing what worked/didn't      → retrospectives/
I mapped relationships visually        → companion .canvas next to the .md, or canvas/ if standalone
I don't know where this goes          → inbox/     (always safe default)
```

**When in doubt, use `inbox/`.** The vault keeper triages inbox items into their proper location with correct frontmatter and cross-links.

---

## Canvas Files (Multimodal Assets)
