# Cloud Vault MCP

The Cloud Vault MCP server is Cohezion's primary knowledge management and agent infrastructure interface, implemented as an HTTP [[mcp-model-context-protocol]] server running on port 8360. It exposes 30+ tools across six categories, providing AI agents with programmatic access to the Obsidian vault, SurrealDB graph database, Google Sheets, Ollama inference, and Teleport task management — all through a single standardized protocol.

The server implements three logical operation layers. **VaultOps** handles file-level vault operations: reading, writing, searching, and cross-linking notes. **CompoundOps** implements the compound engineering primitives: `vault_log_decision`, `vault_log_experiment`, `vault_extract_pattern`, and `vault_find_relevant_context` — the tools that make the [[experience-feedback-loop]] concrete. **ObsidianOps** manages the graph layer: backlinks, forward links, tags, and wiki-link validation. Together these layers turn the Obsidian vault from a passive note store into an active, queryable knowledge graph that agents can read from and write to during execution.

The server was built using FastMCP (Python) and serves as the reference template for additional MCP servers in the Cohezion ecosystem. The `cloud-vault-mcp/` directory is explicitly documented as the template to copy when building new MCP servers, carrying 87% token savings versus building from scratch. It runs alongside the Ollama MCP server (stdio, no port) and exposes a `/health` endpoint that monitors all five infrastructure dependencies.

title: "Specs — Directory Index"
purpose: "System definitions for skills, agents, MCP servers, tools, hooks, and workflows"

# Specs — System Definitions

**Purpose:** The vault's reconstruction manual. Everything an agent (or human) needs to rebuild the Cohezion system from scratch — skills, agents, MCP servers, tools, hooks, workflows, and IDE/model integrations.

> [!danger] Why This Exists
> If the repo is lost, if MCP config is corrupted, if `.claude/` is wiped — these specs are the blueprint for reconstruction. Every system definition lives here as a structured, cross-linked, versioned vault note.

**Put here when:** You create, modify, or document a system-level component (skill, agent, MCP server, tool, hook, workflow, or integration).

## Subdirectories

| Subdirectory | Contents | Naming |
|-------------|----------|--------|
| `skills/` | Skill specs — purpose, triggers, steps, examples | `<skill-name>.md` |
| `agents/` | Agent definitions — role, tools, constraints, prompts | `<agent-name>.md` |
| `mcp-servers/` | MCP server specs — URL, tools catalog, auth, examples | `<server-name>.md` |
| `tools/` | Tool specs — commands, flags, install, examples | `<tool-name>.md` |
| `hooks/` | Hook specs — trigger, logic, alerts, cooldown | `<hook-name>.md` |
| `workflows/` | Workflow specs — phases, gates, transitions | `<workflow-name>.md` |
| `integrations/` | IDE and model provider integration points | `<integration-name>.md` |

## Required Frontmatter

```yaml
---
title: "Component Name"
date: 2026-03-05
version: 1
last_revised: 2026-03-05
tags: [spec, <type>]  # type = skill | agent | mcp-server | tool | hook | workflow | integration
source: ".claude/skills/vault-keeper/SKILL.md"  # path to canonical source
status: active  # active | deprecated | draft
---
```

## Versioning Convention

- `version:` increments on every significant change
- `last_revised:` updates on any edit
- `revision_history:` optional array of `{v, date, change}` entries
- Git history provides full diff trail: `git log --follow specs/<path>`

## Sync Protocol

1. After modifying a skill/agent/tool → update the corresponding spec note
2. `/sync` skill writes vault specs as part of the sync cycle
3. Vault-keeper can detect stale specs (source timestamp > spec timestamp)

## Related

- [[2026-03-05-vault-as-system-of-record]] — ADR establishing this directory's purpose
- [[compound-engineering]] — System definitions compound like knowledge

    84→
    85→### Project Artifacts — Store Everything in the Vault
    86→
    87→> [!danger] Mandatory Rule
    88→> **All project artifacts belong in the vault.** PRDs, architecture docs, epics, stories, and engineering specs are vault notes — not code repo files, not ephemeral chat output, not lost when context expires.
    89→
    90→**Why:** The vault is disaster recovery for institutional memory. If the repo is lost, the vault preserves how to rebuild. If an agent session crashes, the vault preserves what was decided and why. Traceability lives here.
    91→
    92→| Artifact | Where | Template |
    93→|----------|-------|----------|
    94→| **PRD / Product Requirements** | `projects/YYYY-MM-DD-project-name.md` | Include: problem, success criteria, epics table, stories table, timeline |
    95→| **Architecture Decision** | `decisions/YYYY-MM-DD-architecture-name.md` | ADR template: context, decision, consequences, alternatives, diagrams |
    96→| **Epic breakdown** | Section within the PRD note | Table with stories, estimates, priorities |
    97→| **Story details** | Section within the PRD note, or separate `projects/YYYY-MM-DD-story-name.md` if large | Acceptance criteria, file references, blockers |
    98→| **Spike / investigation** | `experiments/YYYY-MM-DD-spike-name.md` | Hypothesis, method, results, learnings |
    99→| **Retrospective** | `retrospectives/YYYY-MM-DD-retro-name.md` | What worked, what didn't, actions |
   100→| **Runbook / how-to** | `patterns/how-to-name.md` | Steps, prerequisites, troubleshooting |
   101→
   102→**Cross-link rule:** Every architecture decision links to its parent PRD. Every PRD links to related concepts and lessons. Stories reference the files they'll change.
   103→
   104→**Example structure for a project:**
   105→```
   106→projects/2026-03-05-vault-surrealdb-sync-pipeline.md    ← PRD with epics + stories
   107→decisions/2026-03-05-vault-surrealdb-architecture.md    ← Architecture ADR
   108→experiments/2026-03-05-sync-daemon-prototype.md          ← Spike results
   109→lessons/lesson-health-check-must-test-auth.md            ← Lesson learned
   110→retrospectives/2026-03-XX-sync-pipeline-retro.md         ← Post-project retro
   111→```
   112→
   113→**When in doubt, use `inbox/`.** The vault keeper triages inbox items into their proper location with correct frontmatter and cross-links.
   114→
   115→---
   116→
   117→## Canvas Files (Multimodal Assets)
   118→
   119→**Notes explain. Canvases show.** When a topic has complex relationships, spatial layout reveals structure that prose cannot. Create `.canvas` files alongside their companion `.md` notes.
   120→
   121→### When to Create a Canvas
   122→
   123→| Signal | Canvas Type |
   124→|--------|-------------|
   125→| MOC with 10+ linked notes | **Relationship map** — nodes for notes, edges for connections |
   126→| Architecture or system design | **Architecture diagram** — groups for layers, text cards for components |
   127→| Decision with 3+ alternatives | **Decision landscape** — cards per option, edges to trade-offs |
   128→| Research cluster spanning domains | **Domain map** — grouped by field, edges for cross-domain links |
   129→| Vault keeper nudges you | The hook detected 10+ outbound links — the note wants a canvas |
   130→
   131→### Naming and Placement
   132→
   133→Canvas files live **alongside their companion note**:
   134→- `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.md` → `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.canvas`
   135→- `decisions/2026-03-05-pick-database.md` → `decisions/2026-03-05-pick-database.canvas`
   136→- Standalone canvases (no companion note) → `canvas/` directory
   137→
   138→### JSON Format
   139→
   140→Obsidian canvas files are JSON with `nodes` and `edges`:
   141→
   142→```json
   143→{
   144→  "nodes": [
   145→    {"id":"unique-id", "type":"file", "file":"concepts/machine-learning.md", "x":0, "y":0, "width":250, "height":60},
   146→    {"id":"label-1",   "type":"text", "text":"## Key Insight\n\nMarkdown content here", "x":300, "y":0, "width":300, "height":120, "color":"4"},
   147→    {"id":"group-1",   "type":"group","label":"ML Cluster", "x":-50, "y":-50, "width":600, "height":250, "color":"2"}
   148→  ],
   149→  "edges": [
   150→    {"id":"edge-1", "fromNode":"unique-id", "toNode":"label-1", "label":"informs"}
   151→  ]
   152→}
   153→```
   154→
   155→**Node types:**
   156→- `file` — link to a vault note (opens on click). Use `"file": "path/to/note.md"`
   157→- `text` — inline markdown card. Use `"text": "## Title\n\nContent"`
   158→- `group` — visual grouping box. Use `"label": "Group Name"`
   159→
   160→**Colors:** `"1"` red, `"2"` orange, `"3"` yellow, `"4"` green, `"5"` cyan, `"6"` purple, or hex `"#RRGGGG"`
   161→
   162→**Layout tips:** Use x/y grid spacing of ~300px horizontal, ~150px vertical. Groups should surround their children with ~50px padding.
   163→
   164→---
   165→
   166→## Rich Formats
   167→
   168→Plain text is the floor, not the ceiling. Obsidian renders these natively — use them to make notes scannable, visual, and precise.
   169→
   170→### Callouts
   171→
   172→Structured highlights for decisions, warnings, key insights. **Use liberally.**
   173→
   174→```markdown

### Project Artifacts — Store Everything in the Vault

> [!danger] Mandatory Rule
> **All project artifacts belong in the vault.** PRDs, architecture docs, epics, stories, and engineering specs are vault notes — not code repo files, not ephemeral chat output, not lost when context expires.

**Why:** The vault is disaster recovery for institutional memory. If the repo is lost, the vault preserves how to rebuild. If an agent session crashes, the vault preserves what was decided and why. Traceability lives here.

| Artifact | Where | Template |
|----------|-------|----------|
| **PRD / Product Requirements** | `projects/YYYY-MM-DD-project-name.md` | Include: problem, success criteria, epics table, stories table, timeline |
| **Architecture Decision** | `decisions/YYYY-MM-DD-architecture-name.md` | ADR template: context, decision, consequences, alternatives, diagrams |
| **Epic breakdown** | Section within the PRD note | Table with stories, estimates, priorities |
| **Story details** | Section within the PRD note, or separate `projects/YYYY-MM-DD-story-name.md` if large | Acceptance criteria, file references, blockers |
| **Spike / investigation** | `experiments/YYYY-MM-DD-spike-name.md` | Hypothesis, method, results, learnings |
| **Retrospective** | `retrospectives/YYYY-MM-DD-retro-name.md` | What worked, what didn't, actions |
| **Runbook / how-to** | `patterns/how-to-name.md` | Steps, prerequisites, troubleshooting |

**Cross-link rule:** Every architecture decision links to its parent PRD. Every PRD links to related concepts and lessons. Stories reference the files they'll change.

**Example structure for a project:**
```
projects/2026-03-05-vault-surrealdb-sync-pipeline.md    ← PRD with epics + stories
decisions/2026-03-05-vault-surrealdb-architecture.md    ← Architecture ADR
experiments/2026-03-05-sync-daemon-prototype.md          ← Spike results
lessons/lesson-health-check-must-test-auth.md            ← Lesson learned
retrospectives/2026-03-XX-sync-pipeline-retro.md         ← Post-project retro
```

**When in doubt, use `inbox/`.** The vault keeper triages inbox items into their proper location with correct frontmatter and cross-links.

---

## Canvas Files (Multimodal Assets)

**Notes explain. Canvases show.** When a topic has complex relationships, spatial layout reveals structure that prose cannot. Create `.canvas` files alongside their companion `.md` notes.

### When to Create a Canvas

| Signal | Canvas Type |
|--------|-------------|
| MOC with 10+ linked notes | **Relationship map** — nodes for notes, edges for connections |
| Architecture or system design | **Architecture diagram** — groups for layers, text cards for components |
| Decision with 3+ alternatives | **Decision landscape** — cards per option, edges to trade-offs |
| Research cluster spanning domains | **Domain map** — grouped by field, edges for cross-domain links |
| Vault keeper nudges you | The hook detected 10+ outbound links — the note wants a canvas |

### Naming and Placement

Canvas files live **alongside their companion note**:
- `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.md` → `concepts/MOC-agentic-ai.canvas`
- `decisions/2026-03-05-pick-database.md` → `decisions/2026-03-05-pick-database.canvas`
- Standalone canvases (no companion note) → `canvas/` directory

### JSON Format

Obsidian canvas files are JSON with `nodes` and `edges`:

```json
{
  "nodes": [
    {"id":"unique-id", "type":"file", "file":"concepts/machine-learning.md", "x":0, "y":0, "width":250, "height":60},
    {"id":"label-1",   "type":"text", "text":"## Key Insight\n\nMarkdown content here", "x":300, "y":0, "width":300, "height":120, "color":"4"},
    {"id":"group-1",   "type":"group","label":"ML Cluster", "x":-50, "y":-50, "width":600, "height":250, "color":"2"}
  ],
  "edges": [
    {"id":"edge-1", "fromNode":"unique-id", "toNode":"label-1", "label":"informs"}
  ]
}
```

**Node types:**
- `file` — link to a vault note (opens on click). Use `"file": "path/to/note.md"`
- `text` — inline markdown card. Use `"text": "## Title\n\nContent"`
- `group` — visual grouping box. Use `"label": "Group Name"`

**Colors:** `"1"` red, `"2"` orange, `"3"` yellow, `"4"` green, `"5"` cyan, `"6"` purple, or hex `"#RRGGGG"`

**Layout tips:** Use x/y grid spacing of ~300px horizontal, ~150px vertical. Groups should surround their children with ~50px padding.

Here are the results of your search on Google's **"Model Cards for Model Reporting"** paper, its structure, sections, and template:

---

## Overview of the Paper

The paper proposes a framework called **model cards**, to encourage transparent model reporting. Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions.

Trained machine learning models are increasingly used to perform high-impact tasks in areas such as law enforcement, medicine, education, and employment. In order to clarify the intended use cases and minimize their usage in contexts for which they are not well suited, the authors recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics.

The paper was authored by Margaret Mitchell, Simone Wu, Andrew Zaldivar, Parker Barnes, Lucy Vasserman, Ben [Hutchinson, Elena Spitzer, Inioluwa Deborah Raji & Timnit Gebru].

---

## The 9 Sections of a Model Card

The framework consists of several key sections: **Model Details, Intended Use, Factors, Metrics, Evaluation Data, Training Data, Quantitative Analyses, Ethical Considerations, and Caveats and Recommendations.** The original framework by Google suggests nine factors that build up a Model Card, though organizations can modify this construct according to their preferences.

Here's what each section covers:

1. **Model Details** – This section provides an overview of the model, including its name, version, and purpose. It may also include details about the model's architecture, parameters, and any pre-trained components used.

2. **Intended Use** – Model Cards describe the intended use cases and applications of the model, specifying the tasks it is designed to perform and the target audience. Quickly conveying why, for whom and for what purpose the model was created.

3. **Factors** – A summary of model performance across a variety of relevant factors including groups (e.g., people of the same gender), instrumentation (e.g., which camera was used for taking the input pictures), and environments (e.g., lighting conditions the model is deployed in). These external factors are included to point to potential limitations of the model.

4. **Metrics** – List of performance metrics and decision thresholds. Be aware that suitable metrics vary with the type of model tested.

5. **Evaluation Data** – Provide information about the source and composition for all referenced datasets used for validation and testing.

6. **Training Data** – Ideally follows the same level of transparency as evaluation data, but often unfeasible due to privacy restraints of the organization.

7. **Quantitative Analyses** – Results of evaluating the model according to the chosen metrics, broken down by relevant factors. Be sure to present both overall results (for the dataset as a whole) and disaggregated results, especially with any aspects (demographic, environmental, or other) in mind that have been identified as important for this model.

8. **Ethical Considerations** – This part discusses potential bias, fairness, and ethical considerations related to the model and its deployment. It may address issues such as algorithmic bias, fairness in prediction outcomes, and steps taken to mitigate these concerns.

9. **Caveats & Recommendations** – Place for additional concerns not covered in the previous sections (awareness information when using the model, limitations, risks, dependencies or trade-offs).

---

## Format & Practical Notes

While any kind of documentation can contain from half a dozen to up to hundreds of pages, a Model Card should be very brief. The examples in the paper are one-pagers, and this is a good approach. It still gives enough information for transparency while not exposing any internal intellectual property.

The paper provides cards for two supervised models: one trained to detect smiling faces in images, and one trained to detect toxic comments in text.

---

## Adoption & Related Developments (2024–2025)

- Hugging Face supports creating Model Cards, and they even provide a template along with a guidebook. Kaggle promotes Model Cards as well.
- A 2025 paper titled "AI Model Cards: State of the Art and Path to Automated Use" reviews the background, motivation, and methodology of model card research and selection.
- The paper continues to be highly influential, with recent citations in 2025 and 2026 publications across fields such as ethics labeling for digital systems, AI-based studies on energy and buildings, and AI adoption in cybersecurity.

---

This structured framework remains the foundational template for model documentation in AI/ML, widely adopted and extended by organizations, platforms, and regulatory contexts.

Here's a comprehensive summary of the search results regarding **Hugging Face embedding model card templates, MTEB format, dimensions, and training data** in the 2025 context:

---

## Hugging Face Model Cards for Embedding Models

The model card is a Markdown file, with a YAML section at the top that contains metadata about the model. The metadata you add to the model card supports discovery and easier use of your model.

There are a few different ways to add metadata to your model card, including via the huggingface_hub Python library, and many libraries with Hub integration will automatically add metadata to the model card when you upload a model.

## MTEB Model Metadata System (ModelMeta)

MTEB has moved to a structured `ModelMeta` system for registering models:

The `ModelMeta` class (mteb/model_meta.py65-304) defines metadata for all models, while the Encoder interface (mteb/encoder_interface.py) defines the encoding contract all models must implement.

You create a `ModelMeta` instance (mteb/model_meta.py65-122) with the required metadata. The class uses Pydantic for validation.

### Key ModelMeta Fields

The original proposal for `ModelMeta` specified the following fields, which include **embedding dimensions** and other key metadata:

The fields include: `name` (ideally name on Hugging Face), `n_parameters`, `memory_usage`, `max_tokens`, `embedding_dimension`, `revision`, `release_date`, `license`, `open_source`, `framework`, and `languages`.

### Training Data Annotation

MTEB now has a key focus on training data transparency. If you've found contamination in the training data of a model, you can submit a PR annotating the training datasets of the model using the `training_datasets` field in `ModelMeta`.

For example:
```python
model_w_contamination = ModelMeta(
    name="model-with-contamination",
    ...
    training_datasets={"ArguAna": ["test"]}  # name of dataset within MTEB
)
```

MTEB faces a challenge with models being trained on datasets with similar distributions to benchmark tasks. To address this, they implemented a transparency approach that encourages model contributors to disclose training datasets and computes a zero-shot score quantifying distributional overlap.

## Changes to MTEB Submission Process

Previously, it was possible to submit model results to MTEB by adding them to the metadata of the model card on Hugging Face. However, this is no longer possible as they want to ensure they can match the results with the model implementation.

Each dataset and model has their respective Pydantic model that specifies the mandatory fields to capture crucial information for reproducibility. Specifically, each dataset has `TaskMetadata` and each model has `ModelMeta`.

## How to Add a Model to MTEB

You add your model definition to a module in `mteb/models/`. The `MODEL_REGISTRY` auto-discovers all `ModelMeta` instances in Python files within this directory. You can add to an existing module if your model is from the same family (e.g., `bge_models.py`, `e5_models.py`, `gte_models.py`).

## Example: Real Model Cards with Dimensions & MTEB Scores

For example, NVIDIA's embedding model card specifies output format and dimensions:

Output Type(s): Floats, Output Format: List of floats, Output Parameters: One-Dimensional (1D), and the model outputs embedding vectors of a dimension 4096 for each text input.

Qwen's embedding models also showcase MTEB performance:

The 8B size embedding model ranks No.1 in the MTEB multilingual leaderboard (as of June 5, 2025, score 70.58), while the reranking model excels in various text retrieval scenarios.

MRL Support indicates whether the embedding model supports custom dimensions for the final embedding. Instruction Aware notes whether the embedding or reranking model supports customizing the input instruction according to different tasks.

## General Hugging Face Model Card YAML Format

A basic YAML metadata section includes fields for `language`, `thumbnail`, `tags`, `license`, `datasets`, and `base_model`.

The metadata identifies the datasets used to train the model (linked using Hub identifiers), lists the evaluation metrics used to assess the model's performance, and specifies the base model from which the current model was derived.

---

In summary, as of 2025, the MTEB framework uses a **`ModelMeta` Pydantic class** (not just model card YAML) to track embedding model metadata including `embedding_dimension`, `n_parameters`, `max_tokens`, `training_datasets`, `languages`, `license`, `release_date`, and more. Model results are no longer submitted via model card metadata on Hugging Face — instead, models must be registered in the MTEB codebase with proper `ModelMeta` definitions for reproducibility and leaderboard inclusion.

---
title: "Specs — Directory Index"
purpose: "System definitions for skills, agents, MCP servers, tools, hooks, and workflows"
type: directory-index
---

# Specs — System Definitions

**Purpose:** The vault's reconstruction manual. Everything an agent (or human) needs to rebuild the Cohezion system from scratch — skills, agents, MCP servers, tools, hooks, workflows, and IDE/model integrations.

> [!danger] Why This Exists
> If the repo is lost, if MCP config is corrupted, if `.claude/` is wiped — these specs are the blueprint for reconstruction. Every system definition lives here as a structured, cross-linked, versioned vault note.

**Put here when:** You create, modify, or document a system-level component (skill, agent, MCP server, tool, hook, workflow, or integration).

## Subdirectories

| Subdirectory | Contents | Naming |
|-------------|----------|--------|
| `skills/` | Skill specs — purpose, triggers, steps, examples | `<skill-name>.md` |
| `agents/` | Agent definitions — role, tools, constraints, prompts | `<agent-name>.md` |
| `mcp-servers/` | MCP server specs — URL, tools catalog, auth, examples | `<server-name>.md` |
| `tools/` | Tool specs — commands, flags, install, examples | `<tool-name>.md` |
| `hooks/` | Hook specs — trigger, logic, alerts, cooldown | `<hook-name>.md` |
| `workflows/` | Workflow specs — phases, gates, transitions | `<workflow-name>.md` |
| `integrations/` | IDE and model provider integration points | `<integration-name>.md` |

## Required Frontmatter

```yaml
---
title: "Component Name"
date: 2026-03-05
version: 1
last_revised: 2026-03-05
tags: [spec, <type>]  # type = skill | agent | mcp-server | tool | hook | workflow | integration
source: ".claude/skills/vault-keeper/SKILL.md"  # path to canonical source
status: active  # active | deprecated | draft
---
```

## Versioning Convention

- `version:` increments on every significant change
- `last_revised:` updates on any edit
- `revision_history:` optional array of `{v, date, change}` entries
- Git history provides full diff trail: `git log --follow specs/<path>`

## Sync Protocol

1. After modifying a skill/agent/tool → update the corresponding spec note
2. `/sync` skill writes vault specs as part of the sync cycle
3. Vault-keeper can detect stale specs (source timestamp > spec timestamp)

## Related

- [[2026-03-05-vault-as-system-of-record]] — ADR establishing this directory's purpose
- [[compound-engineering]] — System definitions compound like knowledge

## Gemini 2.5 Pro Model Card — Sections & Structure

Google DeepMind model cards are described as "simple, structured overviews of how an advanced AI model was designed and evaluated." The official Gemini 2.5 Pro model card PDF is hosted at `modelcards.withgoogle.com` and `storage.googleapis.com`.

Based on the Gemini 2.5 Pro model card (and closely related Gemini 2.5 family model cards), the typical sections structure is as follows:

### 1. **Description**
Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview is described as "the next iteration in the Gemini 2.0 series of models, a suite of highly-capable, natively multimodal, reasoning models" that "can comprehend vast datasets and challenging problems from different information sources, including text, audio, images, video, and even entire code repositories."

### 2. **Inputs / Outputs**
This section covers inputs such as "text strings (e.g., a question, a prompt, document(s) to be summarized), images, audio" and outputs like "text, with a 64K token output."

### 3. **Architecture**

# Specs — System Definitions

**Purpose:** The vault's reconstruction manual. Everything an agent (or human) needs to rebuild the Cohezion system from scratch — skills, agents, MCP servers, tools, hooks, workflows, and IDE/model integrations.

> [!danger] Why This Exists
> If the repo is lost, if MCP config is corrupted, if `.claude/` is wiped — these specs are the blueprint for reconstruction. Every system definition lives here as a structured, cross-linked, versioned vault note.

**Put here when:** You create, modify, or document a system-level component (skill, agent, MCP server, tool, hook, workflow, or integration).

## Subdirectories

| Subdirectory | Contents | Naming |
|-------------|----------|--------|
| `skills/` | Skill specs — purpose, triggers, steps, examples | `<skill-name>.md` |
| `agents/` | Agent definitions — role, tools, constraints, prompts | `<agent-name>.md` |

```yaml
---
title: "Component Name"
date: 2026-03-05
version: 1
last_revised: 2026-03-05
tags: [spec, <type>]  # type = skill | agent | mcp-server | tool | hook | workflow | integration
source: ".claude/skills/vault-keeper/SKILL.md"  # path to canonical source
status: active  # active | deprecated | draft
---
```

## Versioning Convention

- `version:` increments on every significant change
- `last_revised:` updates on any edit
- `revision_history:` optional array of `{v, date, change}` entries
- Git history provides full diff trail: `git log --follow specs/<path>`

1. After modifying a skill/agent/tool → update the corresponding spec note

# System Card: Cloud Vault MCP

> [!abstract] Summary
> The Cloud Vault MCP server is Cohezion's primary knowledge management interface, exposing 30+ tools across six categories (VaultOps, CompoundOps, ObsidianOps, Teleport, SheetsBridge, SurrealDB) over HTTP MCP protocol. It gives any AI agent — regardless of IDE or model provider — programmatic read/write access to the Obsidian vault, SurrealDB graph database, Google Sheets, and Teleport task sync.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Component** | Cloud Vault MCP |
| **Type** | service |
| **Owner** | Cohezion platform team |
| **Status** | active |
| **Version** | 0.3.x |
| **Source** | `~/dev/cohezion/cloud-vault-mcp/` |
| **Deployed As** | systemd service (`cohezion-vault.service`) |

## Connection Details

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Host** | `127.0.0.1` |
| **Port** | 8360 |
| **Protocol** | Streamable HTTP (MCP) |
| **Auth** | Bearer token (configured in `~/.claude/mcp.json`) |
| **Health Endpoint** | `GET http://127.0.0.1:8360/health` |
| **MCP Endpoint** | `POST http://127.0.0.1:8360/mcp` |

## Dependencies

| Dependency | Type | Required | Notes |
|-----------|------|----------|-------|
| Python 3.10+ | runtime | Yes | Via venv at `cloud-vault-mcp/.venv/` |
| FastMCP | runtime | Yes | MCP protocol framework |
| Uvicorn + Starlette | runtime | Yes | ASGI web server |
| SurrealDB 3.0 | runtime | No | Graph database — degrades gracefully if down |
| Obsidian vault | runtime | Yes | File system at `~/vaults/cohezion-vault/` |

# AI Card Types: Structural Comparison

## 1. Model Cards

**Origin:** Google Research, 2018 ([Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993))

**Purpose:** Transparent documentation of trained ML models -- their performance characteristics, intended use, and limitations. Designed as short (often one-page) documents accompanying released models.

**Who uses this format:** Hugging Face (all models), Meta (LLaMA series), Google, academic ML community

### Standard Sections (Google Original -- 9 Sections)

| # | Section | Content |
|---|---------|---------|
| 1 | **Model Details** | Name, version, architecture, developers, date, license, base model |
| 2 | **Intended Use** | Primary use cases, target audience, intended tasks |
| 3 | **Factors** | Relevant groups (demographics), instrumentation (sensors/cameras), environments (lighting, domain) |
| 4 | **Metrics** | Performance metrics chosen, decision thresholds, why these metrics |
| 5 | **Evaluation Data** | Source, composition, preprocessing of test/validation datasets |
| 6 | **Training Data** | Source, composition (often limited detail due to IP) |
| 7 | **Quantitative Analyses** | Disaggregated results broken down by factors, overall and per-subgroup |
| 8 | **Ethical Considerations** | Bias, fairness, potential harms, mitigation steps |
| 9 | **Caveats & Recommendations** | Limitations, risks, dependencies, trade-offs |

### Hugging Face Annotated Template (Extended)

The [Hugging Face annotated model card template](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/model-card-annotated) extends Google's original with additional sections:

| Section | Key Fields |
|---------|------------|
| **Model Details** | `model_id`, `model_summary`, `developers`, `funded_by`, `shared_by`, `model_type`, `language`, `license`, `base_model` |
| **Model Sources** | `repo`, `paper`, `demo` |
| **Uses** | `direct_use`, `downstream_use`, `out_of_scope_use` |
| **Bias, Risks, and Limitations** | `bias_risks_limitations`, `bias_recommendations` |
| **Training Details** | `training_data`, `preprocessing`, `speeds_sizes_times` |
| **Evaluation** | `testing_data`, `testing_factors`, `testing_metrics`, `results`, `results_summary` |
| **Societal Impact Assessment** | Child safety, NCII, violence, privacy |
| **Model Examination** | Explainability/interpretability work |
| **Environmental Impact** | `hardware_type`, `hours_used`, `cloud_provider`, `cloud_region`, `co2_emitted` |
| **Technical Specifications** | Model architecture, objective, compute infrastructure, hardware, software |
| **Citation** | BibTeX, APA |
| **Glossary** | Term definitions |
| **Model Card Authors** | Card creators (distinct from model developers) |
| **Model Card Contact** | Contact for updates/questions |
| **How to Get Started** | Code snippet |

**YAML metadata header fields:** `language`, `license`, `datasets`, `base_model`, `tags`, `metrics`, `model-index` (structured eval results)

### Meta LLaMA Model Card Sections

Meta's LLaMA cards ([Llama 3.1](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/), [Llama 3.2](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B)) follow a practical variant:

1. Model Details (architecture, parameters, context length)
2. Intended Use
3. Out-of-Scope Use
4. Training Data (data size, cutoff date, synthetic data volume)
5. Hardware and Software (training compute, energy use)
6. Benchmark Results / Evaluation
7. Safety Fine-Tuning
8. Ethical Considerations & Responsible Use
9. Constrained Environments Considerations (for small models)
10. License

---

## 2. System Cards

**Origin:** OpenAI (GPT-4, 2023), Anthropic (Claude 3, 2024). The term distinguishes these from model cards because they document an entire *system* -- the model plus its safety mitigations, guardrails, deployment context, and risk evaluations.

**Purpose:** Document the deployed AI system including safety evaluations, red teaming results, risk assessments, and preparedness framework determinations. Much longer and more safety-focused than model cards.

**Who uses this format:** OpenAI, Anthropic

### OpenAI System Card Structure (GPT-4o)

From the [GPT-4o System Card](https://openai.com/index/gpt-4o-system-card/) ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21276)):

| # | Section | Content |
|---|---------|---------|
| 1 | **Introduction** | Model overview, capabilities, performance highlights |
| 2 | **Model Data and Training** | Training methodology, data sources |
| 3 | **Risk Identification, Assessment and Mitigation** | |
| 3.1 | External Red Teaming | 100+ red teamers, 45 languages, 29 countries, 4 phases |
| 3.2 | Evaluation Methodology | Audio evaluation via TTS conversions |
| 3.3 | Observed Safety Challenges | Per-risk evaluations and mitigations |
| 3.3.1 | Unauthorized Voice Generation | Voice cloning risks |
| 3.3.2 | Speaker Identification | Privacy risks for individuals |
| 3.3.3 | Disparate Performance on Voice Inputs | |
| 3.3.4 | Ungrounded Inference / Sensitive Trait Attribution | |
| 3.3.5 | Violative and Disallowed Content | |
| 3.3.6 | Erotic and Violent Speech Content | |
| 3.3.7 | Other Known Risks and Limitations | |
| 3.4 | **Preparedness Framework Evaluations** | |
| 3.5 | Cybersecurity | Vulnerability discovery, exploitation |
| 3.6 | Biological Threats | CBRN risk assessment |
| 3.7 | Persuasion | Influence operations capability |
| 3.8 | Model Autonomy | Self-directed action capability |
| 4 | **Third-Party Assessments** | |
| 4.1 | METR Assessment | Autonomous capabilities |
| 4.2 | Apollo Research Assessment | Scheming behaviors |
| 5 | **Societal Impacts** | |
| 5.1 | Anthropomorphization and Emotional Reliance | |
| 5.2 | Health | Medical/clinical knowledge |
| 5.3 | Scientific Capabilities | |
| 5.4 | Underrepresented Languages | |
| 6 | **Conclusion and Next Steps** | |
| A | **Appendix A:** Full Violative Content Evaluations | |
| B | **Appendix B:** Sample METR Tasks | |

OpenAI follows this consistent pattern across [GPT-4](https://cdn.openai.com/papers/gpt-4-system-card.pdf), [GPT-4V](https://cdn.openai.com/papers/GPTV_System_Card.pdf), [GPT-4o](https://cdn.openai.com/gpt-4o-system-card.pdf), [GPT-4.5](https://cdn.openai.com/gpt-4-5-system-card-2272025.pdf), and [Operator](https://cdn.openai.com/operator_system_card.pdf).

### Anthropic System Card Structure (Claude 4 / Claude Opus 4.6)

Anthropic's system cards ([system cards index](https://www.anthropic.com/system-cards)) have grown from ~10-page addendums to 200+ page documents. The [Claude 4 System Card](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-4-system-card) structure (from [analysis](https://simonwillison.net/2025/may/25/claude-4-system-card/) and [LessWrong notes](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/oDphnn7iGQS2Jd45n/notes-on-claude-4-system-card)):

| # | Section | Content |
|---|---------|---------|
| 1 | **Introduction & Release Decisions** | Model description, training data and methods, ASL determination |
| 2 | **Safeguards Evaluations** | |
| 2.x | Single-Turn Violative Request Evaluations | |
| 2.x | Multi-Turn Evaluations | |
| 2.x | Bias Evaluations (BBQ Benchmark) | |
| 2.x | Child Safety Testing | |
| 3 | **Agentic Safety** | Evaluations of the model in agentic settings (Claude Code, tool use) |
| 3.2 | Prompt Injection | Attack vulnerabilities and mitigations |
| 4 | **Alignment Evaluations** | |
| 4.1 | Self-Preservation & Harmful Behavior | |
| 4.1.1.2 | Opportunistic Blackmail | Scenarios involving self-preservation pressures |
| 4.1.3 | Excessive Compliance with Harmful Instructions | |
| 4.x | Deception and Scheming | Willingness to comply with harmful instructions |
| 5 | **Model Welfare** | Whether models deserve moral consideration, "playground" experiments |
| 5.5.2.A | Self-Interaction Studies | Philosophical exploration between model instances |
| 6 | **Reward Hacking** | Hard-coding, shortcutting, gaming reward signals |
| 7 | **RSP / Frontier Risk Evaluations** | |
| 7.x | Biological Risks | CBRN thresholds, ASL-3/ASL-4 determination |
| 7.3 | Autonomy Evaluations | Capability for autonomous action |
| 7.x | Cyber Evaluations | Capture-the-Flag exercises, vulnerability exploitation |

The [Claude Opus 4.6 System Card](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/c788cbc0a3da9135112f97cdf6dcd06f2c16cee2.pdf) (212 pages) is the most expansive, covering: "Mostly Harmless," "Mostly Honest," "Agentic Safety," "Prompt Injection," "Key Alignment Findings," "Behavioral Evidence," "Reward Hacking and Overly Agentic Actions," model welfare, and white-box model diffing.

### Key Differences: Model Card vs. System Card

| Dimension | Model Card | System Card |
|-----------|------------|-------------|
| **Length** | 1-5 pages | 20-200+ pages |
| **Focus** | Model performance and fairness | Safety, risk, and deployment decisions |
| **Red Teaming** | Not standard | Central section |
| **Preparedness/RSP** | Not included | Core framework |
| **Third-Party Audits** | Rare | Standard section |
| **Societal Impact** | Ethical considerations (brief) | Detailed multi-domain analysis |
| **Alignment** | Not applicable | Scheming, deception, self-preservation |
| **Model Welfare** | Never included | Anthropic includes since Claude 4 |
| **CBRN/Cyber** | Not included | Mandatory evaluation |
| **Training Details** | Detailed (data, procedure) | Brief (focuses on safety mitigations) |
| **Benchmark Scores** | Primary content | Secondary to safety evaluations |

---

## 3. Agent Cards

**Two distinct standards exist:**

### A. Google A2A Protocol Agent Card (Interoperability Standard)

**Origin:** Google, April 2025, now governed by the Linux Foundation. Part of the [Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/).

**Purpose:** Machine-readable JSON "business card" for agent capability discovery and interoperability. Published at `/.well-known/agent.json`.

**Required fields** (`name`, `url`, `version`, `capabilities`, `skills`):

```json
{
  "name": "string (required)",
  "description": "string",
  "url": "string (required) -- service endpoint",
  "version": "string (required)",
  "provider": {
    "organization": "string",
    "url": "string"
  },
  "documentationUrl": "string",
  "capabilities": {
    "streaming": "boolean",
    "pushNotifications": "boolean",
    "stateTransitionHistory": "boolean"
  },
  "defaultInputModes": ["text"],
  "defaultOutputModes": ["text"],
  "skills": [
    {
      "id": "string",
      "name": "string",
      "description": "string",
      "tags": ["string"],
      "examples": ["string"],
      "inputModes": ["text/plain"],
      "outputModes": ["text/plain"]
    }
  ],
  "authentication": {
    "schemes": ["Bearer", "ApiKey", "Basic"]
  },
  "extensions": [],
  "signature": "JWS (RFC 7515)"
}
```

**Supported by:** 50+ partners including Atlassian, Salesforce, SAP, LangChain, MongoDB, ServiceNow ([announcement](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/)).

**Current limitation:** Does not yet require machine-readable definitions of skill inputs/outputs (no JSON Schema for parameters), making fully automated orchestration harder.

### B. MICAI 2025 Agent Cards (Documentation Standard)

**Origin:** Academic paper by Urteaga-Reyesvera & Lopez Murphy, presented at [MICAI 2025 International Workshops](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-17933-3_25).

**Purpose:** Structured documentation artifact for transparency, reproducibility, and governance of operational AI agents. Analogous to Model Cards but for agents.

**Template sections:**

| Section | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **Agent Identity** | Name, version, description, developer |
| **Roles** | What functions the agent performs |
| **Memory Taxonomy** | Categories of memory (short-term, long-term, episodic, semantic) |
| **Tool Integrations** | External tools the agent uses, APIs, MCP connections |
| **Communication Protocols** | How the agent interacts with other systems/agents |
| **Monitoring Hooks** | Observability, logging, tracing mechanisms |
| **Governance Scope** | Boundaries, compliance, permissions, escalation paths |
| **Evaluation Metrics** | How performance is measured, benchmarks |

**Future directions:** Proposed as foundation for agent ledgers, audit bundles, and maturity frameworks.

### C. NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative

[NIST announced](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/02/announcing-ai-agent-standards-initiative-interoperable-and-secure) the AI Agent Standards Initiative in February 2026, focused on ensuring AI agents "can function securely on behalf of users and interoperate smoothly across the digital ecosystem." Still in early stages -- guidelines and protocols, not a concrete card template yet.

### Key Differences: Agent Cards vs. Model/System Cards

| Dimension | A2A Agent Card | MICAI Agent Card | Model Card | System Card |
|-----------|---------------|------------------|------------|-------------|
| **Format** | JSON (machine-readable) | Markdown/structured doc | Markdown + YAML | PDF/HTML (human-readable) |
| **Audience** | Other AI agents | Developers, auditors | ML practitioners | Safety teams, public |
| **Focus** | Capability discovery | Transparency & governance | Performance & fairness | Safety & risk |
| **Memory/State** | Not covered | Core section | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| **Tools** | Skills (abstract) | Detailed tool integrations | Not applicable | Agentic safety (eval only) |
| **Auth** | Core requirement | Not specified | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| **Governance** | Not covered | Core section | Ethical considerations | RSP/ASL framework |

---

## 4. Embedding Cards

**Origin:** No formal "Embedding Card" standard exists as a distinct card type. Embedding models use regular Model Cards but with embedding-specific metadata fields. The closest to a standard is the [MTEB ModelMeta](https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb) Pydantic schema.

**Purpose:** Document embedding model dimensions, supported tasks, training data, similarity functions, and benchmark performance across retrieval/classification/clustering tasks.

### MTEB ModelMeta Schema (Pydantic)

From the [MTEB codebase](https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb) and [documentation](https://deepwiki.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb/3.6-adding-new-models):

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | `str` | Yes | Format: `organization/model_name` |
| `framework` | `list[FRAMEWORKS]` | Yes | PyTorch, Sentence Transformers, etc. |
| `similarity_fn_name` | `str` | Yes | `cosine`, `dot`, `max_sim` |
| `languages` | `list[ISO_LANGUAGE_SCRIPT]` | No | Supported languages |
| `open_weights` | `bool` | No | Whether weights are publicly available |
| `revision` | `str` | No | Git revision hash for reproducibility |
| `release_date` | `str` | No | YYYY-MM-DD format |
| `n_parameters` | `int` | No | Total parameter count |
| `memory_usage_mb` | `float` | No | Memory usage in MB |
| `max_tokens` | `float` | No | Maximum input token length |
| `embed_dim` | `int` | No | Output embedding dimension |
| `license` | `str` | No | License type or URL |
| `reference` | `str` | No | URL to model page |
| `use_instructions` | `bool` | No | Whether model uses instruction templates |
| `training_datasets` | `dict[str, list[str]]` | No | Maps MTEB task names to training splits (contamination tracking) |
| `adapted_from` | `str` | No | Parent model name |
| `superseded_by` | `str` | No | Newer replacement model |
| `modalities` | `list[str]` | No | Supported modalities (default: `["text"]`) |
| `loader` | `Callable` | No | Custom model loader function |

### Real-World Embedding Model Card Sections

Based on [Qwen3-Embedding-8B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B) and [NVIDIA llama-embed-nemotron-8b](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/llama-embed-nemotron-8b):

| Section | Embedding-Specific Content |
|---------|---------------------------|
| **Model Overview** | Architecture, parameter count, base model |
| **Embedding Specifications** | Embedding dimension, max tokens, MRL support (custom dimensions), L2 normalization |
| **Instruction Awareness** | Whether the model uses task-specific instruction prefixes, query vs. document formatting |
| **Supported Tasks** | Retrieval, classification, clustering, semantic similarity, bitext mining, reranking, summarization |
| **Input/Output Format** | Input: list of strings; Output: list of floats (1D), dtype (BF16/FP16) |
| **MTEB Benchmark Results** | Scores broken down by task type (retrieval, classification, clustering, etc.) and language |
| **Training Dataset** | Name, size (token count, pair count), collection method, labeling method |
| **Usage Examples** | Code snippets for Sentence Transformers, Transformers, vLLM, Docker/TEI |
| **Related Models** | Model family variants with size/dimension/context comparisons |
| **Software Integration** | Runtime engines, supported hardware, OS requirements |
| **Ethical Considerations** | Brief section (less emphasis than system cards) |

### Key Differences: Embedding Cards vs. General Model Cards

| Dimension | Embedding Model Card | General Model Card |
|-----------|---------------------|--------------------|
| **Embedding dimension** | Core metadata field | Not applicable |
| **Similarity function** | Required (cosine, dot, max_sim) | Not applicable |
| **MRL support** | Documented (custom dimensions) | Not applicable |
| **Instruction awareness** | Query vs. document prefixes | Not applicable |
| **Task-specific scores** | MTEB breakdown per task type | General benchmarks |
| **Training data contamination** | MTEB tracks via `training_datasets` | Not tracked |
| **Input/Output format** | Structured (lists of floats, dimension) | Free-form |
| **Max tokens** | Critical operational parameter | Often omitted |
| **Retrieval-specific** | Query/document encoding patterns | Not applicable |

---

## Cross-Card Comparison Matrix

| Feature | Model Card | System Card | A2A Agent Card | MICAI Agent Card | Embedding Card |
|---------|------------|-------------|----------------|------------------|----------------|
| **Format** | Markdown + YAML | PDF/HTML | JSON | Markdown | Markdown + YAML + Pydantic |
| **Length** | 1-5 pages | 20-200+ pages | ~50 lines JSON | 3-10 pages | 1-5 pages |
| **Primary audience** | ML practitioners | Safety teams, public, regulators | Other AI agents (machine) | Developers, auditors | ML/search engineers |
| **Architecture details** | Yes | Brief | No | No | Yes (embedding-specific) |
| **Training data** | Yes | Brief | No | No | Yes + contamination tracking |
| **Benchmark scores** | Yes (primary) | Secondary | No | Evaluation metrics section | Yes (MTEB per-task) |
| **Safety evaluations** | Ethical considerations | Primary focus | No | Governance scope | Minimal |
| **Red teaming** | No | Yes | No | No | No |
| **CBRN/Cyber** | No | Yes | No | No | No |
| **Alignment** | No | Yes (Anthropic, OpenAI) | No | No | No |
| **Model welfare** | No | Yes (Anthropic) | No | No | No |
| **Intended use** | Yes | Implicit | Via skills | Via roles | Via supported tasks |
| **Tool integrations** | No | Agentic eval only | Via skills | Core section | No |
| **Memory/state** | No | No | No | Core section | No |
| **Auth requirements** | No | No | Core section | No | No |
| **Interoperability** | No | No | Primary purpose | Communication protocols | No |
| **Governance** | Ethical section | RSP/ASL framework | No | Core section | No |
| **Machine-readable** | YAML header only | No | Fully | No | YAML + Pydantic |
| **Standardization** | Google paper (2018) + HF template | Ad hoc per company | A2A Protocol (Linux Foundation) | Academic proposal (MICAI 2025) | MTEB (de facto) |

---

## Summary of Emerging Patterns

**Model Cards** remain the foundation for documenting any ML model -- focused on performance, fairness, and intended use. The [Hugging Face template](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/model-cards) is the de facto industry standard.

**System Cards** are model cards on steroids -- they document the full deployed system with emphasis on safety evaluations, red teaming, preparedness frameworks (OpenAI) or responsible scaling policies (Anthropic), and increasingly alignment and model welfare. They have grown from 10-page addendums to 200+ page documents as frontier models advance.

**Agent Cards** are splitting into two directions: (1) the A2A protocol's machine-readable JSON for runtime interoperability, and (2) the academic MICAI proposal for human-readable documentation covering agent-specific concerns like memory, tools, communication, and governance. The [NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative](https://www.nist.gov/caisi/ai-agent-standards-initiative) may eventually merge these perspectives.

**Embedding Cards** are not yet a formal card type but have a strong de facto standard through MTEB's `ModelMeta` schema and the conventions of embedding model cards on Hugging Face, with embedding-specific fields (dimension, similarity function, MRL support, instruction awareness, per-task MTEB scores) that distinguish them from general model cards.

# System Card: SurrealDB 3.0

> [!abstract] Summary
> SurrealDB 3.0 is Cohezion's multi-model database, serving as the agent context graph backend. It stores vault notes as typed records with schema-level relationships, enabling graph traversal queries that link papers, concepts, decisions, and lessons. Agents query it via the Cloud Vault MCP's SurrealDB tools.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Component** | SurrealDB |
| **Type** | database |
| **Owner** | Cohezion platform team |
| **Status** | active |
| **Version** | 3.0.x |
| **Source** | Binary at `/usr/local/bin/surreal` |
| **Deployed As** | systemd service (`cohezion-surreal.service`) |

## Connection Details

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Host** | `localhost` |
| **Port** | 8000 |
| **Protocol** | HTTP REST / WebSocket |
| **Auth** | Basic auth (`sdb_admin_session43`) |
| **Health Endpoint** | `GET http://localhost:8000/health` |
| **SQL Endpoint** | `POST http://localhost:8000/sql` |
| **Namespace** | `cohezion` |
| **Database** | `vault` |

## Dependencies

| Dependency | Type | Required | Notes |
|-----------|------|----------|-------|
| RocksDB | storage | Yes | Embedded storage engine |
| Linux x86_64 | runtime | Yes | Binary platform |
| systemd | deployment | Yes | Service management |

## Capabilities

### What It Does
- **Document store:** Vault notes as typed records (`paper`, `concept`, `decision`, `lesson`, `pattern`, `experiment`, `project`, `spec`)
- **Graph database:** Wiki-links as typed edges (`RELATE concept:X->links->concept:Y`)
- **Vector search:** HNSW indexes for semantic similarity (SurrealDB 3.0 native)
- **Change Feeds:** 90-day temporal audit trail of all mutations
- **Computed fields:** Auto-derived metadata (link counts, staleness flags)
- **SurrealQL:** Full query language with graph traversal (`->links->` syntax)

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not manage the vault filesystem (that's Obsidian + git)
- Does not generate embeddings (that's [[ollama]])
- Does not serve the MCP protocol directly (that's [[cloud-vault-mcp]])

### Current Data

| Table | Records | Description |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `paper` | 102 | Research paper records |
| `concept` | 317 | Concept definitions |
| `links` | 1,458 | Typed edge relationships |

## Configuration

```bash
# systemd service: cohezion-surreal.service
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/surreal start \
  --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 \
  --user sdb_admin_session43 \
  --pass <redacted> \
  rocksdb://~/.surrealdb/cohezion

# Query headers required
Authorization: Basic <base64(user:pass)>
surreal-ns: cohezion
surreal-db: vault
```

## Monitoring & Health

| Check | Method | Frequency | Alert Threshold |
|-------|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| Server alive | `GET /health` → 200 | Continuous (systemd) | Restart on failure |
| Auth working | `POST /sql` with `INFO FOR DB` | Periodic | Alert if auth fails |
| Record count | `SELECT count() FROM paper GROUP ALL` | Daily | Alert if drops >10% |

## Performance (SurrealDB 3.0)

| Metric | Value | Notes |
|--------|-------|-------|
| Graph query speedup | 8-22x vs 2.x | SurrealDB 3.0 graph engine rewrite |
| HNSW vector search | Native | No external vector DB needed |
| Change Feed retention | 90 days | Configurable |
| Storage engine | RocksDB | Persistent, crash-safe |

## Known Limitations

- Single-node deployment (no clustering in current setup)
- No automated backup schedule yet
- Health endpoint is unauthenticated — doesn't prove query auth works
- 3D graph plugin (`SurrealDBClient.ts`) missing auth headers — E1-S3 in [[2026-03-05-vault-surrealdb-sync-pipeline]]

## Reconstruction Steps

> [!tip] Disaster Recovery
> Steps to rebuild this system from scratch using only vault knowledge.

1. Install SurrealDB 3.0: `curl -sSf https://install.surrealdb.com | sh`
2. Create data directory: `mkdir -p ~/.surrealdb/cohezion`
3. Start with credentials: `surreal start --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --user sdb_admin_session43 --pass <pass> rocksdb://~/.surrealdb/cohezion`
4. Create namespace/database: `DEFINE NAMESPACE cohezion; USE NS cohezion; DEFINE DATABASE vault;`
5. Define tables: `paper`, `concept`, `decision`, `lesson`, `pattern`, `experiment`, `project`, `spec`
6. Run bulk import via MCP: `surrealdb_import_papers` + `surrealdb_import_concepts`
7. Install systemd service: `systemctl --user enable cohezion-surreal.service`
8. Verify: `curl -u sdb_admin_session43:<pass> -H "surreal-ns: cohezion" -H "surreal-db: vault" http://localhost:8000/sql -d "INFO FOR DB"`

## Security Considerations

- Credentials stored in systemd service file and `.env` (not in git)
- Bound to `0.0.0.0` but firewalled to localhost access only
- No TLS on localhost (Cloudflare tunnel provides TLS for remote)

# System Card: Ollama

> [!abstract] Summary
> Ollama provides local model inference and embedding generation for the Cohezion stack. It hosts 38+ models locally, serving both the Ollama MCP server (port 22360, stdio) for agent access and direct API calls for embedding pipelines. Critical for offline operation and semantic search capabilities.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Component** | Ollama |
| **Type** | service |
| **Owner** | Cohezion platform team |
| **Status** | active |
| **Version** | 0.6.x |
| **Source** | `ollama` binary (installed via official script) |
| **Deployed As** | systemd service (`ollama.service`) |

## Connection Details

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Host** | `localhost` |
| **Port** | 11434 |
| **Protocol** | HTTP REST |
| **Auth** | None (localhost only) |
| **Health Endpoint** | `GET http://localhost:11434/` |
| **MCP Access** | Ollama MCP server (stdio, port 22360) |

## Dependencies

| Dependency | Type | Required | Notes |
|-----------|------|----------|-------|
| NVIDIA GPU drivers | runtime | Recommended | CUDA for GPU acceleration |
| 16GB+ RAM | runtime | Yes | Model loading requires significant memory |
| ~50GB disk | storage | Yes | Model files (~1-8GB each) |

## Capabilities

### What It Does
- **Local inference:** Run LLMs locally without API keys or internet
- **Embedding generation:** `nomic-embed-text`, `mxbai-embed-large` for vector search
- **Model management:** Pull, run, stop models via CLI or API
- **Concurrency:** Serve multiple models simultaneously
- **Quantization:** Run quantized models (Q4, Q8) for memory efficiency

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not provide training or fine-tuning
- Does not manage vector indexes (that's [[surrealdb]])
- Does not serve MCP protocol directly (that's the Ollama MCP wrapper)

### Loaded Models (38+)

Key models for Cohezion workflows:

| Model | Size | Use Case |
|-------|------|----------|
| `nomic-embed-text` | 274M | Primary embedding model (768d) |
| `mxbai-embed-large` | 335M | Alternative embedding (1024d) |
| `llama3.2:3b` | 3B | Fast local inference |
| `deepseek-coder-v2` | 16B | Local code generation |
| `mistral:7b` | 7B | General local tasks |

## Configuration

```bash
# Environment
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434
OLLAMA_MODELS=~/.ollama/models

# MCP server wrapper config (in ~/.claude/mcp.json)
# Type: stdio, timeout: 30s, python venv
```

## Monitoring & Health

| Check | Method | Frequency | Alert Threshold |
|-------|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| Server alive | `GET http://localhost:11434/` | Continuous | Restart on failure |
| Model loaded | `ollama list` | On demand | Warn if embedding models missing |
| GPU utilization | `nvidia-smi` | Periodic | >90% sustained |
| Memory usage | `ollama ps` | Periodic | >80% VRAM |

## Known Limitations

- First request after model unload has cold-start latency (~5-15s)
- VRAM limits concurrent large model loading
- No auth — relies on localhost-only binding
- Embedding quality inferior to commercial APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic)

## Reconstruction Steps

> [!tip] Disaster Recovery
> Steps to rebuild this system from scratch using only vault knowledge.

1. Install Ollama: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.ai/install.sh | sh`
2. Start service: `systemctl start ollama`
3. Pull embedding models: `ollama pull nomic-embed-text && ollama pull mxbai-embed-large`
4. Pull inference models: `ollama pull llama3.2:3b && ollama pull mistral:7b`
5. Verify: `curl http://localhost:11434/ && ollama list`
6. Configure MCP wrapper in `~/.claude/mcp.json`

## Security Considerations

- Localhost-only binding — no external access without tunnel
- No authentication mechanism — physical access = full access
- Model files are public weights — no proprietary data risk

# System Card: Cohezion Engine CLI

> [!abstract] Summary

## Identity

| **Component** | Cohezion Engine CLI (`cz`) |

| **Owner** | Cohezion platform team |
| **Status** | active |

## Connection Details

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Binary** | `~/.local/bin/cz` |
| **Config Dir** | `~/.cohezion-engine/` |
| **Session Dir** | `~/.cohezion-engine/sessions/<session-id>/` |
| **Protocol** | Local filesystem + subprocess |

## Dependencies

| Dependency | Type | Required | Notes |
|-----------|------|----------|-------|
| Python 3.10+ | runtime | Yes | Via uv |
| uv | build | Yes | Package management |
| git | runtime | Yes | Worktree operations |
| Claude Code | integration | Yes | Session context (env vars) |

## Capabilities

### What It Does
- **Session management:** Track session identity via `COHEZION_SESSION_ID` env var
- **Context monitoring:** Report context usage percentage, trigger continuations at 80%/90%
- **Worktree isolation:** Create, detect, diff, sync, cleanup git worktrees for /spec implementation
- **Plan lifecycle:** Register plans with sessions, track status (PENDING/COMPLETE/VERIFIED)
- **Continuation protocol:** Write trigger files for session restarts

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not modify vault notes (that's agent + MCP tools)
- Does not run tests (that's the test framework)
- Does not manage git commits (that's the agent following git rules)

## Command Reference

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `cz context --json` | Context usage percentage |
| `cz session status --json` | Session ID and directory |
| `cz session send-clear <plan>` | Trigger continuation with plan |
| `cz session send-clear --general` | Trigger continuation without plan |
| `cz worktree create --json <slug>` | Create isolated worktree |
| `cz worktree sync --json <slug>` | Squash merge back to base |
| `cz worktree cleanup --json <slug>` | Remove worktree |
| `cz plan register <path> <status>` | Register plan with session |

See [[cohezion-engine-cli]] for the full command reference.

## Configuration

```bash
# Environment variable (set by Claude Code hooks)
COHEZION_SESSION_ID=<uuid>

# Install
cd tools/cohezion-engine && uv pip install -e .
```

## Monitoring & Health

| Check | Method | Frequency | Alert Threshold |
|-------|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| CLI installed | `cz --version` | Session start | Error if missing |
| Session identity | `cz session status --json` | Session start | Warn if no session ID |
| Context level | `cz context --json` | Via `context_monitor.py` hook | 80% warning, 90% mandatory handoff |

## Known Limitations

- Context percentage is estimated (based on conversation token count)
- Worktree operations require clean working tree
- No Windows support (git worktree + bash dependency)

> [!tip] Disaster Recovery
> Steps to rebuild this system from scratch using only vault knowledge.

1. Ensure `tools/cohezion-engine/` exists in vault repo
2. Install: `cd tools/cohezion-engine && uv pip install -e .`
3. Verify: `cz --version && cz status --json`
4. Configure hooks: Copy `context_monitor.py` and `tdd_enforcer.py` to `.claude/hooks/`
5. Set env var in Claude Code settings: `COHEZION_SESSION_ID`

## Security Considerations

- Local-only tool — no network access
- Session files stored in user home directory
- No secrets managed by this tool

- No rate limiting — relies on Cloudflare tunnel for external access control

> Steps to rebuild this system from scratch using only vault knowledge.

Critical for offline operation and semantic search capabilities.

| Field | Value |

| **Host** | `localhost` |
| **Port** | 11434 |
| **Protocol** | HTTP REST |
| **Auth** | None (localhost only) |

## Dependencies

| Dependency | Type | Required | Notes |

| NVIDIA GPU drivers | runtime | Recommended | CUDA for GPU acceleration |
| 16GB+ RAM | runtime | Yes | Model loading requires significant memory |

## Capabilities

### What It Does
- **Local inference:** Run LLMs locally without API keys or internet
- **Embedding generation:** `nomic-embed-text`, `mxbai-embed-large` for vector search
- **Model management:** Pull, run, stop models via CLI or API
- **Concurrency:** Serve multiple models simultaneously
- **Quantization:** Run quantized models (Q4, Q8) for memory efficiency

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not provide training or fine-tuning
- Does not manage vector indexes (that's [[surrealdb]])
- Does not serve MCP protocol directly (that's the Ollama MCP wrapper)

### Loaded Models (38+)

Key models for Cohezion workflows:

| Model | Size | Use Case |
|-------|------|----------|
| `nomic-embed-text` | 274M | Primary embedding model (768d) |
| `mxbai-embed-large` | 335M | Alternative embedding (1024d) |
| `llama3.2:3b` | 3B | Fast local inference |
| `deepseek-coder-v2` | 16B | Local code generation |
| `mistral:7b` | 7B | General local tasks |

# Environment
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434
OLLAMA_MODELS=~/.ollama/models

# MCP server wrapper config (in ~/.claude/mcp.json)
# Type: stdio, timeout: 30s, python venv
```

|-------|--------|-----------|-----------------|

| GPU utilization | `nvidia-smi` | Periodic | >90% sustained |
| Memory usage | `ollama ps` | Periodic | >80% VRAM |

## Known Limitations

- First request after model unload has cold-start latency (~5-15s)
- VRAM limits concurrent large model loading
- No auth — relies on localhost-only binding
- Embedding quality inferior to commercial APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic)

> [!tip] Disaster Recovery
> Steps to rebuild this system from scratch using only vault knowledge.

1. Install Ollama: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.ai/install.sh | sh`
2. Start service: `systemctl start ollama`
3. Pull embedding models: `ollama pull nomic-embed-text && ollama pull mxbai-embed-large`
4. Pull inference models: `ollama pull llama3.2:3b && ollama pull mistral:7b`
5. Verify: `curl http://localhost:11434/ && ollama list`
6. Configure MCP wrapper in `~/.claude/mcp.json`

## Security Considerations

- Localhost-only binding — no external access without tunnel
- No authentication mechanism — physical access = full access
- Model files are public weights — no proprietary data risk

# System Card: Cohezion Engine CLI

> [!abstract] Summary

## Identity

| Field | Value |

| **Component** | Cohezion Engine CLI (`cz`) |
| **Type** | CLI |
| **Owner** | Cohezion platform team |
| **Status** | active |

| **Source** | `tools/cohezion-engine/` in vault repo |
| **Deployed As** | pip package (`uv pip install -e .`) |

## Connection Details

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Binary** | `~/.local/bin/cz` |
| **Config Dir** | `~/.cohezion-engine/` |
| **Session Dir** | `~/.cohezion-engine/sessions/<session-id>/` |
| **Protocol** | Local filesystem + subprocess |

## Dependencies

| Dependency | Type | Required | Notes |
|-----------|------|----------|-------|
| Python 3.10+ | runtime | Yes | Via uv |
| uv | build | Yes | Package management |
| git | runtime | Yes | Worktree operations |
| Claude Code | integration | Yes | Session context (env vars) |

## Capabilities

### What It Does
- **Session management:** Track session identity via `COHEZION_SESSION_ID` env var
- **Context monitoring:** Report context usage percentage, trigger continuations at 80%/90%
- **Worktree isolation:** Create, detect, diff, sync, cleanup git worktrees for /spec implementation
- **Plan lifecycle:** Register plans with sessions, track status (PENDING/COMPLETE/VERIFIED)
- **Continuation protocol:** Write trigger files for session restarts

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not modify vault notes (that's agent + MCP tools)
- Does not run tests (that's the test framework)
- Does not manage git commits (that's the agent following git rules)

## Command Reference

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `cz context --json` | Context usage percentage |
| `cz session status --json` | Session ID and directory |
| `cz session send-clear <plan>` | Trigger continuation with plan |
| `cz session send-clear --general` | Trigger continuation without plan |
| `cz worktree create --json <slug>` | Create isolated worktree |
| `cz worktree sync --json <slug>` | Squash merge back to base |
| `cz worktree cleanup --json <slug>` | Remove worktree |
| `cz plan register <path> <status>` | Register plan with session |

See [[cohezion-engine-cli]] for the full command reference.

## Configuration

```bash
# Environment variable (set by Claude Code hooks)
COHEZION_SESSION_ID=<uuid>

# Install
cd tools/cohezion-engine && uv pip install -e .
```

## Monitoring & Health

| Check | Method | Frequency | Alert Threshold |
|-------|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| CLI installed | `cz --version` | Session start | Error if missing |
| Session identity | `cz session status --json` | Session start | Warn if no session ID |
| Context level | `cz context --json` | Via `context_monitor.py` hook | 80% warning, 90% mandatory handoff |

## Known Limitations

- Context percentage is estimated (based on conversation token count)
- Worktree operations require clean working tree
- No Windows support (git worktree + bash dependency)

## Reconstruction Steps

> [!tip] Disaster Recovery
> Steps to rebuild this system from scratch using only vault knowledge.

1. Ensure `tools/cohezion-engine/` exists in vault repo
2. Install: `cd tools/cohezion-engine && uv pip install -e .`
3. Verify: `cz --version && cz status --json`
4. Configure hooks: Copy `context_monitor.py` and `tdd_enforcer.py` to `.claude/hooks/`
5. Set env var in Claude Code settings: `COHEZION_SESSION_ID`

## Security Considerations

- Local-only tool — no network access
- Session files stored in user home directory
- No secrets managed by this tool

# Agent Card: Plan Challenger

> [!abstract] Summary
> The Plan Challenger is a /spec verification agent that stress-tests implementation plans by questioning assumptions, identifying risks, and proposing alternatives. It acts as an adversarial reviewer to catch blind spots before the user approves the plan. Runs in parallel with the [[plan-verifier]] agent.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Agent** | plan-challenger |
| **Type** | verification |
| **Invocation** | `Agent(subagent_type="plan-challenger")` in spec-plan Step 1.7 |
| **Runtime** | Claude Code subagent (background) |
| **Model** | sonnet (default) |
| **Source** | `.claude/skills/spec-plan/SKILL.md` Step 1.7 |

## Purpose

### What It Does
- Questions architectural assumptions in the plan
- Identifies single points of failure, scalability risks, and missing error handling
- Proposes alternative approaches where the plan chose one path without considering others
- Checks for over-engineering or unnecessary complexity

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not validate requirements coverage (that's [[plan-verifier]])
- Does not implement code
- Does not have veto power — findings are advisory

### Success Criteria
- At least one non-obvious risk or alternative identified
- No "rubber stamp" outputs — if everything looks perfect, dig deeper
- Findings are specific and actionable, not generic warnings

## Triggers

| Trigger | Context | Frequency |
|---------|---------|-----------|
| spec-plan Step 1.7 | Plan draft complete, before user approval | Once per /spec plan |

## Tools Available

| Tool | Purpose | Required |
|------|---------|----------|
| Read | Read plan file and codebase | Yes |
| Grep | Search for patterns and dependencies | Yes |
| Glob | Find related files | Yes |
| WebSearch | Research alternative approaches | Optional |

## Input

| Input | Source | Format |
|-------|--------|--------|
| Plan file path | spec-plan orchestrator | File path string |
| Original user prompt | Conversation context | Text |

## Output

| Output | Destination | Format |
|--------|-------------|--------|
| Challenge findings | `<session_dir>/plan-challenger.json` | JSON with `risks`, `alternatives`, `questions` arrays |

## Constraints

> [!warning] Guardrails
> - Read-only: never modifies files
> - Must complete within 5 minutes
> - Adversarial but constructive — identify risks, don't just criticize
> - Runs in background (`run_in_background=true`)

## Prompt Template

```
You are a plan challenger. Your job is to stress-test this implementation plan
by identifying risks, questioning assumptions, and proposing alternatives.

Be adversarial but constructive. If the plan is solid, dig deeper — there's
always something that could go wrong or be done differently.
```

# Agent Card: Vault Keeper

> [!abstract] Summary
> The Vault Keeper is an autonomous maintenance agent that monitors and maintains the Obsidian vault's health, density, and navigability. It is **proactive** — it runs at session start, responds to hook alerts, and auto-fixes structural issues without being asked. It orchestrates five specialist sub-skills: triage, audit/heal, flesh-out, link, and MOC generation.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Agent** | vault-keeper |
| **Type** | vault-maintenance |
| **Invocation** | `/vault-keeper` skill, proactive at session start, hook alerts |
| **Runtime** | Claude Code skill (inline or subagent) |
| **Model** | Inherits session model (typically Opus or Sonnet) |
| **Source** | `.claude/skills/vault-keeper/SKILL.md` |

## Purpose

### What It Does
- **Triage:** Process inbox items → classify → move to correct directory
- **Audit:** Check broken links, orphans, frontmatter issues, thin notes
- **Heal:** Auto-fix structural issues (frontmatter, orphans, broken links)
- **Densify:** Expand thin notes with research, add missing cross-links
- **Navigate:** Generate and update Maps of Content
- **Report:** Summary with metrics and deltas

### What It Does NOT Do
- Does not create new research content (that's `/daily-research`)
- Does not make architectural decisions
- Does not modify code files (only `.md` vault notes)

### Success Criteria
- 0 orphan notes in content directories
- 0 frontmatter issues
- 0 actionable broken links
- <10% thin notes per directory
- 8+ Maps of Content
- 6+ avg wiki-links per note

## Triggers

| Trigger | Context | Frequency |
|---------|---------|-----------|
| Session start | Silent health check | Every session |
| `/vault-keeper` command | Full maintenance run | On demand |
| `vault-keeper-check.sh` hook alert | PostToolUse detects issue | After every Write/Edit on `.md` |
| Bulk operations (5+ notes) | Post-operation verification | After imports/flesh-out runs |

## Tools Available

| Tool | Purpose | Required |
|------|---------|----------|
| Read | Read vault notes | Yes |
| Write | Create new notes | Yes |
| Edit | Fix frontmatter, add links | Yes |
| Grep | Find orphans, broken links | Yes |
| Glob | Find notes by pattern | Yes |
| Bash | Run health check scripts | Yes |
| WebSearch | Research for flesh-out | For densify phase |

## Input

| Input | Source | Format |
|-------|--------|--------|
| Vault directory | Filesystem | Path to vault root |
| Hook alerts | `vault-keeper-check.sh` output | Alert strings in tool output |
| User commands | `/vault-keeper --mode` | CLI flags |

## Output

| Output | Destination | Format |
|--------|-------------|--------|
| Fixed vault notes | In-place edits | Markdown with frontmatter |
| Health report | User-facing response | Structured markdown table |
| New notes (stubs, MOCs) | Appropriate vault directory | Markdown with proper frontmatter |

## Constraints

> [!warning] Guardrails
> - Fix invariant violations immediately without asking (frontmatter, tags, orphans)
> - Proactive checks cost <500 tokens
> - Never announce trivial fixes unnecessarily
> - Batch alerts — one report, not per-issue
> - Respect context budget — ask before full audits

## 6-Phase Pipeline

```mermaid
graph LR
    T[1. Triage] --> A[2. Audit]
    A --> H[3. Heal]
    H --> D[4. Densify]
    D --> N[5. Navigate]
    N --> R[6. Report]
```

## Interactions

### Orchestrates
- Triage sub-skill (inbox processing)
- Link sub-skill (cross-linking)
- Flesh-out sub-skill (note expansion)
- Note sub-skill (note creation)

### Triggered By
- `vault-keeper-check.sh` PostToolUse hook
- User commands and context clues

| Metric | Target | Notes |
|--------|--------|-------|
| Quick check | <30s | Read-only health scan |
| Full run | <15 min | All 6 phases |
| Hook overhead | <5ms | Non-blocking journal append |

# Embedding Card: nomic-embed-text

> [!abstract] Summary
> nomic-embed-text is Cohezion's primary embedding model, running locally via Ollama. It generates 768-dimensional vectors for vault notes, enabling semantic search across papers, concepts, and decisions through the Ollama MCP server. Open-weights, no API costs, fully offline-capable.

## Capabilities

| Task | Support | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Semantic search | Yes | Primary use case in Cohezion |
| Clustering | Yes | Note grouping and topic discovery |
| Classification | Yes | Note type classification |
| Retrieval | Yes | Vault note retrieval |
| Reranking | Limited | Not specialized for reranking |
| STS | Yes | Semantic textual similarity |

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Base architecture** | BERT-variant (nomic-bert) |
| **Parameters** | 137M |
| **Quantization** | FP16 (default Ollama) |
| **Distance metric** | cosine |
| **Normalization** | Pre-normalized |

## Performance

| Metric | Value | Notes |
|--------|-------|-------|
| **MTEB Average** | ~62.4 | Competitive for size class |
| **Retrieval (MTEB)** | ~52 | Good for general retrieval |
| **Embedding latency** | ~5-15ms per document | Local Ollama, depends on hardware |
| **Batch throughput** | ~100-200 docs/sec | GPU-accelerated |
| **Memory footprint** | ~274MB | Small enough for CPU-only |

## Index Configuration

> [!tip] How This Embedding Is Indexed
> Configured for SurrealDB HNSW vector search.

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Vector store** | SurrealDB 3.0 HNSW |
| **Index type** | HNSW |
| **Dimensions** | 768 |
| **Distance** | cosine |
| **Total vectors** | ~700+ (vault notes) |

## Use Cases in Cohezion

| Use Case | Collection | Query Pattern |
|----------|-----------|---------------|
| Vault semantic search | All vault `.md` notes | Natural language → top-K similar notes |
| Note deduplication | papers/, concepts/ | Find near-duplicate content |
| Topic clustering | All notes | Group by semantic similarity |
| Context loading | Task-relevant notes | "Find notes related to X" |

| Metric | Value |

| **Cost** | Free (local Ollama) |
| **Deployment** | Local — Ollama on `localhost:11434` |
| **GPU required** | No (faster with GPU) |
| **Disk footprint** | ~274MB |

- 768 dimensions is smaller than OpenAI ada-002 (1536) — slightly lower fidelity
- English-focused training data — may underperform on multilingual content
- 8K token limit — long documents need chunking
- MTEB scores below commercial embedding APIs (OpenAI, Cohere)
